    • Where it's used: bound at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:169-172; injected as IOptions<RefreshSessionSettings> into AuthSessionIssuer (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:57, read for the reuse grace at :601, the lost-response recovery window at :624 and the cap at :707), into EFRefreshSessionStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:38, which routes by DataSourceName at :357), and into RefreshSessionCleanupService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/RefreshSessionCleanupService.cs:51, snapshotted at :55). The design-time context helper supplies an instance so dotnet ef can build a model that includes the table (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/DbContexts/Design/DesignTimeDbContextHelper.cs:174-175). The app Identity services do not take it: the issuer owns it, so ADC's AuthenticationService has no reference to it.

    UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry.cs:20 · Level 1 · class (internal sealed partial)

    • What it is: the fallback IPermissionRegistry (and, since it also implements IPermissionCatalog, the fallback catalog) for a host that wired the CQRS pipeline without declaring any role-to-permission grants. It grants nothing, so a permission-gated command or query is denied rather than allowed, and it logs one warning naming the call that would fix it (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/UnconfiguredPermissionRegistry.cs:6-11).
    • Depends on: IPermissionRegistry and IPermissionCatalog (:20), IRequiresPermission by reference in the doc comment (:9), and Microsoft.Extensions.Logging for the source-generated log message (:1).
    • Concept introduced: failing closed, and only where it costs nothing. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the direction a misconfiguration fails in: a registry that answered "no permission model, therefore allow" would silently open every gated request, so this one denies, and now that it doubles as the fallback IPermissionCatalog it renders an empty catalog rather than throwing, so a role-administration screen on an unconfigured host reads as "this host grants nothing yet" instead of failing (:225-228). [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] assesses whether an operator can tell why: the log message spells out the remedy verbatim (:264-267, naming AddAuthorizationPolicies() / AddPermissions(...) and the required ordering before AddApplicationDecorators()). The second half of the doc comment (:12-17) is the more interesting teaching point and is an availability story rather than a security one: the two authorization decorators are registered unconditionally and take an IPermissionRegistry constructor dependency, so without any registration the whole pipeline fails to activate and a small app with no Identity module answers 500 on every read, not only the gated ones. This type turns a total activation failure into a correct, noisy denial on the subset of requests that actually declare a permission.
    • Walkthrough: two fields, two catalog properties, and three methods.
      • private static readonly HashSet<string> None = [] (:221) is the single empty grant set every permission call returns, and private int _warned (:223) is the one-time-warning latch.
      • IReadOnlyList<string> Roles => [] (:229) and IReadOnlyList<string> Permissions => [] (:232) are the IPermissionCatalog members: both always empty, so an unconfigured host's role editor renders no roles and no permissions to pick from rather than erroring.
      • GetPermissions(string role) (:235-239) warns then returns None.
      • HasPermission(IEnumerable<string> roles, string permission) (:242-249) argument-guards both parameters (:244-245) before warning and returning false, so a caller bug still surfaces as an ArgumentException rather than being swallowed by the stub.
      • WarnOnce() (:256-262) uses Interlocked.Exchange(ref _warned, 1) == 0 (:258) so concurrent requests produce exactly one log line. The comment (:251-255) explains why the warning is deferred to the first permission check instead of emitted at startup: a host with no permission-gated request is correctly configured and simply never needs a registry, so warning at boot would cry wolf. Reading the catalog properties never triggers the warning, only GetPermissions/HasPermission do.
      • LogNoPermissionsConfigured (:264-267) is a [LoggerMessage] source-generated Warning, which is why the class is partial.
    • Why it's built this way: it is registered with TryAddSingleton from inside AddApplicationDecorators() (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:141), and the surrounding comment (:119-123) states both halves of the rule: TryAdd so a host that already declared its grants (via AddAuthorizationPolicies() or AddPermissions(...), both of which run before this call) keeps its own registry and never constructs this type, and here rather than in AddApplication() so the registration lands exactly where the decorators that need it are wired. Adding IPermissionCatalog to the same fallback type, rather than a second stub class, means the one TryAddSingleton call keeps both ports covered from the same no-op instance.
    • Where it's used: reached through the IPermissionRegistry dependency of the authorization command and query decorators in the CQRS pipeline (see group 05), and through the IPermissionCatalog dependency of IRoleAdministrationService's GetCatalogAsync on a host that never configured a registry.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: internal, so it is not part of the framework's public API and cannot be referenced or asserted against from a consumer's code.

    ILoginProtectionService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ILoginProtectionService.cs:10 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the application-layer contract for brute-force and rate-limit protection on authentication endpoints: lockout checks, failed-attempt increments, successful-login resets, and registration rate-limiting per IP address.

    • Depends on: Result from MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ILoginProtectionService.cs:1).

    • Concept introduced: rate limiting as a first-class application concern. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses brute-force protection on auth flows, and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether such a policy is extracted to a port so the application layer can reason about it without coupling to a specific store (the doc comment at :7-8 names both a distributed and an in-memory cache as valid backers). Returning Result from CheckLockoutAsync (:18) and CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync (:42) makes "account is locked out" a normal control-flow branch rather than a thrown exception.

    • Walkthrough: five async methods in two scopes.

      • Email-scoped (failed-login lockout): CheckLockoutAsync (:18) returns a failure result when the email is currently locked; IncrementFailedAttemptsAsync (:26) records a failure and, per the doc comment (:20-22), applies exponential-backoff lockout once the maximum is exceeded; ResetFailedAttemptsAsync (:33) clears the counter after a successful login.
      • IP-scoped (registration flood): CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync (:42) and IncrementRegistrationCountAsync (:49) throttle account creation per client IP. Both accept a nullable ipAddress and skip the check when it is null, so a host that cannot resolve the caller IP degrades to no limit rather than blocking everyone; CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync returns Result.Success() in that case (doc comment, :36-37).

      All five take a CancellationToken with a default argument, per convention.

    • Why it's built this way: keeping the protection policy behind an interface lets the shared authentication workflow compose it in while the concrete cache mechanics stay in the implementation; the null-IP skip keeps the limiter from becoming an availability hazard (ADR-029).

    • Where it's used: injected into AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> (constructor parameter at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:77), which calls all five across its login and registration flows: CheckLockoutAsync (:131), IncrementFailedAttemptsAsync on both the unknown-email and wrong-password branches (:146, :161), ResetFailedAttemptsAsync on success (:178), CheckRegistrationRateLimitAsync (:197) and IncrementRegistrationCountAsync (:256). The concrete, cache-backed LoginProtectionService (tuned by LoginProtectionSettings, bound at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:155-158) implements it, and the framework registers that pairing at :135.

    IPasswordResetTokenService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IPasswordResetTokenService.cs:10 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the two-method port behind the forgot-password workflow: issue a single-use reset token for an email address, and validate-then-consume a token presented back by the user. Implementations keep the token material outside the database, hashed at rest, and enforce both the per-email request throttle and the per-token validation-attempt cap (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IPasswordResetTokenService.cs:5-9).

    • Depends on: Result and its generic form from MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions (:1), plus the UserIdentifierType alias. Its Infrastructure adapter is PasswordResetTokenService, backed by ICacheService and tuned by PasswordResetSettings.

    • Concept introduced: a single-use credential without a schema change. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how a secondary credential is minted, stored, and retired; [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses whether short-lived state earns a place in the durable store. A reset token is not durable data: it is valid for minutes and must stop working the instant it is redeemed. Putting it in columns on the user row costs a migration in every consumer and needs a sweeper to reap expired rows, because expiry is not something a table enforces; a self-contained signed payload needs no store but then cannot be single-use, since a signed token that has not expired stays valid however many times it is presented. This port takes the third path and hides the choice: the handlers see two Result-returning methods, and the cache substrate is entirely the implementation's business (ADR-091).

      The second teaching point is in the return shapes. ValidateAndConsumeAsync is documented to collapse unknown, expired, mismatched, and attempt-capped into one generic failure (:32-35), so the redeem endpoint cannot be used to distinguish a wrong token from an expired one from an address that was never issued a token. The issue path is throttled rather than refused loudly, for the same anti-enumeration reason the forgot-password handler answers success to every input.

    • Walkthrough: two members.

      • Task<Result<string>> IssueAsync(string email, UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (:23) returns the raw token to email, or a failure when the per-email request throttle has been exceeded. The doc comment (:12-15) states the replace semantics: issuing overwrites any token already outstanding for that address, so requesting a new link immediately stops the older one from working. The userId parameter is what the token resolves back to at redeem time, which is why the redeem call never has to trust an identifier supplied by the caller.
      • Task<Result<UserIdentifierType>> ValidateAndConsumeAsync(string email, string token, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (:36) validates the presented token against the outstanding record and consumes it on success, so a token never redeems twice (:25-28), returning the account the token belongs to.

    • Why it's built this way: taking email on both methods, rather than treating the token as self-describing, is what lets the implementation key its records by address and enforce the per-address throttle and the one-active-token rule at the same key. Returning Result<UserIdentifierType> rather than a boolean means the redeem handler gets the account identity from the token store itself. See PasswordResetTokenService for the mechanics the port hides: a 32-byte random token (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/PasswordResetTokenService.cs:39), only its digest stored, an attempt counter, and an address normalized through Email before it becomes a cache key (:34-45) so User@x.com and user@x.com cannot hold independent tokens for one account.

    • Where it's used: injected into the shared ForgotPasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (constructor parameter at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ForgotPassword/ForgotPasswordHandlerBase.cs:39, called at :72, where a throttled issue is logged and still answered as success) and into ResetPasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ResetPassword/ResetPasswordHandlerBase.cs:45, redeemed at :61-62). Both apps' sealed subclasses take the same dependency, for example ADC's ForgotPasswordHandler and ResetPasswordHandler. The framework registers the concrete as scoped at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:165.

    AuthSignInMetrics

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1099 · Level 3 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the OpenTelemetry instrument for password sign-in outcomes: one MMCA.Common.Auth meter carrying one counter, mmca.auth.signin, tagged by a low-cardinality outcome. It is declared in the same file as AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>, after the log companion (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1092-1099).
    • Depends on: System.Diagnostics.Metrics for Meter and Counter<long> (BCL, AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:2), Error and TwoFactorErrors (its TwoFactorRequiredCode) for classifying a second-factor failure. Nothing else.
    • Concept introduced: an outcome tag, never an identity, on a security metric. [Rubric §13, Observability] assesses whether the system exposes the signals an operator needs, and [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether telemetry leaks personal data. The doc comment (:1092-1098) sets the rule in one line: tags carry only the low-cardinality outcome, never an address, a user id or a client IP. Seven fixed values keep the series count bounded however many accounts exist, and a rise in invalid_credentials or locked_out is visible without the metric pipeline ever holding who was attempted. The same comment records a packaging consequence: a host exports the meter by registering its name, the Aspire service defaults already do, and the name is duplicated there as a literal because MMCA.Common.Aspire has no reference to Application (:1093-1096).
    • Walkthrough: eleven internal members.
      • MeterName = "MMCA.Common.Auth" (:1102).
      • Seven outcome constants (:1105-1123): Success ("success", a token pair was issued), InvalidCredentials ("invalid_credentials": unknown address, wrong password, no password credential, or a request that failed validation), LockedOut ("locked_out"), SecondFactorRequired ("second_factor_required": the password verified and no code was supplied), SecondFactorFailed ("second_factor_failed"), EmailNotConfirmed ("email_not_confirmed") and Rejected ("rejected": the app gate or the issuance refused the account).
      • A private Meter built from MeterName (:1125) and the SignIns counter (:1128), created as mmca.auth.signin with unit {attempt}, one count per LoginAsync call.
      • ForSecondFactorFailure(IEnumerable<Error> errors) (:1140-1141) maps a failed challenge to second_factor_required when any error carries TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorRequiredCode (no code supplied) and to second_factor_failed for anything else, a wrong code, a replay, or a redemption that could not be persisted.
      • Record(string outcome) (:1145-1146) adds 1 to the counter with the single outcome tag.
    • Why it's built this way: a static class with a static meter matches how .NET metrics are meant to be created (one instrument per process, recorded from anywhere), and keeping it internal beside the workflow means the outcome vocabulary changes in the same file as the branches that emit it. Counting a validation failure as invalid_credentials rather than adding an eighth value keeps the tag set small and matches what the caller is told.
    • Where it's used: only by AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>'s LoginAsync, which records Success once the tokens are issued (AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:293) and routes every failure through the private SignInFailed helper (:976-984), which calls Record (:981) and then writes the matching Warning through AuthenticationServiceLog. The second-factor branch picks its tag through ForSecondFactorFailure (:253). No usage outside the defining file; the background is ADR-041.

    AuthenticationServiceLog

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1051 · Level 5 · class (internal static partial)

    • What it is: the source-generated log-message companion of AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>, declared in the same file after the base closes. It carries two messages, PasswordRehashRejected and SignInFailed, and the EmailLogHash helper that makes an address safe to put in the second (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1051-1090).
    • Depends on: Microsoft.Extensions.Logging for ILogger, LogLevel and the [LoggerMessage] generator (AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:6), System.Security.Cryptography and System.Text for the SHA-256 digest (:4-5), the Email value object for normalizing the address, and the solution-wide UserIdentifierType alias for the user-id parameter (:1059).
    • Concept: a non-generic log companion beside a generic base, and an address that never reaches a log. [Rubric §13, Observability] assesses structured, allocation-free logging with stable message templates, and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] covers keeping a public type's shape free of incidental requirements. The [LoggerMessage] source generator needs a partial method on a partial type. Putting it on the public abstract base would force that base to be partial and make the generated method generic over TUser; the doc comment (:1047-1050) names the alternative taken: "a separate non-generic companion so the public base does not have to be partial". The class is internal, so it is not part of the framework's public surface. [Rubric §11, Security] applies to the sign-in line: a failed sign-in is logged with a 12-hex-character (48-bit) prefix of the SHA-256 of the normalized address, never the address, and the comment (:1065-1071) gives both halves of the reasoning: it is the same digest the login-protection counters key on, so the two log streams correlate, and a 48-bit prefix matches too many addresses to name one.
    • Walkthrough: three members and one private constant.
      • EmailLogHashLength = 12 (:1054), private, the number of hex characters a log line carries.
      • PasswordRehashRejected(ILogger logger, UserIdentifierType userId, string errorCodes) (:1059) logs at LogLevel.Warning (:1057) with the template "Password rehash for user {UserId} was refused by the aggregate ({ErrorCodes}); the sign-in is unaffected and the stored hash is unchanged" (:1058). The template states the consequence for an operator reading it: the sign-in already succeeded and nothing was written.
      • SignInFailed(ILogger logger, string outcome, string emailHash) (:1062-1063) logs at Warning with "Password sign-in failed ({Outcome}) for address hash {EmailHash}", where Outcome is one of the AuthSignInMetrics tag values.
      • EmailLogHash(string? email) (:1074-1089) normalizes a blank address to the empty string (:1077-1080), otherwise takes Email.Create(email)'s normalized value and falls back to Trim().ToLowerInvariant() for a malformed address (:1084, under a scoped CA1308 suppression that names the RFC 5321 lowercase rule it matches, :1083), and returns the first 12 uppercase hex characters of the SHA-256 digest (:1088).
    • Why it's built this way: a refused rehash is a domain answer (the aggregate's RehashPassword returned a failure), not an exception, so it never reaches the best-effort wrapper's own failure log and metric; that message is what makes the branch visible. Logging the error codes joined with ", " rather than the error messages keeps the line free of any user-facing text. A failed sign-in needs a per-address handle for an investigation (the same address failing repeatedly) without writing personal data, which is what the truncated digest gives. The background is ADR-133 (the stored hash carries its work factor and is upgraded on sign-in), ADR-096 (best-effort side effects never fail the primary operation) and ADR-041.
    • Where it's used: PasswordRehashRejected is called once, from the private RehashPasswordIfNeededAsync of AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> when IPasswordRehashableUser.RehashPassword fails (AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:1023-1030). SignInFailed and EmailLogHash are called together from the base's private SignInFailed helper (:982), which every failing branch of LoginAsync returns through. Both use the base's overridable Logger property as the sink, which defaults to NullLogger.Instance (:153), so the lines are emitted only by an app subclass that overrides Logger with an injected logger. No usage outside the defining file.

    SoftDeletedUserCache

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUserCache.cs:19 · Level 5 · class (static)

    • What it is: the shared cache contract for the soft-deleted user marker (BR-133), which now means "deleted or locked": the key shape, the marker lifetime, and the helpers that write and clear it. The API middleware reads the marker on every authenticated request and answers 401 while it is set; the module that soft-deletes a user, an administrator's lock (UserAdministrationServiceBase) and a machine-client revocation write it, and an unlock clears it (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUserCache.cs:6-12).

    • Depends on: ICacheService from MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces (:2), CrossServiceCacheKeys for the unqualified key prefix, the UserIdentifierType alias, and System.Globalization.CultureInfo (BCL, :1).

    • Concept introduced: revoking a stateless credential without a per-request lookup. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether a revoked principal actually loses access, and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether such a concern is factored so both ends share one definition. A JWT is a bearer credential: signature validation never asks "is this account still active?", so soft-deleting or locking a user leaves an already-issued access token passing validation until it expires (ADR-047). The textbook fixes (a deny-list, or an account-status query on every request) reintroduce exactly the per-request state that stateless JWT was chosen to avoid. This type is the middle path: a short-lived cache marker written at deletion or lock time and read cheaply on the hot path.

      The remarks (:13-18) explain why the constants live in the Application layer rather than next to the middleware that reads them: a downstream application deleting an account has to write the exact same key the middleware reads, and a private constant in the presentation layer is unreachable from an application-layer command handler. Same reasoning as IdempotencyHeaders, applied one layer up.

    • Walkthrough: six static members, no state.

      • A private DefaultClockSkew of 5 minutes (:22), the JWT bearer library's default, which the framework never overrides.
      • MarkerDuration => TimeSpan.FromMinutes(20) (:41). The remarks (:27-40) justify the number rather than leaving it magic: the marker must outlive every access token issued before the delete or lock. A host that does not run Identity registers no validator query, and the Identity host's query checks deletion only, so the marker is the only thing that rejects a deleted user's token on the first and a locked user's on any host. A token is accepted until its expiry plus the bearer clock skew, so the marker lasts the default 15-minute access-token lifetime (the BR-205 default on ITokenService) plus the 5-minute skew. It is a constant because the static helper cannot reach the JWT settings; a host with a longer lifetime or skew writes a longer marker through MarkerDurationFor. Only positive markers are written.
      • MarkerDurationFor(TimeSpan accessTokenLifetime, TimeSpan? clockSkew = null) (:51-55) returns the lifetime plus the skew (the 5-minute default when null), never less than MarkerDuration (:53-54).
      • KeyFor(UserIdentifierType userId) (:73-74) builds {CrossServiceCacheKeys.Prefix}user:deleted:{userId} through string.Create(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, ...). The remarks (:62-66) name the bug the invariant culture prevents: an identifier renders differently under some cultures (digit shapes, group separators), so a culture-sensitive key would be written under one request's culture and missed under another, silently letting a deleted user keep making requests. The second paragraph (:67-71) explains the prefix: the Identity service writes the marker and every other service's middleware reads it, so the key must not be qualified with each host's own namespace, or a service that does not host Identity would never see a lock.
      • MarkDeletedAsync(ICacheService cache, UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (:84-92) null-guards the cache (:89) and writes true under KeyFor(userId) for MarkerDuration (:91). It returns the task without awaiting, so there is no extra async state machine for a one-call passthrough.
      • MarkDeletedForAsync(cache, userId, TimeSpan duration, ...) (:103-112) is the same write with an explicit lifetime, for a host whose access tokens outlive MarkerDuration.
      • ClearMarkerAsync(cache, userId, ...) (:129-137) removes the marker through ICacheService.RemoveAsync (:136), so a token issued after an unlock is accepted at once. The remarks (:122-128) explain why that is enough on every replica: another replica may still hold a local copy, but the middleware never reads one, it reads the marker from the shared store.

    • Why it's built this way: publishing the key shape and the TTL as framework API is what keeps the writers and the reader honest, and it is a precondition for the module boundary in ADR-047: Identity owns the delete and the lock, every service hosts the middleware, and the only thing they share is a cache entry rather than a database. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness] applies directly: an extracted service can enforce the revocation without a reference to the Identity database.

    • Where it's used: read by SoftDeletedUserMiddleware, which builds the key (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:85) and, when it caches a deleted answer itself, sizes it with MarkerDurationFor(tokens.AccessTokenLifetime, ...) or falls back to MarkerDuration when no ITokenService is registered (:183-189). Written through SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter, the default ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter, which writes for MarkerDurationFor(tokenService.AccessTokenLifetime) and clears through ClearMarkerAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:17-25). The shared delete workflow calls that writer (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:214) and swallows any non-cancellation fault (:216) so a failed marker cannot turn a successful erasure into an error the caller would retry. MachineClientService writes the marker for a revoked client's service account with a lifetime computed from its own token lifetime (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:231-234).

    • Caveats / not-in-source: the marker is best effort on both ends by design. The middleware fails open on a cache fault (SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:98), and the writers log and continue. The exposure that leaves is bounded by the access-token lifetime, which is the trade-off ADR-047 accepts explicitly.

    AuthenticationValidators

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationValidators.cs:26 · Level 5 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: a tiny parameter object that bundles the three FluentValidation validators the authentication workflow needs (login, registration, refresh), the optional Terms of Service version registration requires, and, when the host registered one, the sign-in second-factor challenge, into one injectable dependency.
    • Depends on: FluentValidation's IValidator<T> (NuGet, :1) over the request DTOs LoginRequest, RegisterRequest, and RefreshTokenRequest (all in MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth), IOptions<LegalAcceptanceOptions> and LegalAcceptancePolicy from MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal for the terms check, and ITwoFactorAuthenticator for the optional challenge.
    • Concept introduced: the parameter object as a constructor-arity guardrail. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses whether a class stays a single, cohesive responsibility rather than sprawling into a god class, and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether cross-cutting dependencies are grouped so a class can grow without exploding its constructor. The doc comment (:6-11) states the exact motive: collapsing three closely-related dependencies into one keeps the app's AuthenticationService below the application-service constructor-arity ceiling (a god-class analyzer guardrail) without giving up per-request validation. Because the request DTOs already live in MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth, the bundle is app-agnostic, which is why it could be hoisted out of the apps into the framework. The same move is now used twice more: the terms options and the second-factor authenticator ride in here so adopting either feature adds no constructor argument to the app's subclass. The pressure is real rather than theoretical: ADC's subclass already carries a long primary constructor (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs:52-70, the bundle at :57).
    • Walkthrough: two constructors and five get-only members.
      • The primary constructor (:26-30) takes the three IValidator<T> instances plus an optional IOptions<LegalAcceptanceOptions>? legalAcceptance = null.
      • A second public constructor (:45-51) takes the same four arguments, legalAcceptance without a default, plus a required ITwoFactorAuthenticator twoFactor, chains to the primary and sets TwoFactor. Its doc comment (:32-44) gives the selection rule: the container picks it only when an ITwoFactorAuthenticator is registered (by AddTwoFactorAuthentication(configuration)), so a host that has not adopted two-factor resolves the primary constructor and is unchanged. The class-level RS0027 suppression (:25) records why the shipped constructor keeps its optional parameter: removing the default would break every three-argument call, and the longer overload has no optional parameter, so positional calls bind unambiguously.
      • Login (:54), Register (:57) and Refresh (:60) surface the validators by name.
      • CurrentTermsVersion (:66) returns LegalAcceptancePolicy.ResolveCurrentVersion(legalAcceptance?.Value): the Terms of Service version registration requires, or null when acceptance is not configured.
      • TwoFactor (:73) is the sign-in challenge, or null when the host registered none. Its doc comment (:68-72) fixes precedence: AuthenticationServiceBase uses it only when its own twoFactor constructor argument is null, so an explicit argument wins. Beyond the one resolver call the type has no logic.
    • Why it's built this way: a sealed grouping type with get-only properties is the cheapest way to fold cohesive dependencies into one constructor slot, so the workflow base can validate each request shape, and challenge a second factor, without pushing its constructor or the app's over the arity limit; DI resolves the underlying services and composes them into this one object, choosing the constructor by what is registered. Two of the three validators (LoginRequestValidator, RefreshTokenRequestValidator) come from the framework assembly, while IValidator<RegisterRequest> is satisfied by the app's own RegisterRequestValidator, so the bundle is the point where framework and app validation meet.
    • Where it's used: injected into AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> (constructor parameter at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:78), whose LoginAsync, RegisterAsync, and RefreshTokenAsync call validators.Login (:170), validators.Register (:307), and validators.Refresh (:407) respectively before doing any work, which re-exposes CurrentTermsVersion as a protected property (:141) that RegisterAsync tests (:316), and whose ChallengeSecondFactorAsync resolves twoFactor ?? validators.TwoFactor (:862). It is registered by each app's Identity module rather than by the framework, since one of its dependencies is app-owned: MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:42 and MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:46, both TryAddScoped<AuthenticationValidators>(). AddTwoFactorAuthentication registers the authenticator the longer constructor picks up (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:63, with the by-type registration precondition stated at :38-40), and the terms options are bound by the opt-in AddLegalAcceptance(configuration) (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:140-146).

    IAuthenticationService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IAuthenticationService.cs:12 · Level 5 · interface

    • What it is: the application-layer contract for the Identity module's authentication workflows: login, registration, token refresh, per-device and global session revocation, session and sign-in history listing, external (OAuth) login, and the two credential-proved sign-ins (a redeemed sign-in link and a verified passkey).

    • Depends on: LoginRequest, RefreshTokenRequest, RegisterRequest, AuthenticationResponse, RegistrationOutcome, RefreshSessionSummaryResponse, SignInSummaryResponse, SignInLinkErrors and PasskeyErrors (the defaults' failures), Result, Error, and the UserIdentifierType alias.

    • Concept introduced: default interface methods for optional capabilities. [Rubric §1, SOLID] (interface segregation and dependency inversion): four members ship a default implementation in the interface itself, so an implementation that has not adopted a capability inherits a safe answer and need not override anything. ExternalLoginAsync (:150-158) returns a not-supported Error ("Auth.ExternalLoginNotSupported", :158) (ADR-036); SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync (:174-180) and SignInWithPasskeyAsync (:197-203) reject through SignInLinkErrors.NotSupported and PasskeyErrors.NotSupported, so an implementation that has not adopted sign-in links (ADR-116) or passkeys (ADR-139) keeps compiling and never opens a session through that path; and HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync (:217-220) answers false, which the remarks (:213-216) justify as the recoverable direction: refusing to delete the last passkey can be undone, a locked-out account cannot. [Rubric §11, Security]: every sign-in member returns Result<AuthenticationResponse>, so auth outcomes flow as values and no exception leaks credential detail to the caller.

      The second concept the signatures teach is that a session is a device, not a user. LoginAsync, RegisterAsync and RefreshTokenAsync all take optional ipAddress and userAgent (:25-26, :41-42, :56-57) recorded on the session row, and the doc comments state the invariant each time: signing in opens a session for the calling device and leaves the user's other devices signed in (:15-16), and refreshing rotates the presenting device's session only (:46-47).

    • Walkthrough: twelve methods, all async, all ending in a CancellationToken.

      • LoginAsync(LoginRequest, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...) returns Result<AuthenticationResponse> (:23-27).
      • RegisterAsync(RegisterRequest, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...) (:39-43); the ipAddress does double duty, feeding ILoginProtectionService's registration rate limit and the new session row (:35). The summary (:30-32) adds one outcome to the contract: when the host requires a confirmed address and the new account is unconfirmed, the result is a success carrying RegistrationOutcome.ConfirmationPending and no session is opened.
      • RefreshTokenAsync(RefreshTokenRequest, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...) (:54-58) exchanges an expired access token plus a valid refresh token for a rotated pair, recording the caller's IP and user agent on the rotated session.
      • RevokeTokenAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, string? refreshToken = null, ...) (:69-72) signs one device out. The documented fallback is the interesting part (:61-63): passing no token, or one that does not belong to this user, revokes every session the user holds, which the comment calls the safe reading of "log me out" from a caller that cannot produce its refresh token.
      • RevokeAllSessionsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...) (:81-83) signs every device out: a password change, an admin lockout, or an explicit "sign out everywhere".
      • GetSessionsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, Guid? currentSessionId = null, ...) (:98-101) lists live sessions newest first with the caller's own device marked. currentSessionId is the caller token's sid claim and is used only to set RefreshSessionSummaryResponse.IsCurrent; passing null marks no row (:91-94).
      • GetSignInsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, Guid? currentSessionId = null, ...) (:115-118) lists the user's sign-in history: one row per sign-in however often its refresh token rotated, ended sign-ins included with how they ended, newest first, capped at the newest 50, over what the session store retains (RefreshSessions:RetentionDays, 30 by default) (:104-106). currentSessionId sets SignInSummaryResponse.IsCurrent the same way.
      • RevokeSessionByIdAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, Guid sessionId, ...) (:134-137) revokes one named device. The remarks (:124-128) fix two behaviors as contract: an unknown id and another account's id both return NotFound and are indistinguishable, so a caller cannot probe for another user's sessions; and revoking an already-revoked session changes nothing and also returns NotFound with the code Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked (:126-128), so a device list can tell the user the device was already signed out instead of claiming this request signed it out.
      • ExternalLoginAsync(loginProvider, providerKey, email, firstName, lastName, ...) (:150-158), the default-implemented OAuth path.
      • SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, string? ipAddress = null, string? userAgent = null, ...) (:174-180) opens a session for an account whose owner has just redeemed a single-use sign-in link; the caller has already spent the token, and this member applies the same account gates a password sign-in does and mints the pair (:161-163).
      • SignInWithPasskeyAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...) (:197-203) does the same after a verified passkey assertion, and the resulting access token carries mfa=passkey (:183-186).
      • HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...) (:217-220) asks whether the account still has a password or an external login, before its last passkey is deleted (:206-208).

      The doc comment (:6-9) also records a scope decision: password change is not on this interface. It is dispatched directly through its own command handler at the controller layer.

    • Why it's built this way: concentrating the token-issuing and session-management workflows behind one port keeps the Identity controllers thin and lets the protection and rate-limit policy (ILoginProtectionService) compose in; the defaulted members keep the contract stable across hosts that do and do not enable social login, sign-in links or passkeys, and route every credential-proved sign-in through the same account gates and issuance. Encoding the anti-probing and idempotent-revoke rules in remarks rather than leaving them to an implementation makes them testable expectations of every implementer.

    • Where it's used: implemented by AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> (which realises every member except the default ExternalLoginAsync) and, through it, by each app's sealed AuthenticationService; consumed by the API controller bases (AuthControllerBase, OAuthControllerBase, TwoFactorControllerBase), by RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase for the sign-in link redemption, and by the passkey sign-in flow.

    RefreshSessionSignIn

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionSignIn.cs:19 · Level 5 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: one sign-in as the session store aggregates it: its identifier, the instant its earliest retained session was issued, and its newest session (the head), which carries the last activity, the device and how the sign-in ended (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionSignIn.cs:5-9).
    • Depends on: RefreshSession from MMCA.Common.Domain.Auth (:1). Nothing else.
    • Concept introduced: a sign-in is a rotation chain, not a row. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses whether read shapes match what the data means, and [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether a read stays bounded as data grows. Every refresh rotates a session into a new row, so a user who stayed signed in for a month owns hundreds of rows for one sign-in. This record is the unit a sign-in history needs: one entry per chain, its start, and only its newest row. SignInId is the chain's shared RefreshSession.SignInId, or, for a row written before that column existed, the row's own Id (:10-13), so older data still lists. Head is read-only: a store may return it untracked, so a mutation on it is never persisted (:15-18).
    • Walkthrough: a positional sealed record with three members (:19): Guid SignInId, DateTime StartedAt (the UTC issue instant of the earliest retained session, :14) and RefreshSession Head. Value equality and immutability come from the record; there is no behavior.
    • Why it's built this way: aggregating in the store, and handing back this small projection, is what lets IRefreshSessionStore's GetRecentSignInsAsync bound its read by the number of sign-ins requested rather than by the user's total row count, so a sign-in that rotated a thousand times costs one entry. Carrying the whole head rather than a flattened DTO leaves the response shaping (device, end reason, current marker) to the application layer.
    • Where it's used: returned by IRefreshSessionStore.GetRecentSignInsAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IRefreshSessionStore.cs:80-83); produced by EFRefreshSessionStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:96) and by the test double InMemoryRefreshSessionStore; consumed by SignInHistory (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:45), which sits behind the issuer's ListSignInsAsync that AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>'s GetSignInsAsync calls. Background: ADR-097.

    IRefreshSessionStore

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IRefreshSessionStore.cs:21 · Level 6 · interface

    • What it is: persistence for RefreshSession rows, one hashed refresh session per signed-in device (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IRefreshSessionStore.cs:5-6). Sessions are added, looked up by token hash or by id, listed per user (live, unrevoked, all, or aggregated into sign-ins), counted per user, rotated, and saved.

    • Depends on: RefreshSession from MMCA.Common.Domain.Auth (:1), RefreshSessionSignIn for the sign-in aggregate, and the UserIdentifierType alias. The shipped implementation is EFRefreshSessionStore; the test double is InMemoryRefreshSessionStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryRefreshSessionStore.cs:27).

    • Concept introduced: a repository whose contract is deliberately missing an Update. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses interface segregation, and [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses whether the persistence contract expresses the aggregate's rules. The doc comment (:8-14) explains the shape: sessions are mutated only through RefreshSession.Revoke on instances this store returned, so an implementation that tracks its entities persists a revocation with no update method at all, and TryRotateAsync is the one exception because rotation is a claim, not a mutation. The requirement that makes that safe is stated as a contract obligation, not left implicit: implementations must return tracked instances from every lookup except FindByIdUntrackedAsync, which is untracked by design and for reading only, because a no-tracking read anywhere else would accept revocations and rotations and drop them silently at save time (:15-19). This is the same trap called out for composed EF queries elsewhere in the framework, promoted here to interface documentation.

      The second concept is lookup by hash, never by token (:8, :37). The store never sees plaintext: callers hash first with RefreshSession.HashToken and search on the digest, which is what lets the table hold only digests. [Rubric §11, Security] applies directly.

    • Walkthrough: eleven members.

      • AddAsync(RefreshSession session, ...) (:26) stages an insert.
      • FindByTokenHashAsync(string tokenHash, ...) (:37) finds by digest including revoked and expired rows, and the comment (:29-32) marks that as load-bearing: a rotated token that comes back is found on its revoked row, which is the BR-206 reuse signal, so a store that filtered revoked rows out would report a replay as "unknown token" and never revoke the family.
      • GetUnrevokedByUserAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...) (:45-47) returns the user's un-revoked sessions oldest first, expired ones included since they still occupy a row, which is what makes both family revocation and cap eviction deterministic (:40-41).
      • GetAllByUserAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, ...) (:59-61) returns every session row the user holds, revoked and expired included, oldest first, as tracked instances. Account erasure needs the whole set: a revoked row still carries the IP address and user agent captured at issue time, so anonymizing only the un-revoked rows would leave the rest behind (:50-54).
      • GetRecentSignInsAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, int maxSignIns, ...) (:80-83) returns the user's newest maxSignIns sign-ins as RefreshSessionSignIn entries, newest first by StartedAt, aggregated in the store: one entry per RefreshSession.SignInId with its earliest issue instant and only its newest row (:64-68). A row with no SignInId (written before the column existed) is its own sign-in unless it was rotated away, in which case its successor stands for it (:68-69). Two obligations follow (:71-73): the returned heads are for reading only (the shipped EF store reads them untracked), and an implementation must bound what it reads by maxSignIns, never by the user's total row count.
      • GetUserIdsWithLiveSessionsAsync(DateTime now, ...) (:93-95) returns each user holding at least one live session at now exactly once, where live means not revoked and ExpiresAt strictly after now (RefreshSession.IsActiveAt), evaluated as one query in the store (:86-88).
      • CountLiveSessionsByUserAsync(IReadOnlyCollection<UserIdentifierType> userIds, DateTime now, ...) (:106-109) counts live sessions for many users in one grouped query, never one per user; a requested user with no live session is absent from the result and duplicates count once (:98-102). The EF store implements the two live-session reads at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:221 and :236.
      • FindByIdAsync(Guid id, UserIdentifierType userId, ...) (:121-124) takes the owner as part of the query rather than as a check the caller performs afterwards. The comment (:112-115) gives the reason: a session id is a value a client hands back, so scoping the query to the owner is what makes another account's id indistinguishable from a nonexistent one. That is an authorization decision encoded in a signature.
      • FindByIdUntrackedAsync(Guid id, ...) (:141-142) re-reads a session as the database holds it now, bypassing any tracked copy, revoked and expired rows included (:127-136). The rotation loser needs it: its tracked instance was read before the winner's conditional update and still shows the row live, so only a fresh read can say when and why the row was revoked. The instance is for reading only, so a mutation on it is never persisted. The default returns null, which the caller treats as "cannot tell" and answers with the conservative BR-206 family revocation; the shipped EF store overrides it with a no-tracking query (EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:277).
      • SaveChangesAsync(...) (:147) persists staged inserts and revocations.
      • TryRotateAsync(RefreshSession presented, RefreshSession successor, DateTime revokedAt, ...) (:177) is the one exception to the no-update rule, and it ships a default interface implementation. It argument-guards both sessions (:183-184), revokes the presented session as RefreshSession.ReasonRotated linked to the successor's hash (:186), then stages and saves the successor (:191-192). The bool return is the whole point (:154-160): two requests presenting the same still-live token both read an un-revoked row, so a check-then-act rotation would mint two successors from one token and the presented row could never fire reuse detection again. Returning false tells the caller it lost the claim. The caller then re-reads the row through FindByIdUntrackedAsync to tell a sibling rotation inside the reuse grace (a 409 with nothing revoked) or a sign-out or cap eviction (that request fails alone) from a genuine replay (the family is revoked). The default body is atomic only per instance, which is all an in-memory or test store can offer; the shipped EF store replaces it with a conditional ExecuteUpdateAsync the database arbitrates (EFRefreshSessionStore.cs:304, the update at :322).

    • Why it's built this way: hashed-at-rest, per-device session rows are what turn refresh-token rotation into something a user can inspect and revoke per device, and what let reuse detection revoke a whole family (ADR-050, BR-205/206). Keeping the contract in Application means the workflow that uses it is independent of EF, so an extracted Identity service can bring its own store. Making rotation a claim rather than a mutation is the difference between a race that mints two live tokens and a race one side of which is answered as a replay. Pushing the sign-in aggregation into the store keeps a history page's cost proportional to the page, not to how often the user's tokens rotated.

    • Where it's used: registered as scoped against the EF implementation at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:173, scoped, like the unit of work it shares a DbContext with, so a login and its session insert commit together. Consumed by AuthSessionIssuer, not by AuthenticationServiceBase (injected at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:56) for the owner-scoped lookups behind targeted revocation (:298, :338), the unrevoked-session reads behind sign-out and family revocation (:242, :683), cap eviction (:708), the insert of a new session (:491) and the successor lookup of a lost-response recovery (:634). The sign-in aggregate is read by SignInHistory (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:45), the all-sessions read behind account erasure by RefreshSessionRevocation (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionRevocation.cs:81), and the live-session reads by UserSessionsAdministrationService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:80, :99).

    RefreshSessionRevocation

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/RefreshSessionRevocation.cs:21 · Level 6 · class (public static)

    • What it is: a shared static helper with two steps. RevokeAllAsync (public) revokes every un-revoked refresh session a user holds; RevokeAndAnonymizeAllAsync (internal) is the account-erasure step. Used wherever a credential-rotation path needs to make sure a stale token cannot keep authenticating after the event that should have invalidated it.

    • Depends on: IRefreshSessionStore (nullable: a host that never registered one, because refresh sessions are opt-in, is a no-op), RefreshSession (.Revoke, RefreshSession.ReasonSignedOut), and the BCL TimeProvider.

    • Concept introduced: a credential-rotation event is a call site, not a feature flag. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether changing a credential actually invalidates the sessions issued under the old one. Because refresh sessions are opt-in (RefreshSessionSettings.Enabled), a change-password or reset-password handler cannot assume a store exists; the doc comment states this directly (:23-26), and refreshSessions is null (:37-40) is checked first so the call degrades to a no-op rather than throwing, meaning the same handler code runs unchanged on a host that never enabled the feature.

    • Walkthrough: one static method, RevokeAllAsync(IRefreshSessionStore? refreshSessions, TimeProvider? timeProvider, UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken) (:31-35). It returns immediately on a null store (:37-40) or an empty session list (:44-47), otherwise stamps now from the supplied timeProvider or TimeProvider.System (:42), calls session.Revoke(now, RefreshSession.ReasonSignedOut) on every un-revoked session in a loop (:49-52), and saves once (:54).

      RevokeAndAnonymizeAllAsync (:69-90) is the erasure variant. It reads every session through IRefreshSessionStore.GetAllByUserAsync, revokes the un-revoked ones as RefreshSession.ReasonAccountDeleted, and calls Anonymize() on every row, revoked ones too, since each still carries the IP address and user agent captured at issue time (:57-64, :81-89). It saves nothing: the store returns tracked rows, so the caller's own unit-of-work save persists the changes together with the erasure. It is used by DeleteUserHandlerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:178).

    • Why it's built this way: a static class with no instance state keeps the helper a one-line call from any handler that needs it (RevokeAllAsync is public so an app-side IUserAdministrationService can run the same step after locking an account or changing its role instead of re-implementing it, class doc :16-19), and centralizing the null-store check here means every caller gets the same opt-in-safe behavior instead of re-deriving it.

    • Where it's used: the documented mechanism behind IUserAdministrationService<TUserDto>'s SetLockedAsync obligation (see that type); also ChangePasswordHandlerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ChangePassword/ChangePasswordHandlerBase.cs) and ResetPasswordHandlerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ResetPassword/ResetPasswordHandlerBase.cs).

    AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:74 · Level 8 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the shared authentication workflow (password login, registration, refresh-token rotation, per-device and global revocation, session and sign-in history listing, and the sign-in-link and passkey sign-ins) hoisted once into the framework, generic over the app's User aggregate. It realises IAuthenticationService and leaves the genuinely app-specific decisions to a small set of abstract and virtual hooks a sealed subclass overrides (class doc comment, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:29-48).

    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork and IRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType> (persistence, G07), IPasswordHasher, ILoginProtectionService, AuthenticationValidators and IAuthSessionIssuer (the five required constructor parameters, :75-79), and two optional ones: an ITwoFactorAuthenticator? and IOptions<EmailConfirmationSettings>? (:80-81, both default null so a subclass that adopts neither passes nothing), the IAuthUser credential contract plus AuditableAggregateRootEntity<TIdentifierType> as the TUser constraint (:82) and, where a host adopts the matching feature, IEmailConfirmableUser (matched in CheckEmailConfirmed), IPasswordRehashableUser (matched in the sign-in rehash) and IUserPreferences (matched when seeding the registration culture), PasswordCredential (the stored-credential test), BestEffort, the companions AuthenticationServiceLog and AuthSignInMetrics, ILogger and NullLogger (:6-7), ITokenService (reached only through the issuer's TokenService property), TwoFactorOutcome, TwoFactorErrors and AuthClaimTypes (the mfa claim values), SignInLinkErrors and PasskeyErrors, RegistrationOutcome, Email (normalizing the login and register address), ClaimsPrincipalExtensions (principal.GetUserId(), principal.FindMultiFactorMethod() and principal.FindAuthTime()), Result and Error, and the request and response DTOs. The base itself takes no session store, no session settings, no clock and no logger (:74-81): the first three belong to the issuer, and the logger is an overridable property instead.

    • Concept introduced: the Template Method that de-duplicates a whole vertical slice. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses idiomatic pattern use: this is a textbook Template Method, the invariant sequence of an operation living in the base while the variable steps are deferred to subclass hooks, and the class doc comment lists the hooks with what each app supplies (:35-46). [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] (DRY across services) and [Rubric §1, SOLID] also apply: a fix to the lockout order or the rotation logic is written once for every app. [Rubric §11, Security]: the base encodes the security posture directly, validate first, an ILoginProtectionService lockout and rate-limit gate (ADR-029), an untracked-then-tracked dual fetch (ADR-004), an opt-in upgrade of an outdated password hash on sign-in (ADR-133), a refusal of every interactive sign-in for a machine client's service account (ADR-140), and, through IAuthSessionIssuer, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection (ADR-050, BR-205/206). [Rubric §13, Observability]: every password sign-in is counted by outcome and every failure logged without the address. [Rubric §7, Microservices Readiness]: the workflow depends only on ports, so it runs unchanged whether the Identity module is in-monolith or its own service.

      The division of labour is the other concept to absorb before reading the code (:49-54): this class decides who is signed in, and IAuthSessionIssuer decides what they are handed. Once a caller is proved, the multi-device refresh sessions (hashed at rest), BR-205 rotation with BR-206 reuse detection, the per-user session cap, and the sid and mfa claims on the minted access token are the issuer's job, so this workflow never touches a RefreshSession row. Every session-shaped member below is a single delegation to the issuer; the reuse, replay, expiry and cap rules are taught on AuthSessionIssuer.

    • Walkthrough (members in teaching order):

      • Constructor, arming fields and protected accessors (:74-153): a primary constructor takes the five required collaborators plus the two optional ones; when twoFactor is null the challenge falls back to AuthenticationValidators.TwoFactor, and an explicit argument wins (parameter doc, :62-68). A private constant PasswordRehashOperation = "password-rehash" (:85) is the best-effort operation name and metric tag for the sign-in rehash. Two private fields arm the minted token for one request: _multiFactorMethod (:97), the second-factor method that satisfied this request (a plain field because the service is scoped and one request issues one token pair, remarks :93-96), and _authenticatedAt (:105), the sign-in instant (auth_time) a presented token carried, armed only by RefreshTokenAsync so the rotated token keeps it unchanged; a sign-in leaves it null and the issuer stamps the instant of the session it opens (:99-104). Protected read-only properties re-expose UnitOfWork (:108), TokenService (:120), which returns sessionIssuer.TokenService, the issuer's stamping instance, so minting through it is what puts sid on the token (remarks, :112-118), and a Repository resolved lazily as unitOfWork.GetRepository<TUser, UserIdentifierType>() (:123-124). A protected CurrentTermsVersion (:141) forwards validators.CurrentTermsVersion, so adopting Terms of Service acceptance adds no constructor dependency here or in the app's subclass; when it is non-null, RegisterAsync has already refused a request whose AcceptedTerms is false before CreateUser runs, so a CreateUser override stamps that version on the new user (doc comment :126-140). A protected virtual ILogger Logger (:153) defaults to NullLogger.Instance; its doc comment (:143-152) says it is the sink for both the failed sign-in Warnings and the rehash line, that an app wanting them overrides it with its own injected logger, and that it is a virtual property rather than a constructor argument so the constructor stays within the framework's dependency ceiling. Token lifetimes and the session cap are not members of this class: they are configuration read by the issuer.

      • LoginAsync (:164-298): every call is counted once on the MMCA.Common.Auth meter by outcome, and every outcome but success writes one Warning carrying the outcome and a truncated hash of the normalized address (remarks, :156-163). Each failing branch returns through the private SignInFailed(outcome, request.Email, failure) helper (:976-984), which records the AuthSignInMetrics outcome and logs through AuthenticationServiceLog before handing the failure back unchanged. The sequence: validate the request (a failure counts as invalid_credentials, :170-177), check lockout (ADR-029 and BR-212, locked_out, :180-187), normalize the raw email into an Email value object (:191) so the EF predicate compares same-typed converted values (an invalid address yields a null value object that simply matches no user). Step 1 is an untracked fetch via the FindUntrackedByEmailAsync hook (:195) to verify credentials without change-tracker overhead. The gate is CanSignInWithPassword(untracked) (:201, private helper at :941-942): the account must exist, must not be a machine client's service account (ADR-140), and must carry stored password material (HasStoredCredential, :935, through PasswordCredential.IsStored); an external-OAuth account (ADR-036) carries none. All three refusals answer the identical generic 401 after the identical BurnPasswordVerificationCost(request.Password) call (:203) and IncrementFailedAttemptsAsync (:204), so none of them can be told apart, by status or by timing, from an unknown address (comment, :197-200). passwordHasher.VerifyPassword runs next (:212) and fails the same way on a wrong password. Only after the password check does the app gate (ValidateLoginCandidateAsync, :226, outcome rejected) run, deliberately: reaching it proves the caller owns the account, so its distinct status message (for example a deactivated-account rejection) is told to the account's owner rather than to anyone sweeping addresses, and running it first would make account state readable with no credential at all and skip the failed-attempt counter (comment, :222-225). Two more gates follow the same rule, for the same reason: CheckEmailConfirmed(untracked) (:239, outcome email_not_confirmed, hook at :832-842), off unless the host both supplied EmailConfirmationSettings.RequireConfirmedEmail and the app's User implements IEmailConfirmableUser, and ChallengeSecondFactorCountingFailuresAsync(untracked.Id, request, cancellationToken) (:248-249, private helper at :876-889, outcome chosen by AuthSignInMetrics.ForSecondFactorFailure). That helper runs the overridable ChallengeSecondFactorAsync hook (:858-864) and counts a TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalidCode failure against the account through IncrementFailedAttemptsAsync exactly like a wrong password (:883-886), so the lockout at the top of the method throttles code guessing per account; a missing code is the ordinary first leg of the challenge and is not counted (:866-871). Step 2 is a tracked re-fetch by id (:262), purely about the instance the app's CreateAccessToken hook mints from, and the second lookup turns a race that deleted the account between the two steps into a clean 404, counted as invalid_credentials because it reads as an unknown address (:265-271). Then ResetFailedAttemptsAsync (:274), and _multiFactorMethod = MultiFactorMethodFor(secondFactor.Value) (:277, private helper at :897-906, mapping a verified TOTP or recovery code to the mfa claim value and any unrecognized outcome to null) arms the field in a try/finally around the private IssueTokensCoreAsync (:278-286), which does not repeat the challenge this request already ran (:280-281), so the claim lands only on this response and disarms whether or not the call throws. A refused issuance is counted as rejected (:288-291), a success is recorded (:293), and then RehashPasswordIfNeededAsync(issued, user, request.Password) (:295) runs before return issued (:297).

      • RegisterAsync (:301-398): validate (:307), refuse unaccepted terms when a version is configured (:316-319, returning LegalAcceptanceErrors.TermsNotAccepted), IP rate-limit (ADR-029 and BR-213, :322-326), reject a duplicate email through the EmailExistsAsync hook (:328-333), hash the password (:335), build the user through the CreateUser hook and unwrap it with TryGetValue (:336-340), seed the account's language from the request culture (SeedRegistrationCulture, :342-346, private helpers at :771-779 and :788-798), AddAsync and save (:348-353), run the OnUserRegisteredAsync post-commit hook to pick up the instance the first access token is minted from (:382), and increment the IP registration count (:385). The culture seed exists because the confirmation email is composed later, outside this request, in the recipient's stored culture (ADR-027); it applies only to a User that implements IUserPreferences and has no culture yet, and stores nothing for the invariant culture, the pseudo-locale or a culture that resolves to the default (doc comments, :764-770, :781-787). Next, registration opens no session exactly when sign-in would refuse the new account: if CheckEmailConfirmed(tokenUser) fails, the result is a success carrying RegistrationOutcome.ConfirmationPending (:387-393), and because the same virtual gate decides both, a subclass override moves them together. Otherwise the session is opened last (:397): it carries the user id, which a store-generated key only has once the insert has run.

        The save is wrapped in a deliberately broad catch (Exception) (:355) whose comment (:358-371) is the teaching material. The email lookup above is a check-then-act: two concurrent registrations for the same address both pass it, and the loser only fails on the insert, against the unique index every consumer puts on Email (ADC unfiltered, Store filtered on IsDeleted). Without the catch, that race surfaces as a generic 500 instead of the 409 a serialized pair would have produced. The catch cannot name DbUpdateException, because Application has no EF Core dependency by layer rule, so the re-check is what narrows it (:372-377): if the address exists now, the concurrent registration is the cause and the caller gets the same conflict the serial path returns through the shared EmailAlreadyExistsFailure() helper; anything else rethrows untouched and still reaches the exception middleware. The re-check passes CancellationToken.None on purpose: it has to run even when the caller's token is what aborted the save, or a cancelled save could never be classified.

      • RefreshTokenAsync (:401-473): validate (:407), pull claims from the expired JWT via TokenService.GetPrincipalFromExpiredToken (:415, the issuer's instance; signature still checked, only lifetime skipped), read the identifier with principal.GetUserId() (:425, rides the standard sub claim, also accepts the NameIdentifier form the bearer handler maps it to, and parses through IParsable so the identifier alias can change shape without editing this file), load the tracked user (:432, a missing user answered by CreateRefreshUserMissingError, :435), run the refresh app gate (:439), and hand the presented refresh token to sessionIssuer.RotateAsync (:460-466) together with a mint callback over CreateAccessTokenForSession. The issuer resolves the session behind the token (reuse detection included), rotates it, and answers with a token pair whose access token carries the successor's sid. Two claims ride the rotation, both read off the presented access token, whose signature was already validated, and both armed in one try/finally around the successor mint and cleared together (:468-472): the step-up the user already performed, _multiFactorMethod = principal.FindMultiFactorMethod() (:450; dropping it would quietly demote a signed-in session every access-token lifetime and make every IRequiresMfa use case unreachable without a fresh sign-in, comment :445-449), and the sign-in instant, _authenticatedAt = principal.FindAuthTime() (:455), carried unchanged because a refresh is not a sign-in, so a stolen refresh token cannot make its session look recently signed in; a token with no auth_time rotates into one with none (comment, :452-454, ADR-139).

      • RevokeTokenAsync (:476-490): load the user (a NotFound when absent), then delegate to sessionIssuer.SignOutAsync(userId, refreshToken, ...) (:487). Only a live session belonging to this user identifies the device to sign out; when the token is absent or identifies no live session of this user, the issuer revokes every live session instead, rather than reporting success for a revocation that reached nothing.

      • RevokeAllSessionsAsync (:493-506): the unconditional form of the same thing, through sessionIssuer.SignOutEverywhereAsync (:503).

      • GetSessionsAsync (:510-518) and GetSignInsAsync (:522-530): no user lookup, so each is one call to the issuer, sessionIssuer.ListActiveAsync (:515) for live devices and sessionIssuer.ListSignInsAsync (:527) for the sign-in history, wrapped in a success (remarks, :509, :521).

      • RevokeSessionByIdAsync (:538-542): an expression-bodied delegation to sessionIssuer.RevokeSessionAsync. Ownership is checked by the issuer's store query, so another account's id and a nonexistent id produce the same NotFound (remarks, :533-537); an already-revoked session writes nothing and returns NotFound with Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked, matching the interface contract (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/IAuthenticationService.cs:126-128).

      • SignInVerifiedEmailOwnerAsync (:558-586): the sign-in-link path. A missing account or a service account reads as an invalid link (:564-570), the app gate runs (:572), and the second factor is challenged with no code (:578): any outcome other than NotEnrolled is refused with SignInLinkErrors.SecondFactorRequired (:579-583), because the link proves only mailbox access and honoring it would let that alone bypass an enrolled factor (remarks, :553-555). The email-confirmation gate is skipped on purpose: redeeming the link is the proof that gate asks for (:549-550). It then mints through IssueTokensCoreAsync (:585).

      • SignInWithPasskeyAsync (:604-633): the passkey path. A missing account or a service account answers PasskeyErrors.AssertionFailed (:610-616), the app gate runs (:618), and with no second-factor challenge _multiFactorMethod is armed to AuthClaimTypes.MultiFactorMethodPasskey around the issuance (:624-632): a passkey is possession of the authenticator plus its own user verification, so it satisfies the second factor itself, and RefreshTokenAsync carries mfa=passkey across rotations like otp (remarks, :597-601).

      • HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync (:641-653): a vanished account answers false (:646-649); otherwise a non-empty stored password hash counts, and so does the virtual HasExternalLoginAsync (:651-652, hook at :664-665, default false).

      • IssueTokensAsync (:694-716): the protected open-and-respond an app-level sign-in that proves no factor (external login) mints through. It null-guards the user (:700) and, for anyone but a service account, runs the second-factor challenge with no code first, refusing an enrolled account with TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorRequired and opening no session (:701-713; doc :680-686). It ends in the private IssueTokensCoreAsync (:728-746), the core every framework sign-in (password, registration, sign-in link, passkey) calls directly once it has settled the factor itself. The core refuses a service account with the generic Auth.InvalidCredentials 401 (:734-738), which makes it the backstop behind every path-specific refusal (doc :672-678), and otherwise delegates to sessionIssuer.IssueAsync(user.Id, sessionId => CreateAccessTokenForSession(user, sessionId), ...) (:740-745): the access token is a callback because it carries the session's id, which exists only once the issuer has opened the session.

      • The private mechanics are login-side only. ChallengeSecondFactorCountingFailuresAsync (:876-889) is the counting wrapper described under LoginAsync. MultiFactorMethodFor (:897-906) maps an unrecognized outcome to null, so an enum that grew cannot silently mint an mfa claim. HasStoredCredential (:935) delegates to PasswordCredential.IsStored, and CanSignInWithPassword (:941-942) adds the existence and service-account checks. BurnPasswordVerificationCost (:958-966) skips a blank password and otherwise calls the hasher's own passwordHasher.BurnVerificationCost(password) (:965), so a branch that never reaches the real check still pays the key-derivation cost. The remarks (:949-957) explain both choices: the burn costs what verifying the most expensive record the hasher can have stored costs (for the shipped hasher, the larger of its current and legacy work factors), so an unknown address costs the same as an account still on an older record, and it does not verify against fixed decoy material because a hasher that rejects wrong-sized material before deriving anything (the shipped one does) would answer a decoy instantly and silently reopen the timing gap. SignInFailed (:976-984) is the record-and-log helper above.

        RehashPasswordIfNeededAsync (:1004-1035) is the work-factor upgrade. It returns at once unless the issuance succeeded and the app's User opts in by implementing IPasswordRehashableUser (:1006-1009). Otherwise it runs inside BestEffort.ExecuteAsync(PasswordRehashOperation, Logger, ..., CancellationToken.None) (:1011-1034): when passwordHasher.NeedsRehash(rehashable.PasswordHash) reports the stored hash is current it does nothing (:1016-1019); otherwise it hashes the verified plaintext and hands the new material to rehashable.RehashPassword(hash, salt) (:1021-1022), logs AuthenticationServiceLog.PasswordRehashRejected with the joined error codes and returns if the aggregate refuses (:1023-1030), and saves through the unit of work on its own (:1032). The remarks (:992-1000) give the ordering its reason: it runs after the tokens are issued and saves separately, so the session save never carries the user row, and a refused invariant, a concurrency conflict or a dropped connection cannot fail a sign-in that has already succeeded; any non-domain failure is logged and counted by the best-effort wrapper, and the record is simply upgraded on a later sign-in. CancellationToken.None is deliberate: the sign-in is complete, and an abandoned request must not surface as a cancellation from this step. EmailAlreadyExistsFailure() (:1042-1044) is the 409 shared by the up-front check and the race recovery so the two paths are indistinguishable to a caller. Session resolution, rotation, family revocation and the cap are private to AuthSessionIssuer.

      • The hooks: four are abstract, so a subclass must supply them. FindUntrackedByEmailAsync (:753) and EmailExistsAsync (:759) are deliberately written against the app's concrete User so EF translates the predicate against the app's own mapped columns, and the second explicitly leaves the app to decide whether soft-deleted accounts count (ignoreQueryFilters: true blocks re-registration of an erased address); CreateUser (:762) runs the app's domain factory; CreateAccessToken (:801) mints the app's claim set (for example speaker_id versus customer_id).
