Eight virtual methods can be overridden, besides the Logger property above: CreateAccessTokenForSession (:821-822) calls sessionIssuer.MintForSession(sessionId, _multiFactorMethod, _authenticatedAt, () => CreateAccessToken(user)), so the issuer arms its stamping token service for the duration of the app hook and sid (plus mfa when this request verified a second factor, and auth_time, carried over unchanged on a refresh) is appended to whatever claim set the app passes, which is what keeps the claims additive with no change to CreateAccessToken's signature (remarks, :807-817); CheckEmailConfirmed (:832-842) is the email-confirmation gate, used by both sign-in and registration; ChallengeSecondFactorAsync (:858-864) runs the second-factor challenge through twoFactor ?? validators.TwoFactor (:862) and, with neither, answers TwoFactorOutcome.NotEnrolled with no extra query, which is what keeps the feature free for an app that has not adopted it; HasExternalLoginAsync (:664-665) reports an external login for the last-passkey check; ValidateLoginCandidateAsync (:909) and ValidateRefreshCandidateAsync (:913) add extra gates such as a deactivated-account check (the first also guards the sign-in-link and passkey paths); OnUserRegisteredAsync (:920) runs the post-commit side-effect; and CreateRefreshUserMissingError (:928-929) defaults the vanished-user case to 401 (a token for a missing user is indistinguishable from an invalid one) while letting an app return 404 where its public contract already promises it.

    • Why it's built this way: the untracked-then-tracked dual fetch keeps the common credential-verification path off the change tracker (cheaper, and soft-deleted accounts fall out via EF query filters returning the generic 401) while still giving a tracked instance to mint from (ADR-004). Per-device session rows with hashed tokens, rotation, family revocation on reuse, and a per-user cap are the BR-205/206 model (ADR-050), and keeping them behind IAuthSessionIssuer gives the sign-in decision and the session mechanics one owner each (:49-54). Routing every sign-in path, password or not, through one issuance core is what lets a single check refuse a service account everywhere (ADR-140) and lets the sign-in-link and passkey paths (ADR-116, ADR-139) reuse the app gate and the session mint unchanged. Password material flows through IAuthUser's PasswordHash and PasswordSalt (ADR-032). A successful sign-in is the only moment the verified plaintext is in hand, which is why the hash upgrade lives here, opt-in per app through IPasswordRehashableUser (ADR-133), and why it is best-effort rather than part of the sign-in's success (ADR-096). The whole workflow depends only on abstractions, so it is identical whether the module runs in-process or as an extracted service.

    • Where it's used: subclassed by each app's sealed AuthenticationService, for example MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs:52, which binds TUser = User, adds the Attendee default role (BR-45) and the speaker_id claim (BR-209, claims builder documented at :559), passes the injected AuthenticationValidators and IAuthSessionIssuer through to the base (:57-58), re-lists IAuthenticationService (:70) so it can re-implement RegisterAsync and ExternalLoginAsync outright (:76), and overrides HasExternalLoginAsync (:190). ADC's User opts into the sign-in rehash by implementing IPasswordRehashableUser (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/User.cs:39). MMCA.Store supplies its own subclass with a customer_id claim. Consumed by the Identity API controllers via the IAuthenticationService port.

    • Caveats / not-in-source: ExternalLoginAsync is intentionally not overridden here: the base inherits the interface's default not-supported failure, and OAuth account linking stays in the app subclass because it is coupled to the app's User factory surface (doc comment, :47-48). ADC's subclass does not override Logger, so in ADC both the failed sign-in Warnings and a refused rehash go to the NullLogger and leave no log line; the mmca.auth.signin counter still records every attempt, and a thrown rehash failure is still counted on the MMCA.Common.BestEffort meter (doc comment, :151-152).

    EmailConfirmationSettings

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.EmailConfirmation · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/EmailConfirmation/EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:10 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: the options class bound to the Authentication:EmailConfirmation configuration section (EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:28), controlling token lifetime, throttling, and whether an unconfirmed address blocks sign-in.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations ([Range]) and System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis ([SuppressMessage]) validate the bound values.
    • Concept introduced: the config-bound settings-class shape (a SectionName constant plus init-only, range-validated properties with sane defaults) is the same one the sibling PasswordResetSettings uses elsewhere in this group; see it there for the general pattern rather than re-teaching it here. [Rubric §11, Security] (assesses whether authentication-adjacent behavior is safely configurable): every numeric knob here is range-constrained (EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:43,50,54,58), so a bad value in configuration fails validation instead of silently disabling throttling.
    • Walkthrough: ConfirmationUrl (EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:40) defaults to empty rather than being [Required], deliberately, per its own doc comment (EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:30-34): an unconfigured host still boots and degrades to a token-only, paste-in-by-hand flow. TokenLifetimeMinutes (line 44) defaults to 1440 (one day). MaxValidationAttempts (line 51) caps wrong-token guesses at 5 before the record is discarded. MaxRequestsPerEmail (line 55) and RequestWindowMinutes (line 59) throttle re-issuance per address. RequireConfirmedEmail (line 70) defaults to false.
    • Why it's built this way: the RequireConfirmedEmail default is called out as load-bearing in its own remarks (EmailConfirmationSettings.cs:49-54): turning it on locks out every account whose address was never confirmed, so a host backfills existing rows as confirmed before flipping it, and with it off the whole feature is additive. This is the opt-in shape recorded in ADR-116.
    • Where it's used: read by AuthenticationServiceBase and EmailConfirmationTokenService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/EmailConfirmationTokenService.cs) and registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs; ADC binds it via MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationServiceSettings.cs and consumes it in SendEmailConfirmationHandler.

    LegalAcceptanceOptions

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/LegalAcceptanceOptions.cs:12 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the options class for terms-of-service acceptance, bound from the Legal section (SectionName, LegalAcceptanceOptions.cs:15). Its one setting, CurrentTermsVersion (:21), is the terms version every user must have accepted (for example 2026-10-01); changing it asks every signed-in user to accept again, and null or whitespace turns the feature off.
    • Depends on: nothing; it is a plain options bag.
    • Concept: a feature switch carried by configuration rather than a flag. "Not configured" is a legal state that disables the feature, and LegalAcceptancePolicy.ResolveCurrentVersion is the single place that turns the raw value into a trimmed version or null.
    • Why it's built this way: an opt-in host (ADR-116) that never sets the section changes nothing, so the registration only binds the section (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:145-146, inside AddLegalAcceptance at :104). Related: ADR-070, ADR-116.
    • Where it's used: injected as IOptions<LegalAcceptanceOptions> by LegalAcceptanceControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Legal/LegalAcceptanceControllerBase.cs:48, read at :54) and, optionally, by AuthenticationValidators (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationValidators.cs:30,66), which exposes CurrentTermsVersion to the registration check.

    MachineClientSettings

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettings.cs:19 · Level 0 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the options class for machine clients (OAuth client credentials), bound from the MachineClients section (SectionName, MachineClientSettings.cs:22) by AddMachineClients(configuration) and validated at startup.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party at runtime; its doc comment points at IServiceAccountProvisioner, which an enabled host must register.
    • Concept introduced: the config-bound settings shape is the one EmailConfirmationSettings already shows; what is new here is a lifetime cap derived from another mechanism's window. [Rubric §11, Security] (assesses whether credentials and their revocation are bounded): MaxAccessTokenMinutes is 15 (:33) because revocation works by the soft-deleted marker for the service account, which lives 20 minutes, and a token must lapse within that window minus the bearer handler's 5-minute clock skew (doc comment :27-32).
    • Walkthrough: MinAccessTokenMinutes is 1 (:25). Enabled (:36) defaults to false; while it is false the token endpoint and every administration endpoint answer 404 and the MachineClients table is in no model, so a host that never opts in sees no route and no migration (remarks :8-13). AccessTokenMinutes (:42) defaults to MaxAccessTokenMinutes; nothing renews the token, a program asks again. DataSourceName (:48) names the logical data source that owns the MachineClients table (the Identity database) and defaults to "Default".
    • Why it's built this way: off by default so the feature is additive, and turning it on needs consumer code (an IServiceAccountProvisioner over the app's own User aggregate, remarks :14-17). MachineClientSettingsValidator enforces both at startup: the 1 to 15 range (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettingsValidator.cs:23-27) and, when enabled, a registered provisioner (:37-40). Recorded in ADR-140; the fail-at-startup shape is ADR-070.
    • Where it's used: bound in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:41-45 (inside AddMachineClients, :37); read by MachineClientService, by EFMachineClientStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/MachineClients/EFMachineClientStore.cs:32), and by ApplicationDbContext and DesignTimeDbContextHelper to decide whether the table is in the model.

    ServiceAccount

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/ServiceAccount.cs:13 · Level 0 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the facts a machine token is minted from, for one service account: user id (the token's sub), name, email and role (ServiceAccount.cs:13-17), the same standard claims a person's token carries.
    • Depends on: the UserIdentifierType alias and PiiAttribute on Name and Email (:15-16).
    • Concept: a plain positional record crossing the consumer boundary; no new concept. Role is the host's role name, and its permissions are read from the registry rather than carried here (doc comment :12).
    • Why it's built this way: Common has no user entity, so the consumer's IServiceAccountProvisioner returns this small projection instead of its User aggregate. See ADR-140.
    • Where it's used: returned by IServiceAccountProvisioner.FindAsync and consumed by MachineClientService.IssueTokenAsync (MachineClientService.cs:97-115); ADC builds it in MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/ServiceAccountProvisioner.cs.

    EmailConfirmationErrors

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.EmailConfirmation · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/EmailConfirmation/EmailConfirmationErrors.cs:9 · Level 2 · class

    • What it is: the static Error-factory class for the email-confirmation flow: one factory for a sign-in refused because the address is unconfirmed, one for every failing token redemption.
    • Depends on: Error (the Result-pattern error type taught in the primer).
    • Concept: the same named-code-plus-factory-method convention used by every *Errors class in this codebase (see AuthErrorCodes for the general shape); no new concept here.
    • Walkthrough: EmailNotConfirmedCode (EmailConfirmationErrors.cs:12) and InvalidTokenCode (line 15) are the two error codes. EmailNotConfirmed(source) (lines 25-28) returns Error.Unauthorized, distinct from Auth.InvalidCredentials so a UI can offer to resend the link. InvalidToken(source) (lines 33-36) is the single rejection every failing redemption (unknown, expired, mismatched, or attempt-capped token) collapses to.
    • Why it's built this way: the doc comment on EmailNotConfirmed (lines 474-478) explains it is reachable only after the password has already been proved, so the message can safely tell the account owner what is wrong rather than help an address sweeper enumerate valid accounts; InvalidToken collapsing every failure mode to one message denies an attacker any signal about which reason a redemption failed for.
    • Where it's used: raised by ConfirmEmailHandlerBase.cs (2 sites) and AuthenticationServiceBase.cs, and by EmailConfirmationTokenService.cs; asserted against in EmailConfirmationHandlerBaseTests.cs, EmailConfirmationTokenServiceTests.cs, and ADC's ConfirmEmailHandlerTests.cs.

    LegalAcceptanceErrors

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/LegalAcceptanceErrors.cs:11 · Level 2 · class (static)

    • What it is: the two validation errors of terms acceptance, as factory methods plus their code constants.
    • Depends on: Error (the primer's Result/Error pattern), AuthErrorCodes (TermsNotAcceptedCode aliases AuthErrorCodes.TermsNotAccepted, LegalAcceptanceErrors.cs:14) and LegalAcceptanceErrorCodes (VersionNotCurrentCode, :17).
    • Concept: error factories with stable codes, mirroring EmailConfirmationErrors; no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: TermsNotAccepted(source) (:22) is the registration refusal when a terms version is configured and the box was not ticked ("You must accept the Terms of Service to register."). VersionNotCurrent(source) (:33) refuses an acceptance of any version other than the configured one, including any acceptance while none is configured. Both build Error.Validation with the caller-supplied source.
    • Why it's built this way: the shared code constants let a client switch on a stable string without referencing the Application layer.
    • Where it's used: TermsNotAccepted is returned by AuthenticationServiceBase.RegisterAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:318); VersionNotCurrent by LegalAcceptancePolicy.EnsureAcceptsCurrentVersion (LegalAcceptancePolicy.cs:36).

    MachineClientErrors

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientErrors.cs:6 · Level 2 · class (static)

    • What it is: the error factories of the machine-client flow, plus the code constants the token endpoint switches on.
    • Depends on: Error (the primer's Result/Error pattern).
    • Concept: error factories with stable codes, mirroring EmailConfirmationErrors; no new concept. [Rubric §11, Security] (assesses whether failures leak information): one code covers every authentication failure.
    • Walkthrough: four public codes: InvalidClientCode (MachineClientErrors.cs:9), UnsupportedGrantTypeCode (:12), InvalidRequestCode (:15), RoleNotAllowedCode (:18). InvalidClient(source) (:27) is Error.Unauthorized for an unknown id, wrong secret, revoked or expired client, missing or non-service account, or a forbidden role, all deliberately indistinguishable (doc comment :20-24). UnsupportedGrantType (:33) and InvalidRequest (:39) are Error.Validation for a grant type other than client_credentials and a missing one. RoleNotAllowed (:49) refuses a role granting users:view-as, users:manage, roles:manage or clients:manage. RoleRequired (:55) and NotFound (:61, Error.NotFoundError) use inline codes with no public constant.
    • Why it's built this way: the constants let the API map a refusal onto the RFC 6749 body without string literals: MachineTokenControllerBase.TokenError answers 400 for the two grant-type codes and 401 invalid_client for everything else (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineTokenControllerBase.cs:115-123).

    IEmailConfirmationTokenService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.EmailConfirmation · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/EmailConfirmation/IEmailConfirmationTokenService.cs:15 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the token-lifecycle abstraction for email confirmation: issue a token for an address, validate and consume one presented back.
    • Depends on: UserIdentifierType (the module's identifier-type alias), Result<T>.
    • Concept: an issue/validate-and-consume token contract, mirroring the shape IPasswordResetTokenService uses elsewhere in this group; no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: IssueAsync(email, userId, cancellationToken) (IEmailConfirmationTokenService.cs:28) replaces any token already outstanding for that address, so there is one active token per address, and fails only when the per-address request throttle (EmailConfirmationSettings.MaxRequestsPerEmail/RequestWindowMinutes) has been exceeded. ValidateAndConsumeAsync(email, token, cancellationToken) (line 41) validates against the outstanding token and consumes it on success so it never redeems twice, collapsing unknown/expired/mismatched/attempt-capped failures to the single EmailConfirmationErrors.InvalidToken error.
    • Why it's built this way: consuming on success is what makes redemption single-use; collapsing every failure reason to one error, per its own doc comment (lines 603-606), denies an attacker signal about why a guess failed.
    • Where it's used: implemented by EmailConfirmationTokenService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/EmailConfirmationTokenService.cs), consumed by SendEmailConfirmationHandlerBase.cs and ConfirmEmailHandlerBase.cs, and by ADC's SendEmailConfirmationHandler.cs/ConfirmEmailHandler.cs; registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs.

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/ILegalAcceptanceService.cs:21 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the per-user storage contract behind terms acceptance: read the signed-in user's standing, and record that they accepted a version.
    • Depends on: LegalAcceptanceDTO, Result<T>, and the UserIdentifierType alias.
    • Concept: a deliberately thin consumer boundary. The controller base validates the request first (ILegalAcceptanceService.cs:14, via LegalAcceptancePolicy.EnsureAcceptsCurrentVersion) and re-derives every answer afterwards (:17, via Normalize), so an implementation only has to load and save the accepted version and instant.
    • Walkthrough: GetForCurrentUserAsync(currentUserId, currentVersion, ct) (:26) reads the caller's standing, or a failure such as NotFound. AcceptForCurrentUserAsync(currentUserId, version, ct) (:39) records the acceptance stamped with the implementation's own clock and returns the standing afterwards.
    • Why it's built this way: Common ships no implementation and AddLegalAcceptance deliberately registers none (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:129), because where the accepted version lives is the consumer's User aggregate (see ILegalAcceptingUser in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/ILegalAcceptingUser.cs). Recorded in ADR-116.
    • Where it's used: consumed by LegalAcceptanceControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Legal/LegalAcceptanceControllerBase.cs:46); ADC implements it as LegalAcceptanceService (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/LegalAcceptanceService.cs), registers it in that module's DependencyInjection.cs, and subclasses the controller base as LegalAcceptanceController.

    IMachineClientService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/IMachineClientService.cs:11 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the machine-client contract: the OAuth client credentials grant, and administration of the clients behind it.
    • Depends on: Result<T>, the response and request records in MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients (MachineTokenResponse, MachineClientResponse, MachineClientSecretResponse, CreateMachineClientRequest).
    • Concept: a service a program (not a person) authenticates against with an id and a secret, receiving a short-lived bearer token and no refresh token or session. The feature switch lives on the interface itself, so a controller can resolve it per action and answer 404 while it is off.
    • Walkthrough: IsEnabled (IMachineClientService.cs:14) mirrors MachineClients:Enabled. IssueTokenAsync(grantType, clientId, clientSecret, ct) (:28) runs the grant and fails with MachineClients.InvalidClient, UnsupportedGrantType or InvalidRequest. ListAsync (:37) lists every client, revoked ones included. CreateAsync(request, ct) (:46) provisions the service account, stores the client and returns the primary secret once. RotateAsync (:52) issues a secondary secret, returned once; both work until PromoteAsync (:58) makes it primary and the old one stops at once. RevokeAsync (:67) stops the secrets and writes the soft-deleted marker so tokens already held are rejected.
    • Why it's built this way: two secrets with an explicit promote let a caller rotate without downtime. See ADR-140.
    • Where it's used: implemented by MachineClientService, registered by AddMachineClients (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:49), resolved per request by MachineTokenControllerBase (MachineTokenControllerBase.cs:57) and MachineClientsControllerBase (MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:42-43), and checked by CloudAdapterTripwire.

    IServiceAccountProvisioner

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/IServiceAccountProvisioner.cs:15 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the consumer-implemented contract that creates and reads the service-account users behind machine clients.
    • Depends on: ServiceAccount, Result<T>, the UserIdentifierType alias.
    • Concept: the consumer-supplied-store shape of ADR-116 (compare ILegalAcceptanceService): Common has no user entity, so the app implements this over its own User aggregate. A service account is a user whose IAuthUser.IsServiceAccount is true: no password, no external login, never a person; the framework refuses it on every interactive sign-in path and as a view-as target (remarks IServiceAccountProvisioner.cs:10-14).
    • Walkthrough: CreateAsync(name, role, ct) (:24) creates a passwordless service-account user with the role and returns its id, or the app's own refusal (an unknown role, say). FindAsync(userId, ct) (:33) returns the account, or null when it does not exist, is deleted or locked, or is not a service account, so a token is never minted for a person.
    • Why it's built this way: an enabled host without a registration fails at startup naming it (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientSettingsValidator.cs:37-40). Related: ADR-116, ADR-140.
    • Where it's used: called by MachineClientService at create and on every mint; ADC implements it as ServiceAccountProvisioner (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/ServiceAccountProvisioner.cs:25), registered at MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:57.

    LegalAcceptancePolicy

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Legal · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/LegalAcceptancePolicy.cs:10 · Level 3 · class (static)

    • What it is: the pure rules of terms acceptance, kept out of the controller and the consumer's service so they cannot drift.
    • Depends on: LegalAcceptanceOptions, LegalAcceptanceErrors, LegalAcceptanceDTO, Result.
    • Concept: server-authoritative version checking. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether consent is recorded against what the user actually saw: the client says which version it showed, and the server refuses unless it equals the configured one.
    • Walkthrough: ResolveCurrentVersion(options) (LegalAcceptancePolicy.cs:18) returns the trimmed configured version, or null for null options, null value or whitespace. EnsureAcceptsCurrentVersion(currentVersion, suppliedVersion, source) (:36) succeeds only when a version is configured and the trimmed supplied one matches it with an ordinal comparison; otherwise it fails with LegalAcceptanceErrors.VersionNotCurrent. Normalize(currentVersion, standing) (:50) re-derives the standing through LegalAcceptanceDTO.Evaluate, taking only the accepted version and instant from the consumer's answer, so the result never depends on a consumer filling CurrentVersion or IsCurrent correctly.
    • Why it's built this way: the ordinal match means a client holding stale terms cannot record consent to the new ones, and the no-version-configured failure means there is nothing to accept when the feature is off.
    • Where it's used: LegalAcceptanceControllerBase (LegalAcceptanceControllerBase.cs:54,83,110,125), AuthenticationValidators (AuthenticationValidators.cs:66), and LegalAcceptancePolicyTests.cs (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/Legal/).

    IMachineClientStore

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/IMachineClientStore.cs:10 · Level 5 · interface

    • What it is: persistence for MachineClient rows.
    • Depends on: MachineClient.
    • Concept: a narrow store interface rather than the generic repository; no new concept. Every caller sits behind MachineClients:Enabled, so it never queries a table the model does not carry (doc comment IMachineClientStore.cs:5-9).
    • Walkthrough: ListAsync (:15) returns every client, revoked ones included, oldest first. FindAsync(clientId, ct) (:21) returns a tracked instance, so SaveAsync(client, ct) (:33) persists changes made to it. AddAsync (:27) adds and saves a new client. RecordUseAsync(client, usedOn, ct) (:44) calls MachineClient.RecordUse and saves best effort: a concurrent issuance that saved first wins, because the last-used instant is informational and must never fail a token request.
    • Why it's built this way: the best-effort RecordUseAsync keeps a concurrency conflict on a diagnostic column off the token path. See ADR-140.
    • Where it's used: implemented by EFMachineClientStore over the Identity database, registered with TryAddScoped (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:48), and consumed by MachineClientService.

    MachineClientService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:35 · Level 6 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the framework's IMachineClientService: it runs the client credentials grant and administers clients.
    • Depends on: IMachineClientStore, IServiceAccountProvisioner, ITokenService, IPermissionRegistry, ICacheService, IOptions<MachineClientSettings>, TimeProvider (primary constructor, MachineClientService.cs:35-42); plus MachineClient, MachineClientSecret, AdministrationPermissions, AuthClaimTypes and SoftDeletedUserCache.
    • Concept introduced: a machine token is minted by the raw ITokenService, not the session-stamping wrapper the sign-in workflow uses, so it carries no sid, mfa or auth_time and opens no refresh session; it carries the service account's standard claims and role permissions as a person's token does, plus client_id and token_use=machine (remarks :16-21). [Rubric §11, Security] (assesses least privilege and revocation): four permissions are refused on the backing role, checked at create and again at every mint, and revocation reuses the soft-deleted-user marker of ADR-047.
    • Walkthrough: ClientCredentialsGrantType is "client_credentials" (:45). ForbiddenPermissions (:52-58) lists ViewAsUsers, ManageUsers, ManageRoles and ManageClients: role and client management are included because a client could otherwise grant its own role anything or mint further clients for itself (:47-51). IssueTokenAsync (:66) refuses a missing or foreign grant type, then collapses every other failure to one InvalidClient result: unparsable id or empty secret, unknown client or Accepts false (:90), and an account that is missing, mismatched or holds a forbidden role, re-read on every mint (:97-98). It then mints with GenerateShortLivedAccessToken at AccessTokenMinutes (:103-115), records the use (:117) and returns a Bearer response. CreateAsync (:135) requires a role, checks it against ForbiddenPermissions (:146) and validates the client row on a throwaway hash BEFORE provisioning the account (:160), so a refused create leaves no orphaned account. RotateAsync (:173) and PromoteAsync (:193) delegate to the entity and save. RevokeAsync (:219) saves the revoked row first (:227-228), then writes the marker for the service account with a duration from SoftDeletedUserCache.MarkerDurationFor over the longer of the machine and host access-token lifetimes (:231-234). IsForbiddenRole (:250) reads the role's permissions from the registry.
    • Why it's built this way: saving before marking means no new token is minted once revocation starts, and the marker then makes every service's SoftDeletedUserMiddleware answer 401 to tokens the client already holds (remarks :212-218). The duration assumes the default bearer clock skew, since this layer cannot read the host's JwtBearerOptions (:230). See ADR-140.
    • Where it's used: registered by AddMachineClients (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.MachineClients.cs:49) and reached through the G12 controller bases; covered by MachineClientServiceRevocationMarkerTests.cs (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/MachineClients/) and ADC's MachineClientControllersTests.cs.

    IPermissionGrantCache

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionGrantCache.cs:21 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the read side of the in-memory snapshot of stored (database-granted, as opposed to compiled-into-code) permissions, keyed by role.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party in its own signature; consumed alongside IPermissionRegistry.
    • Concept introduced: the cache-in-front-of-a-store pattern used across this group for data that is read on every authorization check but changes rarely. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] (assesses whether hot paths avoid a database round trip): GetPermissions (IPermissionGrantCache.cs:29) is synchronous and reads the already-loaded snapshot, so it stays off the authorization hot path's I/O.
    • Walkthrough: GetPermissions(string role) (line 99) returns the role's stored permissions, matched case-insensitively, empty when the role has none or the cache has not loaded yet. RefreshAsync (line 107) reloads the whole snapshot from the store; called at startup, on a configured interval, and explicitly by IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator after a grant changes.
    • Why it's built this way: separating the read interface from the invalidation interface (IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator) lets LayeredPermissionRegistry, which only needs to read, depend on a narrower contract than the administration path that needs to force a reload.
    • Where it's used: implemented by PermissionGrantCache (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/PermissionGrantCache.cs), read by LayeredPermissionRegistry (LayeredPermissionRegistry.cs) and StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService, and registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs.

    IPermissionGrantCacheInvalidator

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionGrantCache.cs:53 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the write-triggering half of the cache: forces a reload of one role's grants (or every role) after an administrative change.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party in its own signature.
    • Concept: same cache-invalidation split introduced at IPermissionGrantCache; no new concept here.
    • Walkthrough: InvalidateAsync(string? role = null, ...) (IPermissionGrantCache.cs:61) invalidates the cached grants and reloads them; null means every role.
    • Why it's built this way: kept on a separate, narrower interface from the read side so a caller that only grants or revokes (the administration surface) depends on exactly the capability it needs.
    • Where it's used: implemented alongside IPermissionGrantCache by PermissionGrantCache.cs, called by StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs after a grant or revoke, and registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs.

    PasskeyAttestation

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyAttestation.cs:9 · Level 0 · record

    • What it is: the verified result of a passkey registration: the credential id, the public key, the authenticator's starting signature counter and its transports.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; BCL byte[], IReadOnlyList<string>.
    • Concept: a library-neutral output record, so the WebAuthn library's own types never cross into the core layers (see IPasskeyCeremony); no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: a single positional record line (PasskeyAttestation.cs:9): CredentialId, PublicKey, SignCount (uint) and Transports.
    • Why it's built this way: it carries exactly what PasskeyService needs to build a PasskeyCredential (PasskeyService.cs:100-107) and nothing of the verification library, which keeps Fido2NetLib confined to MMCA.Common.Passkeys (ADR-139, decision 1).
    • Where it's used: returned by IPasskeyCeremony.VerifyRegistrationAsync and produced by Fido2PasskeyCeremony (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys/Fido2PasskeyCeremony.cs).

    PasskeyChallenge

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyChallenge.cs:7 · Level 0 · record

    • What it is: the server-side half of a passkey ceremony in flight: which ceremony it is, which account it was issued to (registration only), and the options JSON exactly as sent to the browser.
    • Depends on: the UserIdentifierType alias (see the primer).
    • Concept: the stored challenge a completion must redeem; the single-use mechanics live in PasskeyChallenges.
    • Walkthrough: the positional record PasskeyChallenge(string Ceremony, UserIdentifierType? UserId, string OptionsJson) (PasskeyChallenge.cs:7) plus two ceremony constants: Register = "register" (line 10) and SignIn = "signin" (line 13). UserId is null for a sign-in, because a discoverable sign-in names no account before the assertion.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the options verbatim lets the completion verify against what was actually issued, and recording the ceremony and account lets PasskeyService refuse a flow redeemed by the wrong ceremony or another account (PasskeyService.cs:80-84).
    • Where it's used: built by PasskeyService (PasskeyService.cs:66, :188), serialized and redeemed by PasskeyChallenges.

    PasskeySettings

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeySettings.cs:19 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: the options class bound to the Passkeys section: the on/off switch, the WebAuthn relying party, the allowed browser origins, and the data source that owns the passkey table.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party.
    • Concept: the same config-bound settings shape as EmailConfirmationSettings; its validation is a separate validator, PasskeySettingsValidator, per the fail-fast configuration contract (ADR-070).
    • Walkthrough: SectionName (PasskeySettings.cs:22) is "Passkeys". Enabled (line 25) defaults to false. RelyingPartyId (line 31) is the registrable domain the passkeys belong to (example.com also covers app.example.com), required when enabled. RelyingPartyName (line 34) is the name the authenticator shows, required when enabled. Origins (line 40) lists the exact scheme, host and port the browser ceremonies may run on, at least one required when enabled. DataSourceName (line 46) defaults to "Default" and names the logical data source holding the PasskeyCredentials table (the Identity database).
    • Why it's built this way: passkeys are an opt-in, so the default is off and a disabled host carries no relying-party configuration at all (ADR-139, decision 2). DataSourceName follows the same gated-table shape as the permission grants (PermissionGrantSettings): the table is mapped only on the named source.
    • Where it's used: bound and validated by PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions and PasskeySettingsValidator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys), read by Fido2PasskeyCeremony, PasskeyService (IsEnabled), EFPasskeyCredentialStore.cs, ApplicationDbContext.cs and DesignTimeDbContextHelper.cs (under MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure); pinned by PasskeyModelGateTests.cs and AddPasskeysTests.cs.

    PasskeyStepUp

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyStepUp.cs:17 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: the rule that decides whether a signed-in caller may register a passkey: their interactive sign-in must be at most ten minutes old.
    • Depends on: BCL ClaimsPrincipal, TimeSpan, DateTimeOffset; the FindAuthTime() principal extension that reads the auth_time claim.
    • Concept introduced: step-up by sign-in age. A sensitive action (planting a new sign-in method on the account) asks "how long ago did this person actually sign in", not "how fresh is this token". [Rubric §11, Security] (assesses how authentication and authorization resist account takeover): the check reads auth_time, which a refresh carries over unchanged, so a stolen refresh token can never keep itself fresh enough to register its own passkey.
    • Walkthrough: MaxSignInAge (PasskeyStepUp.cs:20) is ten minutes. IsSatisfiedBy(principal, now) (lines 26-30) reads the sign-in instant with principal.FindAuthTime() (line 27); a principal with no auth_time never qualifies, and a sign-in stamped slightly in the future (clock skew between hosts, comment at line 29) counts as recent because only now - signedInAt <= MaxSignInAge is tested (line 30).
    • Why it's built this way: per ADR-139 decision 8, the alternatives ("a token under ten minutes old" or "a token carrying mfa") both ride every refresh, since a refresh resets iat and carries mfa; only auth_time measures the sign-in itself.
    • Where it's used: checked by both registration actions of PasskeysControllerBase.cs and by TwoFactorControllerBase.cs (under MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers); the refusal is PasskeyErrors.StepUpRequired; pinned by AuthTimeClaimTests.cs.

    PasskeyStoredKey

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyStoredKey.cs:8 · Level 0 · record

    • What it is: what an assertion is verified against: the stored public key, the last signature counter, and the owning account's WebAuthn user handle.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party.
    • Concept: the input-side twin of PasskeyAttestation, keeping the ceremony contract free of the domain entity; no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: one positional record line (PasskeyStoredKey.cs:8): PublicKey, SignCount (uint), UserHandle.
    • Why it's built this way: PasskeyService builds it from a PasskeyCredential with the handle derived by UserHandleFor (PasskeyService.cs:255), so the verification library sees bytes, never the entity.
    • Where it's used: passed to IPasskeyCeremony.VerifyAssertionAsync, consumed by Fido2PasskeyCeremony.

    PermissionGrantSettings

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/PermissionGrantSettings.cs:9 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: the options class bound to Authentication:PermissionGrants, controlling how long a cached grant snapshot is served, which logical data source owns the grant table, and which role names the administration surface lists.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations ([Range], [Required]).
    • Concept: the same config-bound settings shape as EmailConfirmationSettings; no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: SectionName (PermissionGrantSettings.cs:12) is "Authentication:PermissionGrants". CacheSeconds (line 34) defaults to 30, is range-validated to 5-3600 (line 33), and its remarks (lines 17-32) spell out two things. First the trade-off (lines 18-26): this is the bound on how stale another replica may be after an edit, since invalidation is per process, and the stored grants are read by the token-minting Identity service, so any lag here is added on top of the access token's lifetime (15 minutes by default) before a revoke reaches every service. Second the failure behavior (lines 27-31): each cached entry lives three intervals, so the snapshot outlives the gap before the next reload and survives up to two failed reloads, after which it stops answering and stored grants fail closed. DataSourceName (line 42, [Required] at line 41) defaults to "Default", naming the logical data source a modular host points at its Identity database. KnownRoles (line 54) defaults to an empty list, and its remarks (lines 48-53) explain why it must be configured: neither IPermissionRegistry (which answers questions about a role but does not list roles) nor the grant table (which only knows roles that already have a grant) can enumerate roles on its own; left empty, the surface still works but lists nothing until the first grant exists.
    • Why it's built this way: the 30-second default keeps the revoke window close to the token lifetime itself, at the cost of one small query per Identity replica every 30 seconds and with no broker on the authorization path; raising it trades a longer revoke window for fewer database reads (PermissionGrantSettings.cs:24-26). The three-interval entry lifetime means a transient store outage costs nothing for two reload cycles, while a longer one degrades to denying stored grants (compiled permissions are unaffected, see LayeredPermissionRegistry) rather than serving an arbitrarily old snapshot.
    • Where it's used: read by PermissionGrantCache.cs, PermissionGrantRefreshService.cs, EFPermissionGrantStore.cs, StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs, ApplicationDbContext.cs, and DesignTimeDbContextHelper.cs (all under MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure); registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs; pinned by PermissionGrantModelGateTests.cs and PermissionGrantCacheTests.cs in MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests.

    LayeredPermissionRegistry

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/LayeredPermissionRegistry.cs:30 · Level 1 · class

    • What it is: an IPermissionRegistry decorator that unions the compiled-into-code permission set with the stored (database-granted) set, so a role's effective permissions are "compiled OR granted", never a replacement of one by the other.
    • Depends on: IPermissionRegistry (the inner, compiled registry), IPermissionGrantCache (the stored-grant cache).
    • Concept introduced: the decorator pattern applied to a registry lookup. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] (assesses whether a pattern is used idiomatically and solves a real problem): LayeredPermissionRegistry wraps inner without changing its contract, adding a second data source transparently to every caller of IPermissionRegistry.
    • Walkthrough: the type is a primary-constructor class taking inner and grants (LayeredPermissionRegistry.cs:30-32). GetPermissions(role) (lines 35-52) reads both layers; when the stored set is empty it returns the compiled set as-is (no allocation), and only when both layers contribute does it materialize a HashSet<string> union, per the comment at lines 45-47: this call is a reporting path (administration surface, diagnostics), not the hot authorization path. HasPermission(roles, permission) (lines 55-66) is that hot path: it short-circuits on the compiled registry first (inner.HasPermission), and only falls through to a per-role stored-grant lookup (grants.GetPermissions(role).Contains(permission)) when the compiled check fails; the caller's roles sequence is materialized once (line 62) because both passes would otherwise enumerate it twice.
    • Why it's built this way: separating the always-cheap compiled check from the stored-grant fallback keeps the common case (a permission granted in code) allocation-free and single-pass, per ADR-116, which records the opt-in database-grant layer as additive on top of the existing compiled registry.
    • Where it's used: registered as the IPermissionRegistry implementation in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs (3 sites) when database grants are enabled; exercised directly in MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/LayeredPermissionRegistryTests.cs.

    PasskeyErrors

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyErrors.cs:10 · Level 2 · class

    • What it is: the catalogue of passkey refusals, each a stable code constant plus a factory returning a typed Error.
    • Depends on: Error.
    • Concept: the same per-feature error catalogue as TwoFactorErrors and SignInLinkErrors; the error kind on each factory picks the HTTP status (see the Result pattern in the primer).
    • Walkthrough: seven code constants (PasskeyErrors.cs:13-31), all prefixed Passkeys.; PasskeysNotSupportedCode is named apart from the sign-in-link constant because the error-resource scan resolves codes by name (comment at line 12). The factories, each taking an optional source: NotSupported (line 36, Error.Failure), ChallengeInvalid (line 42, Error.Validation: unknown, expired, used, or the wrong ceremony or account), RegistrationFailed (line 48, Error.Validation), AssertionFailed (line 54, Error.Unauthorized), StepUpRequired (line 63, Error.Forbidden, pointing at PasskeyStepUp), LastPasskey (line 69, Error.Conflict) and NotFound (line 75, Error.NotFoundError).
    • Why it's built this way: AssertionFailed is deliberately one vague message for every sign-in refusal (unknown credential, bad signature, counter); the specific reason goes only to a Warning log in PasskeyService, so a caller cannot probe which credentials exist (ADR-139, decision 7).
    • Where it's used: PasskeyService (8 sites), Fido2PasskeyCeremony, PasskeysControllerBase.cs, AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> and IAuthenticationService (the not-supported default), and PasskeysPanel.razor.cs in MMCA.Common.UI.

    IPasskeyCeremony

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/IPasskeyCeremony.cs:19 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the core contract for the WebAuthn cryptography: build creation and request options, verify an attestation, read a credential id from an assertion, verify an assertion.
    • Depends on: PasskeyAttestation, PasskeyStoredKey, Result; BCL JsonElement.
    • Concept introduced: a library boundary held by a core interface. [Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain] (assesses how third-party code is contained and pinned): every member speaks JSON strings, JsonElement and byte arrays, so the Fido2 package and its native dependencies live only in MMCA.Common.Passkeys, which a host opts into, and the core layers never load them.
    • Walkthrough: CreateRegistrationOptions(userHandle, userName, displayName, excludeCredentialIds) (IPasskeyCeremony.cs:27) returns creation options as JSON, excluding the account's existing credentials so an authenticator is not enrolled twice. VerifyRegistrationAsync(optionsJson, attestation, isCredentialIdUnique, ...) (lines 35-39) verifies against the options as issued and calls back to ask whether the credential id is unused. CreateSignInOptions() (line 43) builds request options naming no credential (a discoverable sign-in). ReadCredentialId(assertion) (line 48) returns the id or null when malformed. VerifyAssertionAsync(optionsJson, assertion, credential, ...) (lines 60-64) checks the signature, user handle and counter, and returns the counter the authenticator reported.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-139 decision 1 keeps the WebAuthn library in one package behind this contract, guarded at build time (EnforcePasskeysBoundary) and test time (PasskeysIsolationTests.cs). The uniqueness callback lets the store answer without the ceremony depending on persistence.
    • Where it's used: implemented by Fido2PasskeyCeremony, registered by PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions, consumed by PasskeyService; its absence while Passkeys:Enabled is true fails startup in CloudAdapterTripwire.cs (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Configuration).

    • Depends on: PasskeyOptionsResponse, PasskeyRegisterRequest, PasskeyResponse, PasskeySignInRequest, AuthenticationResponse, IAuthenticationService, Result.
    • Concept: a two-step begin/complete ceremony, where begin stores a single-use challenge and complete must redeem it (see PasskeyChallenges); no further new concept.
    • Walkthrough: IsEnabled (IPasskeyService.cs:15) mirrors Passkeys:Enabled. BeginRegistrationAsync(userId, userName, displayName, ...) (lines 23-27) and CompleteRegistrationAsync(userId, request, ...) (lines 34-37) run registration for a signed-in account, which must be the one the flow was issued to. ListAsync (line 43) returns the passkeys oldest first; RenameAsync (lines 51-55) relabels one. DeleteAsync (line 65) removes one, the last only while the account still has a password or external login (remarks at lines 58-59, via IAuthenticationService.HasSignInMethodBesidesPasskeysAsync). BeginSignInAsync (line 70) starts an anonymous discoverable sign-in, and CompleteSignInAsync(request, ipAddress, userAgent, ...) (lines 81-85) verifies the assertion and mints the token pair through IAuthenticationService.SignInWithPasskeyAsync.
    • Why it's built this way: the sign-in ends in the app's own authentication service, so a passkey sign-in produces the same token pair, refresh session and sign-in history as any other, stamped mfa=passkey (ADR-139, decision 7).
    • Where it's used: implemented by PasskeyService, registered by PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions, called by PasskeysControllerBase.cs (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Passkeys); pinned by AddPasskeysTests.cs and PasskeysIsolationTests.cs.

    • What it is: the persistence abstraction for stored passkeys: list an account's, find by row id or by WebAuthn credential id, add, update, remove.
    • Depends on: PasskeyCredential.
    • Concept: the same narrow store-behind-an-interface shape as IPermissionGrantStore; each write saves immediately rather than joining a unit of work.
    • Walkthrough: ListForUserAsync(userId, ...) (IPasskeyCredentialStore.cs:16) returns oldest first. FindAsync(userId, id, ...) (line 23) scopes by account, so another account's row reads as missing. FindByCredentialIdAsync(credentialId, ...) (line 29) searches across all accounts, which is what sign-in and the registration uniqueness check need. AddAsync (line 35), UpdateAsync (line 41, for a rename or a recorded use) and RemoveAsync (line 47) each save.
    • Why it's built this way: scoping FindAsync by account makes ownership a property of the query rather than a check every caller must remember. Removal is a hard delete: passkeys are flat bookkeeping with no soft-delete flag (ADR-139, decision 4).
    • Where it's used: implemented by EFPasskeyCredentialStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFPasskeyCredentialStore.cs), registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs, consumed by PasskeyService; faked in PasskeyTestHost.cs.

    IPermissionGrantStore

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionGrantStore.cs:16 · Level 4 · interface

    • What it is: the persistence abstraction behind the stored-grant layer: read every grant, read one role's grants, grant a permission, revoke a permission.
    • Depends on: PermissionGrant (the persisted grant row), Result.
    • Concept: an idempotent grant/revoke pair, so a click repeated by an administration UI is not an error; no new concept beyond that idempotency guarantee.
    • Walkthrough: GetAllAsync(cancellationToken) (IPermissionGrantStore.cs:23) reads every stored row, used to build the in-memory snapshot the authorization path reads. GetPermissionsAsync(role, cancellationToken) (line 31) reads one role's stored permissions for the administration surface. GrantAsync(role, permission, grantedBy, cancellationToken) (lines 42-46) grants a permission, succeeding and writing nothing when the role already has it stored (doc comment lines 33-36). RevokeAsync(role, permission, cancellationToken) (line 60) removes a stored grant, also idempotent; its remarks (lines 51-55) are explicit that this removes only the STORED grant, never a compiled-into-code one, which is exactly what keeps a data edit from disabling an endpoint the code guarantees.
    • Why it's built this way: the "stored grant is additive, never subtractive over compiled permissions" rule enforced here is the same invariant LayeredPermissionRegistry.HasPermission implements: the compiled check always wins first, and revoking a stored grant can never take away a compiled-in permission.
    • Where it's used: implemented by EFPermissionGrantStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFPermissionGrantStore.cs), read by PermissionGrantCache.cs (2 sites) to build the IPermissionGrantCache snapshot, called by IRoleAdministrationService's implementation StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs (2 sites), and registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs.

    PasskeyChallenges

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyChallenges.cs:21 · Level 5 · class

    • What it is: the single-use challenge store for passkey ceremonies, plus the per-account lock that serializes passkey deletions.
    • Depends on: ICacheService, IDistributedLock, PasskeyChallenge; BCL RandomNumberGenerator, JsonSerializer.
    • Concept introduced: read-and-burn under a distributed lock. A challenge must be redeemable exactly once across every replica, so redemption reads the shared store and removes the entry inside one lock, and a contended lock is itself treated as the replay. [Rubric §11, Security] (assesses replay and takeover resistance): a captured flow id cannot be redeemed twice, even by two requests racing on different replicas.
    • Walkthrough: Lifetime (PasskeyChallenges.cs:24) is five minutes. Keys are passkeys:challenge: plus a flow id of FlowIdLength 32 (lines 26-27); the lock lease and wait are 10 and 5 seconds (lines 31-32), sized like the OAuth exchange-code lock. IssueAsync (lines 38-47) generates the flow id from 16 random bytes as lower-case hex (line 42) and stores the serialized challenge for Lifetime (lines 43-44). RedeemAsync (lines 56-83) rejects anything not exactly 32 lower-case hex characters (line 58), takes lock: plus the key (line 64) and returns null when contended (lines 65-69), reads with GetFromSharedStoreAsync rather than a local copy (line 74) so a flow burned on another replica misses, then removes the entry and deserializes it (lines 80-81). LockAccountAsync(userId, ...) (lines 92-94) takes lock:passkeys:user:{userId}, returning null past the wait.
    • Why it's built this way: this is the OAuth exchange-code pattern applied to WebAuthn (ADR-139 decision 5, building on ADR-108 for the lock and ADR-077 for the cache). The account lock lives here because it uses the same lock primitive and timings.
    • Where it's used: consumed by PasskeyService (3 sites), registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Caching.cs and by PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions.

    PasskeyService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Passkeys · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyService.cs:33 · Level 6 · class

    • What it is: the implementation of IPasskeyService: it orchestrates the challenge store, the WebAuthn ceremony, the credential store and the app's authentication service.
    • Depends on: PasskeySettings, IPasskeyCeremony, IPasskeyCredentialStore, PasskeyChallenges, IAuthenticationService, PasskeyCredential, PasskeyErrors; BCL TimeProvider, ILogger<T>.
    • Concept: orchestration over the contracts introduced at IPasskeyCeremony and PasskeyChallenges. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability] (assesses whether failures are diagnosable): every refusal logs its specific reason at Warning through source-generated LoggerMessage methods (PasskeyService.cs:277-281) while the caller sees one generic error.
    • Walkthrough: a sealed partial primary-constructor class (PasskeyService.cs:33-40). IsEnabled (line 43) reads Enabled. UserHandleFor(userId) (lines 48-49) is the account id as UTF-8, opaque and free of personal data. BeginRegistrationAsync (lines 52-69) excludes the account's existing credential ids and issues a Register challenge. CompleteRegistrationAsync (lines 72-115) redeems the challenge and refuses it unless the ceremony is Register and the account matches (lines 80-84), verifies with a uniqueness callback over FindByCredentialIdAsync (lines 87-93), builds the entity with PasskeyCredential.Create (lines 100-107) and adds it (line 113). ListAsync (line 118) and RenameAsync (line 125) are thin. DeleteAsync (lines 153-179) takes the account lock (line 155), answering a Passkeys.Busy conflict when it cannot (line 158), and refuses LastPasskey when one passkey remains and the account has no other sign-in method (lines 170-173). BeginSignInAsync (line 182) issues a SignIn challenge with no account. CompleteSignInAsync (lines 194-218) redeems a SignIn challenge (line 203), verifies (line 209) and hands the user id to SignInWithPasskeyAsync (lines 215-216). The private VerifyAssertionAsync (line 236) reads the credential id (line 238), finds the credential across accounts (line 244), verifies against a PasskeyStoredKey (lines 251-257), then applies the counter rule itself with credential.RecordUse (line 266) before saving the use (line 273).
    • Why it's built this way: the signature-counter check runs here as well as in the library so the cloned-key rule does not depend on the library's own check (ADR-139, decision 6), and the count-then-delete inside the account lock stops two concurrent deletes of the last two passkeys from locking the user out (remarks at lines 148-152).
    • Where it's used: registered as IPasskeyService by PasskeysServiceCollectionExtensions; UserHandleFor is referenced from IPasskeyCeremony's documentation.

    ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SoftDeletedUsers · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:9 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the two-verb contract that writes and clears the soft-deleted user marker (ADR-047). Its summary (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SoftDeletedUsers/ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:3-8) records that the marker now means "deleted or locked": an account erasure and an administrator's lock both write it, for as long as an already-issued access token on this host can still be accepted, and an unlock clears it.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party beyond the UserIdentifierType alias; Task and CancellationToken from the BCL. The cache and the token settings the marker needs are deliberately absent from the contract.
    • Concept introduced: a narrow writer that hides how a revocation is stored and how long it lasts. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses interface segregation and dependency inversion: whether a consumer depends only on what it uses. Writing the marker correctly needs two unrelated things (the shared cache it lives in, and the host's access-token lifetime that decides how long it must live), and the summary states the point of the abstraction directly: "neither workflow needs the cache nor the token settings itself" (ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:6-7). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses session revocation: a JWT stays valid until its exp, so a deleted or locked account's already-issued tokens must be refused by something other than the token. The marker is that something, and the second verb matters as much as the first: without ClearMarkerAsync, a token issued after an unlock would be refused on every host until the marker expired (doc at :19-22).
    • Walkthrough:
      • MarkDeletedAsync(userId, ct) (ISoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter.cs:17): marks the user as deleted or locked, so requests bearing an already-issued token are rejected (:11-13).
      • ClearMarkerAsync(userId, ct) (:26): removes the user's marker from the shared store, so a token issued after an unlock is accepted at once on every host (:19-22).
    • Why it's built this way: two workflows (account erasure and administrator lock/unlock) need the same marker with the same duration rule; putting the rule behind one writer keeps it in one place. The revocation model is recorded in ADR-047.
    • Where it's used: implemented by SoftDeletedUserMarkerWriter and registered as a scoped factory in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:52. Injected into UserAdministrationServiceBase<TUser, TUserDto> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserAdministrationServiceBase.cs:56, which writes the marker at :264 and clears it at :277) and into DeleteUserHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:98, writing at :214). ADC passes it through its UserAdministrationService and DeleteUserHandler (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/).

    IssuedSession

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:725 · Level 0 · record (private sealed, nested)

    • What it is: the two-field result of opening or rotating a refresh session: the plaintext refresh token the client is handed, and the id of the session row it belongs to. It is a private sealed record nested inside AuthSessionIssuer (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:725), not part of the framework's public surface.
    • Depends on: nothing beyond the BCL (string, Guid). It is produced and consumed entirely inside its declaring class.
    • Concept introduced: the plaintext token exists in exactly one place, and it is a return value. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how a bearer credential is stored. RefreshSession rows keep only a digest (RefreshSession.HashToken, used at AuthSessionIssuer.cs:200 and :285 to look up by hash), so once a session is persisted the raw token cannot be recovered from the store at all. The type comment says exactly this (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:720-724): the plaintext "exists nowhere else, since the store keeps only its hash". Modelling the hand-off as a small record rather than an out-parameter or a tuple is what keeps that fact readable: both methods that can produce a token return Result<IssuedSession>, so the compiler shows you the complete list of places raw token material is in flight. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] also applies: a positional record gives value equality and immutability for free, and Guid SessionId names what would otherwise be an anonymous second tuple element.
    • Walkthrough: one positional declaration, IssuedSession(string RefreshToken, Guid SessionId) (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:725). RefreshToken is what goes back to the caller in the AuthenticationResponse; SessionId is what the access token's sid claim carries, which is why the session must be opened before the token is minted (the comment at AuthSessionIssuer.cs:97-98).
    • Why it's built this way: the pairing is load-bearing rather than incidental. A caller that received only the token could not stamp sid, and a caller that received only the id could not answer the client. Returning both together removes the ordering mistake where a token is minted for a session that does not exist yet.
    • Where it's used: returned by OpenSessionAsync (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:469, constructed at :337) and RotateSessionAsync (:350, constructed at :390); unwrapped by IssueAsync (:84-85) and by RotateAsync (:120-121), each of which passes SessionId to the caller's mintAccessToken callback and puts RefreshToken into the response.

    • What it is: the name an invitation creates the account with when the invited address has no account yet (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:68-71).

    • What it is: why a sign-in link was sent. Each purpose has its own lifetime and its own active token (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:58).

    SessionStampingTokenService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737 · Level 1 · class (private sealed, nested)

    • What it is: a pass-through ITokenService that appends up to three claims to every access token minted while it is armed (the current refresh session's sid, an mfa claim when a second factor verified this request, and an auth_time claim carrying the sign-in instant) and behaves as the plain inner service the rest of the time. It is a private sealed class nested inside AuthSessionIssuer (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737).
    • Depends on: ITokenService (the contract it implements and the inner instance it wraps, AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737), AuthClaimTypes for the sid, mfa and auth_time claim names (:776, :781, :787), and the BCL (System.Security.Claims, System.Globalization.CultureInfo).
    • Concept introduced: a decorator used to make a new claim additive. [Rubric §2, Design Patterns] assesses idiomatic pattern use, and this is the Decorator pattern applied to a very specific compatibility problem. Access tokens need to name the session they belong to (and, when relevant, the second factor that satisfied a step-up and the instant the user actually signed in), but the claim set is produced by the app's own CreateAccessToken hook. The obvious fix, adding parameters to that hook, is a compile break in every consumer for claims the app has no decision to make about; the type's own remarks say exactly this (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:732-736). Wrapping the token service instead means the issuer arms the wrapper around the hook call and the claims appear in tokens minted by subclasses that were never edited. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] is the payoff: an additive protocol change with a zero-line consumer diff, three times over.
    • Walkthrough: a primary constructor takes the inner service (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:737).
      • Guid? CurrentSessionId { get; set; } (:740) is the session arming switch: a session id stamps, null mints unchanged.
      • string? CurrentMultiFactorMethod { get; set; } (:746) is the second-factor arming switch, set only when a second factor really verified for this request (doc :742-745).
      • DateTimeOffset? CurrentAuthTime { get; set; } (:749) is the sign-in-instant switch. The remarks on the issuer's arming method explain why plain mutable properties are safe for all three (:161-162): the issuer is resolved per request (scoped, like the store it saves through) and one request mints one token at a time.
      • AccessTokenLifetime (:752) and RefreshTokenLifetime (:755) forward straight to inner, so the lifetime callers read is still the JWT settings' value.
      • GenerateAccessToken(...) (:758-793) is the only member with behavior. When no switch is armed it delegates verbatim (:765-768). Otherwise it copies the app's additionalClaims into a new List<Claim> (:770, so the caller's sequence is never mutated), then independently appends AuthClaimTypes.SessionId formatted as sessionId.ToString("D", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) when CurrentSessionId is set (:772-777, the "D" format being the canonical hyphenated Guid form ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.FindSessionId parses back, see ClaimsPrincipalExtensions), AuthClaimTypes.MultiFactor set to the raw method string when CurrentMultiFactorMethod is set (:779-782), and AuthClaimTypes.AuthTime as Unix seconds typed ClaimValueTypes.Integer64 when CurrentAuthTime is set (:784-790), before delegating with the extended list (:792). The three claims are independent: a token can carry any combination of them.
      • GenerateRefreshToken() (:796) and GetPrincipalFromExpiredToken(string token) (:799-800) are plain forwards.
    • Why it's built this way: putting the stamping behind an ITokenService rather than inside the caller's own method keeps the app hook's signature and semantics untouched while still guaranteeing the claims on the tokens the framework's own flows mint. The escape hatch still applies: an app that mints from its own injected ITokenService reference produces a valid token with none of the three claims, and can restore them by overriding CreateAccessTokenForSession (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:821-822).
    • Where it's used: constructed once per issuer instance (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:67) and exposed as IAuthSessionIssuer.TokenService (:77), which AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> surfaces to subclasses as its protected TokenService property (AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:120). All three switches are armed and disarmed by the four-argument AuthSessionIssuer.MintForSession (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:173-190, with the finally at :184-189 guaranteeing all three disarm even when the hook throws), which the base calls from CreateAccessTokenForSession with its _multiFactorMethod and _authenticatedAt fields (AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:822; _authenticatedAt is read from the presented token's auth_time on a refresh, :455).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the type's own summary (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:727-731) still describes only the sid claim; the mfa and auth_time behavior is documented on the properties and visible in GenerateAccessToken.

    • What it is: what a redeemed sign-in token grants: the SignInLinkPurpose it was issued for and, for an invitation that carried one, the SignInLinkProfile to provision the account with (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:73-76).

    SignInLinkSettings

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkSettings.cs:10 · Level 1 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the options class for sign-in links (ADR-116), bound from the Authentication:SignInLinks configuration section (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkSettings.cs:6-13). It carries the master switch, the page the link opens, the two lifetimes, the throttles, and the two small pieces of behavior that depend on them.
    • Depends on: SignInLinkPurpose; System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations ([Range]) and System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis ([SuppressMessage]).
    • Concept introduced: a capability that is registered but off. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether a security-sensitive feature fails closed. Enabled defaults to false (SignInLinkSettings.cs:20), so registering the capability changes nothing until a host turns it on, and turning it off again makes every outstanding link inert without waiting for it to expire (doc :15-19). The second security decision lives in ComposeLink: the address and the token ride in the URL fragment, which is never sent to a server, so the live token stays out of access logs, request telemetry and Referer headers, and a mail scanner that prefetches the link with a GET never sees, and so never spends, the token (remarks :68-73). The shape follows the same fail-fast stance: every numeric knob is range-validated, and the registration validates on start (see Where it's used), matching the fail-fast contract of ADR-070.
    • Walkthrough:
      • SectionName = "Authentication:SignInLinks" (:13).
      • Enabled (:20), default false.
      • SignInUrl (:31), default empty, deliberately not required (matching EmailConfirmationSettings.ConfirmationUrl, see EmailConfirmationSettings) so an unconfigured host still boots; with it empty no link can be composed and nothing is sent (doc :22-26). The CA1056 suppression (:27-30) explains why it is a string: the empty default is not a valid System.Uri.
      • SignInLifetimeMinutes (:35), [Range(1, 1440)], default 15; InviteLifetimeMinutes (:39), [Range(1, 43200)], default 20160 (14 days).
      • MaxValidationAttempts (:45), [Range(1, 100)], default 5: wrong tokens tolerated for one address before its outstanding tokens are discarded.
      • MaxRequestsPerEmail (:49), [Range(1, 100)], default 3, within RequestWindowMinutes (:53), [Range(1, 1440)], default 60.
      • LifetimeFor(purpose) (:58-59): the invite lifetime for Invite, the sign-in lifetime otherwise.
      • ComposeLink(email, token) (:74-77): null when SignInUrl is blank, otherwise {SignInUrl}#email=...&token=... with both values passed through Uri.EscapeDataString.
    • Why it's built this way: the defaults make the cheap mistake safe (an unconfigured host boots and sends nothing; an unlisted host never issues links), and the fragment rule is the same one the password-reset link uses (ForgotPasswordHandlerBase.ComposeResetLink, cited in the remarks at :69-70), so both emailed-token flows keep the token off the wire. Recorded in ADR-116.
    • Where it's used: bound by AddSignInLinks with .Bind(...), .ValidateDataAnnotations() and .ValidateOnStart() (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:109-112); injected as IOptions<SignInLinkSettings> into SignInLinkTokenService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/SignInLinks/SignInLinkTokenService.cs:42), SendSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/SendSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:48) and RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:62). ADC's architecture tests pin the invitation lifetime (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Architecture/MMCA.ADC.Architecture.Tests/Privacy/InvitationLifetimeTests.cs).
