    IAuthSessionIssuer

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:27 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the contract that issues, rotates and revokes the access/refresh token pair behind a signed-in device. Its summary (IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:8-13) lists what it owns: the multi-device RefreshSession rows (hashed at rest), BR-205 rotation with BR-206 reuse detection, the per-user live-session cap, and the sid/mfa claims stamped on the access token minted for a session. It also lists the user's sign-in history and records a native client's device metadata on a live session.
    • Depends on: ITokenService, AuthenticationResponse, RefreshSessionSummaryResponse, SignInSummaryResponse, DeviceMetadata, RefreshSessionSettings (referenced from the docs), Result/Result<T> (the Result pattern taught in the primer), and the UserIdentifierType alias.
    • Concept introduced: splitting "who is signed in" from "what they are handed". [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses whether each type has one reason to change. The remarks (IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:16-20) draw the line explicitly: credentials, lockout, the second factor and the app's own gates stay with AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>, which calls the issuer only once a caller has been proved, and the base's own summary states the same split from the other side (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:50: "This class decides who is signed in; IAuthSessionIssuer decides what they are handed"). The access token's claim set still belongs to the app, so the issuer takes it as a Func<Guid, string> mintAccessToken callback: the session id the token must carry exists only once the session has been opened or rotated. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses credential lifecycle handling; the rotation and reuse rules are stated on the contract itself, not left to an implementation. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] shows in how the contract grew: the auth_time overload of MintForSession is a default interface member, so an implementation written before it keeps compiling.
    • Walkthrough:
      • TokenService (IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:35): the ITokenService an app mints through. While the issuer is minting for a session it appends sid (and mfa when a second factor verified); at any other time it is the plain registered service (doc at :29-34).
      • IssueAsync(userId, mintAccessToken, ipAddress, userAgent, ct) (:47): opens a new session, evicting the oldest live one when the per-user cap is full, persists it and returns the pair; the user's other sessions are untouched (:37-40).
      • RotateAsync(userId, refreshToken, mintAccessToken, ipAddress, userAgent, ct) (:71): BR-205 rotation. An unknown or expired token fails alone, and so does a token whose session was revoked by a sign-out or evicted by the session cap (that device simply lost its session). A token already rotated, already flagged as reuse, or rotated first by a concurrent request is the BR-206 reuse signal and revokes every live session the user holds; a revoked row with any other or no recorded reason is treated as reuse too. Every rejection carries the same Auth.InvalidRefreshToken error (:54-62).
      • MintForSession(sessionId, multiFactorMethod, mintAccessToken) (:87): runs the callback with TokenService armed to stamp sid and, when not null, mfa (:79-82).
      • MintForSession(sessionId, multiFactorMethod, authenticatedAt, mintAccessToken) (:105-106): the same, also stamping auth_time: authenticatedAt when given (a refresh carrying the presented token's sign-in instant over unchanged), otherwise the instant of the sign-in IssueAsync is opening, and none outside it (:89-93). Its default body ignores authenticatedAt and delegates to the three-argument member, so an older implementation mints no auth_time, and passkey registration (which requires one) stays refused on that host (remarks :100-104).
      • SignOutAsync(userId, refreshToken, ct) (:117): revokes the one live session behind the presented token when it belongs to the user; when the token is absent or identifies no live session of this user, every live session is revoked instead (:108-111).
      • SignOutEverywhereAsync(userId, ct) (:123): revokes every live session and saves.
      • ListActiveAsync(userId, currentSessionId, ct) (:133): live sessions newest first, with expired-but-unrevoked rows left out because a device list must not offer a device that can no longer authenticate (:125-127).
      • ListSignInsAsync(userId, currentSessionId, ct) (:147): the sign-in history, one row per sign-in (a rotation chain, however many times it rotated), live and ended alike, newest first, capped at the newest 50, each with how it ended, covering what the store retains (RefreshSessionSettings.RetentionDays) (:138-141).
      • RevokeSessionAsync(userId, sessionId, ct) (:162): another account's session id and a never-existing id both answer Auth.SessionNotFound; an already-revoked session writes nothing and answers the not-found failure Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked, so the client can say the device was already signed out (:152-157).
      • RecordDeviceAsync(userId, sessionId, device, ct) (:176): records the DeviceMetadata a native client reported on its own session (named by the access token's sid), replacing what was there, and saves; rotation carries it to every successor. Another account's id, a missing id, and a revoked or expired session all answer Auth.SessionNotFound and write nothing (:164-170).
    • Why it's built this way: the remarks (IAuthSessionIssuer.cs:23-24) give the lifetime rule: scoped, like the session store it writes through, so a sign-in and its session insert share the request's unit of work. Keeping the session rules behind one interface means the authentication workflow never touches a session row. The multi-device session model is recorded in ADR-097 and the rotation scheme in ADR-050.
    • Where it's used: implemented by AuthSessionIssuer; registered TryAddScoped in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:182; injected into AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> (AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:79), which delegates to it from TokenService (:120), refresh (RotateAsync, :460), sign-out (:487, :503), session listing (:515), sign-in history (:527), revocation (:542), issuance (IssueAsync, :740) and CreateAccessTokenForSession (the four-argument MintForSession, :822). AuthControllerBase takes it as a [FromServices] parameter and calls RecordDeviceAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:293, :313). ADC's AuthenticationService takes it as a constructor argument and passes it to the base (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs:58,67).

    ISignInLinkTokenService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.SignInLinks · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:18 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the contract that issues and redeems the single-use tokens behind sign-in links (ADR-116), on the design IEmailConfirmationTokenService uses: the token material lives outside the database, hashed at rest, with a per-address request throttle and a per-token validation-attempt cap (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/SignInLinks/ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:6-11).
    • Depends on: SignInLinkPurpose, SignInLinkProfile, SignInLinkGrant, Result<T> from the primer.
    • Concept introduced: a token keyed by address, not by account. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how emailed bearer tokens are issued and spent. The remarks (ISignInLinkTokenService.cs:12-17) explain the key choice: an invitation is issued to an address that may have no account yet, and redeeming it is what creates one, so the token cannot be keyed by a user id. One active token per address and purpose means a new link of one purpose replaces only the outstanding link of that purpose. Redemption is validate-and-consume in one call, so a token never redeems twice, and every failure collapses to one generic error (:48-50).
    • Walkthrough:
      • IssueAsync(email, purpose, profile = null, ct) (:35): issues a token for the normalized address, replacing any token of the same purpose already outstanding (:20-23). profile is supplied only for an invitation; a plain sign-in link never creates an account (:26-29). Returns the raw token to email, or a failure when the per-address request throttle is exceeded (:31-34).
      • ValidateAndConsumeAsync(email, token, ct) (:52): validates the token against the address's outstanding tokens and consumes the one it matches, returning the SignInLinkGrant; unknown, expired, mismatched and attempt-capped all collapse to the same error (:41-51).
    • Why it's built this way: reusing the email-confirmation token design keeps one reviewed shape for every emailed single-use token in the framework. Recorded in ADR-116.
    • Where it's used: implemented by SignInLinkTokenService and registered TryAddScoped by AddSignInLinks (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:115; the remarks at :104-105 note that registering it issues nothing until the app wires the handlers and a controller and sets Authentication:SignInLinks:Enabled). Injected into SendSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/SendSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:46) and RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/SignInLinks/RedeemSignInLinkHandlerBase.cs:60, consumed at :97). ADC issues invitations through it directly in SendSignInLinkInternalCommandHandler (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/SendSignInLink/).

    SignInHistory

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:20 · Level 7 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: the reader that turns a user's refresh-session rows into a sign-in history: the store aggregates the rotation chains and this shapes each one into a SignInSummaryResponse. Shared by the self-service list and the administrator's, so both read a history the same way (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:7-13).
    • Depends on: IRefreshSessionStore (GetRecentSignInsAsync, FindByIdAsync), RefreshSessionSignIn, RefreshSession, SignInSummaryResponse, SignInEndReasons, SignInHistoryEntryKind, optionally IViewAsGrantStore and ViewAsGrant; RefreshSessionDevice for the device column.
    • Concept introduced: a history row is a rotation chain, not a row. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether a read is bounded. Every refresh rotates the session into a new row, so a naive history would list one entry per refresh and grow with activity. Here a sign-in is the chain: it starts at its earliest retained row and was last active at its newest row's issue instant, and the newest row (the head) decides how it ended (remarks :14-19). The store does the aggregation and caps it at MaxEntries (:23, 50), so the read is bounded by sign-ins, never by how many times each rotated. [Rubric §11, Security] applies to the view-as rows: each support view of the account appears in the holder's own history, without the staff user's device or address (:59-62).

      • MaxEntries = 50 (:23).
      • ReadAsync(store, userId, now, currentSessionId, ct, viewAsGrants = null) (:37): reads the capped aggregate (:45), resolves which sign-in the caller is in (:46), shapes it (:49), and when a view-as grant store is present reads the account's recent grants with the same cap (:55) and merges them (:56).

      • SummarizeViewAs (:80): a grant row spans the grant; ended grants report SignInEndReasons.ViewAsEnded (:84-87), past-expiry ones SignInEndReasons.Expired (:88-91); IP and user agent are null, IsCurrent is false, and the kind is SignInHistoryEntryKind.ViewAs (:93-102).
      • Summarize(signIns, now, currentSignInId) (:110): pure; shapes each chain and applies the same ordering and cap (:114-120).
      • ResolveCurrentSignInAsync (:127): the caller's sid is normally its chain's head, since each rotation mints the token for the successor, so it is matched against the heads with no read (:139-143); otherwise (an access token minted before a sibling rotated) one user-scoped primary-key lookup finds it and returns its SignInId, or its own Id for a chain's first row (:145-146, doc :122-126).
      • Summarize(signIn, now, currentSignInId) (:149): last-active is the head's CreatedAt, IP and user agent come from the head, IsCurrent matches the resolved sign-in (:162), and Device comes from head.ToDeviceMetadata() (:163).
      • DescribeEnd(head, now) (:166): a revoked head reports its instant and recorded reason as-is, because the session reasons and SignInEndReasons share their values (:168-173); otherwise a head past ExpiresAt reports Expired, and a live one reports no end (:175).
    • Why it's built this way: the shaping functions are pure and take now as a parameter, so the history is testable without a clock or a store, and the one shared reader keeps the self-service and administrator views identical. The model is recorded in ADR-097; the view-as rows in ADR-137.
    • Where it's used: AuthSessionIssuer.ListSignInsAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:271) and UserSessionsAdministrationService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Administration/UserSessionsAdministrationService.cs:64).     AuthSessionIssuer

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.Sessions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:54 · Level 8 · class (sealed, partial)

    • What it is: the framework's IAuthSessionIssuer: multi-device refresh sessions, hashed at rest (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:14-16). Every issue opens its own RefreshSession, so signing in on a second device leaves the first one signed in (:19-20).
    • Depends on: ITokenService (mints both tokens), IRefreshSessionStore (the session rows), IOptions<RefreshSessionSettings> (the per-user cap, the reuse grace and the lost-response window), TimeProvider (every session instant), an optional ILogger<AuthSessionIssuer> and an optional IViewAsGrantStore, all primary-constructor parameters (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:54-60, doc :42-53); RefreshSession, AuthenticationResponse, RefreshSessionSummaryResponse, SignInSummaryResponse, DeviceMetadata and Error/Result from the primer. Its private helpers are IssuedSession and SessionStampingTokenService; it reads history through SignInHistory and device columns through RefreshSessionDevice. The class is partial because its two log methods are [LoggerMessage] source-generated (:645-658).
    • Concept introduced: refresh-token rotation with family revocation on reuse, a grace window for races, and an opt-in recovery for lost responses. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how bearer credentials are issued, stored and revoked. The class remarks (AuthSessionIssuer.cs:17-41) state the model: the store holds only RefreshSession.HashToken digests; rotation revokes the presented session and links it to its successor; presenting an already-rotated token lands on that revoked row, which is the reuse signal that revokes the user's whole live family (BR-206); two requests presenting the same live token at once are covered by the same rule because the rotation is claimed atomically through IRefreshSessionStore.TryRotateAsync; and an expired session is not a reuse signal. Both paths share one carve-out (:26-29): a token rotated less than RefreshSessionSettings.ReuseGraceSeconds ago (default 10) is a rotation race between sibling requests, answered 409 Conflict (Auth.RefreshSuperseded) with nothing revoked; past the grace it is a replay, unless lost-response recovery is configured (RefreshSessionSettings.LostResponseRecoveryMinutes, off by default) and the presented row's successor was never presented, in which case that successor is rotated in its place (:29-31). A token whose row was revoked by a sign-out, a session-cap eviction or an earlier reuse sweep is not a new theft signal either: that device simply lost its session, so only that request fails. A swept row is dead by construction, so revoking the family again on it would only sign the user out of the sessions they re-established, on demand of anyone holding a swept token (:391-394); a genuine replay lands on a rotated row and still revokes the family. The practical effect: a stolen-and-replayed token costs the attacker the session and costs the user only a re-sign-in, while a double-fired refresh from two tabs, or a refresh whose response never reached the client, does not sign anyone out.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Fields (:67, :74): the nested SessionStampingTokenService wrapped around the injected token service, exposed as TokenService (:77), and _signInInstant, armed only while IssueAsync mints a new session's first access token so that token carries auth_time (doc :69-73).
      • Lifetimes (:79-83): AccessTokenLifetime and RefreshTokenLifetime read the token service and fall back to 15 minutes and 7 days when the value is non-positive, so the expiry reported to clients matches the JWT's actual exp; a host that binds JwtSettings through AddCommonAuthentication fails startup on such a value, so the fallback covers test doubles and token services configured outside that binding (:35-39).
      • IssueAsync (:86): opens the session first (OpenSessionAsync, :99), unwraps it with TryGetValue (:100), saves (:105), then sets _signInInstant to now (:109) and calls mintAccessToken(issued.SessionId) (:113) inside a try whose finally clears it (:117-120). The comment at :97-98 says why the order matters: the token carries the session's id in sid, and a session has an id only once created; the comment at :107-108 says why the instant is stamped here: opening a session is an interactive sign-in, and every refresh carries it over.
      • OpenSessionAsync (:469): generates a refresh token, creates the row through RefreshSession.Create with now + RefreshTokenLifetime (:476-483), runs EnforceSessionCapAsync (:490), stages the insert without saving (:491) and returns an IssuedSession (:493).
      • EnforceSessionCapAsync (:705): reads the user's un-revoked rows, keeps the ones active now, orders oldest first (CreatedAt, then Id), and revokes from the front with ReasonSessionCap until there is room for one more (loop at :714). Its summary (:696-704) records the default cap of 10, the 1-1000 startup range, and that expired-but-unrevoked rows do not count and age out through RefreshSessionCleanupService.
      • RotateAsync (:124): ResolveRotatableSessionAsync (:135), then RotateSessionAsync (:143), each result unwrapped with TryGetValue, then the mint with the successor's id (:154), so the client's current-device marker follows the rotation (comment :150-152).
      • ResolveRotatableSessionAsync (:398): a blank token, an unknown hash, or a row of another user fails alone (:404-416). A revoked row (:418-457) splits four ways: if IsReuseSignal is false (signed out, cap-evicted, or already swept by an earlier reuse event) it fails alone (:420-427); if it was rotated inside the grace (IsWithinRotationGrace) it answers RefreshSupersededError with nothing revoked (:429-434); if FindRecoverableSuccessorAsync finds a never-presented live successor, that successor is logged and returned as the session to rotate (:436-445), and if a sibling just recovered it the answer is RefreshSupersededError (:447-452); otherwise RevokeFamilyOnReuseAsync revokes the family before failing (:454-456). An expired row fails alone (:459-461). Its summary (:382-397) explains why the unknown-hash case must not revoke the family (otherwise anyone holding one of this user's expired access tokens could sign them out everywhere by posting a random token) and why a swept row must not either.
      • FindRecoverableSuccessorAsync (:619): returns nothing unless recovery is configured, the presented row was revoked as Rotated inside the window and has a successor hash (:624-632); looks the successor up by hash and requires the same user (:634-638); a still-live successor is the recovery, and a non-live one counts as superseded only when it was itself rotated within the grace (:640-642). A successor that was ever presented would itself be revoked, which is exactly the two-holders signal that must keep revoking the family (summary :609-618).
      • RotateSessionAsync (:510): builds the successor through session.CreateSuccessor, which continues the presented session's SignInId so the sign-in history folds a rotation chain into one row (:518-526), then asks the store to claim the rotation via TryRotateAsync (:533-535). A lost claim (:537-565) means a concurrent request spent this token first, but the tracked copy was read before that claim and still looks live, so the row is re-read untracked through IRefreshSessionStore.FindByIdUntrackedAsync (:543-545): a sign-out, cap eviction or reuse sweep of the same row fails alone (:546-552), a rotation inside the grace answers RefreshSupersededError (:554-557), and anything else (rotated longer ago than the grace, or unreadable) gets the replay answer through RevokeFamilyOnReuseAsync and Auth.InvalidRefreshToken (:562-564). Rotation replaces one session with one, so the cap is not re-evaluated (:498).
      • IsReuseSignal (:579) and IsWithinRotationGrace (:599): the first treats a revoked row as reuse when it has a successor hash (:581-584) or any reason other than signed-out, session-cap or reuse-detected (:586-588), the conservative answer for rows the code does not recognize; the second is true only for the Rotated reason, with a positive grace and now - RevokedAt under it (:601-606). A row flagged as reuse, signed out or evicted never reaches the grace check, because IsReuseSignal fails it alone first, however recent.
      • RevokeFamilyOnReuseAsync (:666) and RevokeLiveSessionsAsync (:677): the second revokes every un-revoked row with the given reason and returns how many it revoked (:683-693); the first uses it with ReasonReuseDetected, saves, and logs the user id and the count (:668-672). The log message deliberately omits the client IP and user agent, which are personal data and would put a device fingerprint into every log sink (comment :653-654).
      • InvalidRefreshTokenError (:365) and RefreshSupersededError (:376): Error.Unauthorized("Auth.InvalidRefreshToken", ...) is what every failing branch returns except the races, so a caller cannot tell unknown from expired from replayed (doc :359-364); a race answers Error.Conflict("Auth.RefreshSuperseded", ...) so the client keeps its session and retries with the winner's token (:371-380).
      • MintForSession (:164 and :173): the three-argument overload forwards with authenticatedAt: null (:164-165); the four-argument one arms the nested SessionStampingTokenService with the session id, the second-factor method, and authenticatedAt ?? _signInInstant (:177-179), runs the callback, and disarms all three in a finally (:184-189). A null authenticatedAt outside IssueAsync mints no auth_time rather than inventing a sign-in (remarks :168-172).
      • SignOutAsync (:193): revokes only a live session of this user found by token hash (:197-214); anything else degrades to revoking every live session rather than reporting success for a revocation that reached nothing (comment :203-206, fallback :217-218). SignOutEverywhereAsync (:222) always revokes everything.
      • ListActiveAsync (:236): one query for un-revoked rows, then an in-memory filter to the active ones, newest first, flagging the caller's own session and attaching its device metadata through ToDeviceMetadata (:244-258).
      • ListSignInsAsync (:267): delegates to SignInHistory.ReadAsync with the clock's current instant and the optional view-as grant store (:271-277); the read is bounded by the 50-sign-in cap, never by how many times each sign-in rotated (remarks :262-265).
      • RevokeSessionAsync (:293): the ownership check is the user-scoped FindByIdAsync query (:298), so another account's id and a missing id produce the same Auth.SessionNotFound (:299-306); an already-revoked row writes nothing and answers the not-found failure Auth.SessionAlreadyRevoked (:308-315), so the client can say the device was already signed out; the session is the caller's own, so the answer reveals nothing about another account (remarks :280-292).
      • RecordDeviceAsync (:330): the same user-scoped lookup (:338); a missing, revoked or expired session answers Auth.SessionNotFound (:339-346), since a client reporting on a dead session has nothing left to describe (remarks :324-329); otherwise session.RecordDevice(device) (:348), a failure returned as-is, then save (:354).
    • Why it's built this way: every timestamp comes from the injected TimeProvider, so rotation, expiry, the grace window and the recovery window are testable without a clock, and every user-visible failure on the refresh path collapses to one error (the exceptions being the deliberate, retryable 409s) so the endpoint leaks nothing about which rule fired. A lost concurrent rotation is re-read and judged by the same two predicates as a direct lookup, which keeps one rule for one observable situation. The auth_time stamping exists for step-up checks such as passkey registration (ADR-139). The multi-device model, rotation and reuse detection are recorded in ADR-097 and ADR-050; the view-as rows in ADR-137.
    • Where it's used: registered as the scoped IAuthSessionIssuer in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:182; consumed through that interface by AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> and AuthControllerBase. Constructed directly in the Common test suites, among them AuthSessionIssuerSignInHistoryTests.cs, AuthSessionIssuerDeviceTests.cs, AuthSessionIssuerLostResponseRecoveryTests.cs and AuthSessionIssuerReuseGraceTests.cs (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/Sessions/), AuthenticationServiceBaseTests.cs, AuthenticationServiceIdentityCompletionsTests.cs and AuthenticationServiceLegalAcceptanceTests.cs (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/), PasskeyTestHost.cs (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Passkeys.Tests/) and AuthControllerBaseSessionDeviceTests.cs (MMCA.Common/Tests/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API.Tests/Controllers/Auth/), and in ADC's AuthenticationServiceTests.cs (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application.Tests/Users/).

    RecoveryCodeSet

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorService.cs:97 · Level 0 · record

    • What it is: a two-field record pairing a freshly generated set of plaintext recovery codes with their stored hashes.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party.
    • Concept: a plaintext/hash pair returned once, at generation time only, so the plaintext never has to be persisted or re-derived.
    • Walkthrough: Codes (ITwoFactorService.cs:98) is the plaintext shown to the user once; Hashes (line 86) is what the store keeps.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the plaintext out of any store means a database compromise cannot recover usable recovery codes, only their hashes.
    • Where it's used: returned by ITwoFactorService.GenerateRecoveryCodes(), consumed by TotpTwoFactorService.cs and exercised in MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Users/TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs.

    TwoFactorOutcome

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:73 · Level 0 · enum

    • What it is: the result of a second-factor challenge: NotEnrolled = 0, VerifiedTotp = 1, VerifiedRecoveryCode = 2 (ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:76,79,82).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party.
    • Concept: same explicitly-numbered, wire-stable outcome-enum shape used throughout the domain event taxonomy (see DomainEntityState in group-02); NotEnrolled = 0 is the default/no-op value, matching that convention.
    • Walkthrough: three values; NotEnrolled means the account has no active second factor so nothing was challenged, VerifiedTotp means a time-based code from the authenticator app verified, VerifiedRecoveryCode means a single-use recovery code verified and was spent.
    • Why it's built this way: collapsing the challenge result to one enum lets AuthenticationServiceBase decide, in one switch, whether to continue sign-in unchanged (NotEnrolled) or stamp an mfa claim on the issued token (the two verified cases).
    • Where it's used: returned by ITwoFactorAuthenticator.ChallengeAsync, read by AuthenticationServiceBase.cs (7 sites) and TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs (7 sites), and by the disable/regenerate handler bases.

    TwoFactorSettings

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorSettings.cs:15 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: the options class bound to Authentication:TwoFactor, controlling the TOTP parameters (issuer, digits, period, clock-skew window) and the recovery-code and secret sizing.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations ([Range], [Required], [StringLength]).
    • Concept: the same config-bound settings shape as EmailConfirmationSettings; no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: SectionName (TwoFactorSettings.cs:18) is "Authentication:TwoFactor". Issuer (line 26) defaults to "MMCA" and labels the account in the authenticator app; its summary (lines 20-23) says a host sets its own application name there. Digits (line 30) defaults to 6. PeriodSeconds (line 34) defaults to 30. VerificationWindowSteps (line 46) defaults to 1, and its remarks (lines 40-44) explain the trade-off: one step widens acceptance to roughly ninety seconds to tolerate clock skew, while a larger window multiplies how many codes are live at once for an attacker guessing. RecoveryCodeCount (line 50) defaults to 10. RecoveryCodeByteLength (line 57) defaults to 10 bytes (eighty bits). SecretByteLength (line 61) defaults to 20 bytes, the RFC 4226 recommendation.
    • Why it's built this way: every size and window is a documented security/usability trade-off rather than an arbitrary constant, per ADR-116.
    • Where it's used: bound and validated by AddTwoFactorAuthentication(configuration) (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:49-50), read by TotpTwoFactorService and TwoFactorAuthenticator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/).

    ViewAsSettings

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsSettings.cs:34 · Level 0 · class

    • What it is: the options class bound to the ViewAs section that switches read-only view-as support access on and decides which host owns the grant table, how long grant rows are kept, and which data source holds them.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations ([Range], [Required]).
    • Concept: the same config-bound, startup-validated settings shape as TwoFactorSettings (ADR-070). The feature it configures, a staff user seeing the app as one account sees it through a short-lived read-only token, is described by ADR-137 and walked through at ViewAsService.
    • Walkthrough: SectionName (ViewAsSettings.cs:37) is "ViewAs". Enabled (line 40) defaults to false; the class remarks (lines 10-15) list what "off" means: the grant and end endpoints answer 404, the always-present guard middleware refuses any view-as token with 401, the grant table is in no model (so no migration appears), and sign-in history shows no view-as rows. Lines 17-20 list what a host that turns it on must also do: register an IViewAsSubjectResolver, grant users:view-as to its staff role, add the ViewAsGrants migration on the Identity database, and disclose staff access in its privacy notice. HostsGrantStore (line 49) defaults to true; in a multi-service host only the Identity service keeps it, and the others set it false and learn that a grant ended from a marker in the shared ICacheService (remarks lines 23-31, which also state that a service unable to read that cache refuses view-as requests, failing closed). RetentionDays (line 56, [Range(1, 3650)] at line 55) defaults to 90, matching the field-level audit trail's retention. DataSourceName (line 63) defaults to "Default".
    • Why it's built this way: off by default with no table mapped means a host that never opts in carries neither the endpoints nor the schema, and the explicit HostsGrantStore split keeps the grant table in one database per ADR-137.
    • Where it's used: bound in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:193-194, read by ViewAsService (the retention sweep), EFViewAsGrantStore, ApplicationDbContext, DesignTimeDbContextHelper, and the AuthControllerBase, UsersAdminControllerBase and ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase controllers in MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/.

    ViewAsSubject

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsSubject.cs:15 · Level 0 · record

    • What it is: the facts about one account that a view-as token is minted from, plus the two flags that make an account unviewable.
    • Depends on: UserIdentifierType; the [Pii] attribute on its personal fields.
    • Concept: a small app-supplied read model that lets Common stay ignorant of the consumer's user entity; the consumer fills it through IViewAsSubjectResolver.
    • Walkthrough: positional members UserId, Email, Role, FullName, IsDeleted (ViewAsSubject.cs:16-20), with Email (line 17) and FullName (line 19) marked [property: Pii]. IsServiceAccount (line 27) flags the service account behind a machine client (ADR-140), which has no person to support. IsLocked (line 34) flags a locked account: a lock writes the soft-deleted-user marker (ADR-047), so every host would refuse the token on its first call. Both are init properties that default to false.
    • Why it's built this way: carrying the refusal facts on the subject lets ViewAsService decide every refusal in one place before any grant row is written.
    • Where it's used: returned by IViewAsSubjectResolver.FindAsync, consumed by ViewAsService (the refusal checks and the token claims), built in ADC by MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/ViewAsSubjectResolver.cs.

    ITwoFactorService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorService.cs:16 · Level 1 · interface

    • What it is: the TOTP/authenticator-app abstraction: mints secrets, builds the provisioning URI, verifies codes, and generates/hashes/matches recovery codes.
    • Depends on: RecoveryCodeSet (return type of GenerateRecoveryCodes).
    • Concept introduced: a service interface that isolates the cryptographic mechanics of TOTP (RFC 6238-style time-based codes) from the account-state orchestration that lives in ITwoFactorAuthenticator. [Rubric §1, SOLID] (assesses single-responsibility separation): this interface only knows about codes and secrets, never about a user account or a store.
    • Walkthrough: GenerateSecret() (ITwoFactorService.cs:22) mints a fresh Base32 secret. BuildProvisioningUri(secret, accountName) (line 37) builds the otpauth://totp/... URI an authenticator app scans as a QR code; it is deliberately returned as string rather than System.Uri (the [SuppressMessage] at lines 33-36 explains that round-tripping through Uri would re-normalize the percent-encoding the app parses). VerifyCode(secret, code) (line 46) checks a code within the configured number of time steps on each side of the current one. The overload VerifyCode(secret, code, out matchedStep) (line 59) verifies exactly the same way and also reports which time step matched (Unix seconds divided by the period, or 0 when nothing matched), so a caller that keeps per-account state can refuse a replay of a code it already accepted inside the same window. GenerateRecoveryCodes() (line 66) returns a fresh RecoveryCodeSet. HashRecoveryCode(code) (line 74) hashes one plaintext code the way the store keeps it. TryMatchRecoveryCode(code, storedHashes, out matchedHash) (line 83) compares in fixed time to avoid a timing side-channel on which stored hash matched.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping code verification, secret generation, and recovery-code hashing behind one narrow interface means ITwoFactorAuthenticator and the handler bases never touch a raw cryptographic primitive directly. Replay protection stays out of this interface too: the service only reports the matched step, and the stateful "accept each step once" rule lives in the caller.
    • Where it's used: implemented by TotpTwoFactorService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:59 for the step-reporting overload), consumed by the enrollment/regeneration handler bases in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/ and by TwoFactorAuthenticator, which calls the step-reporting overload (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:81) and then rejects any step at or below the last one it cached for that user (TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:198). Registered as a singleton in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:55.

    IViewAsSubjectResolver

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/IViewAsSubjectResolver.cs:8 · Level 1 · interface

    • What it is: the one-method extension point through which the consuming app reads an account's ViewAsSubject.
    • Depends on: ViewAsSubject, UserIdentifierType.
    • Concept: a consumer-implemented port: Common owns the view-as workflow, the app owns its user table.
    • Walkthrough: FindAsync(userId, cancellationToken) (IViewAsSubjectResolver.cs:14) returns the subject, or null when no such account exists.
    • Why it's built this way: Common does not register an implementation (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:192 says the account reader is the consumer's), and ViewAsService takes it as an optional constructor argument, so an enabled host that forgot it gets a ViewAs.NotConfigured failure rather than a DI error.
    • Where it's used: called by ViewAsService.StartAsync; implemented in ADC by ViewAsSubjectResolver (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/Administration/ViewAsSubjectResolver.cs:24) and registered in that module's DependencyInjection.cs.

    TwoFactorErrors

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorErrors.cs:15 · Level 2 · class

    • What it is: the static Error-factory class for the two-factor flow: challenge-required, challenge-invalid, not-enrolled, enrollment-missing, and recent-sign-in-required.
    • Depends on: Error.
    • Concept: same convention as EmailConfirmationErrors; no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: five codes (TwoFactorErrors.cs:18,21,24,27,33). TwoFactorRequired(source) (lines 38-41) is Error.Unauthorized, asking the caller to supply a code or a recovery code. TwoFactorInvalid(source) (lines 51-54) is also Error.Unauthorized; its remarks (lines 46-50) note it is deliberately the same message for a wrong TOTP code and a wrong recovery code, since telling them apart would leak whether a presented value was recovery-code shaped. TwoFactorNotEnrolled(source) (lines 59-62) and TwoFactorEnrollmentMissing(source) (lines 67-70) are both Error.Conflict, for an action attempted on an account with no active factor and on an enrollment that was never started, respectively. RecentSignInRequired(source) (lines 80-83) is Error.Forbidden with code Authentication.TwoFactorRecentSignInRequired (line 33): starting or confirming enrollment from a session whose interactive sign-in (auth_time) is older than the recent-sign-in window. Its remarks (lines 75-79) explain that enrollment adds a way into the account, so it asks for the same recent sign-in as registering a passkey, and that a refresh never renews auth_time, so only a new sign-in clears it.
    • Why it's built this way: Conflict versus Unauthorized is used to distinguish "your account state does not support this action" from "your credentials did not verify", and Forbidden marks "you are signed in, but not recently enough for this", matching the semantics the rest of the auth surface uses for those error kinds.
    • Where it's used: raised by ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs, DisableTwoFactorHandlerBase.cs and RegenerateRecoveryCodesHandlerBase.cs (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/), by TwoFactorAuthenticator and AuthenticationServiceBase.cs; RecentSignInRequired is raised by TwoFactorControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/TwoFactor/TwoFactorControllerBase.cs:136,170). Asserted in TwoFactorHandlerBaseTests.cs, TwoFactorAuthenticatorTests.cs, TwoFactorControllerBaseTests.cs and AuthErrorCodesAlignmentTests.cs.

    ITwoFactorAuthenticator

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:24 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the account-level orchestration for the second-factor challenge at sign-in, one level above ITwoFactorService's pure cryptographic operations.
    • Depends on: UserIdentifierType, TwoFactorOutcome, TwoFactorErrors, Result<T>.
    • Concept: the service-orchestrates-over-a-crypto-primitive layering also seen with IEmailConfirmationTokenService versus its store; no new concept.
    • Walkthrough: ChallengeAsync(userId, code, cancellationToken) (ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:40-43) returns TwoFactorOutcome.NotEnrolled when the account has no active second factor (sign-in continues unchanged, no mfa claim), the verified outcome when a code satisfies the challenge, or a failure: TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorRequiredCode when a code was needed and none arrived, TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalidCode when one arrived and did not verify (doc comment lines 32-39).
    • Why it's built this way: returning an outcome enum rather than a bare boolean lets AuthenticationServiceBase distinguish "no second factor configured" from "verified", which matters for whether it stamps an mfa claim on the issued token.
    • Enrollment confirmation: VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync(userId, secret, code, cancellationToken) (ITwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:65-69) returns a plain bool and verifies a code against the account's PENDING secret under the same single-use time-step guard as ChallengeAsync (doc comment lines 45-64). The secret it receives (param doc lines 57-61) is the pending secret as ITwoFactorStore holds it, in the protected form ITwoFactorSecretProtector.Protect produced; the shipped implementation unprotects it before verifying. ChallengeAsync answers TwoFactorOutcome.NotEnrolled until the factor is active, so the confirm step cannot use it. There is deliberately no recovery-code fallback, because confirming must prove the authenticator app holds the secret. The accepted step is remembered, so the code that confirmed enrollment cannot be replayed against the first challenge inside its window. Implemented at TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:90.
    • Where it's used: implemented by TwoFactorAuthenticator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs), called from AuthenticationServiceBase.cs (2 sites), from ConfirmTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs:83 (VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync), and by the disable and recovery-code regeneration handler bases, and registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs.

    ITwoFactorSecretProtector

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:13 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: protects an account's two-factor shared secret at rest, so the app's ITwoFactorStore only ever holds the protected form.
    • Depends on: Result<T>.
    • Concept: encryption at rest behind a two-method port. Per the interface summary (ITwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:5-12), the enrollment workflow protects the freshly minted secret before it reaches the store, and the shipped ITwoFactorAuthenticator unprotects the stored value when it verifies a code.
    • Walkthrough: Protect(secret) (line 18) turns the plaintext Base32 secret into its stored form. Unprotect(protectedSecret) (line 23) returns Result<string> and never throws: a failure means this host's key ring cannot read the value.
    • Why it's built this way: a database leak alone then yields no usable TOTP secret. The default uses the host's data-protection key ring (summary lines 9-10), so a multi-replica host needs a shared key ring, and the Result return turns a key-ring mismatch into a handled failure instead of an exception in the sign-in path.
    • Where it's used: implemented by DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:15) and registered as a singleton in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:59; called by BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs (protect) and TwoFactorAuthenticator (unprotect); exercised end to end in TwoFactorSecretProtectionEndToEndTests.cs.

    ITwoFactorStore

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorStore.cs:24 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the persistence abstraction for one account's two-factor state: enrollment lifecycle, recovery-code replacement, and single recovery-code consumption.
    • Depends on: UserIdentifierType, ITwoFactorUserState (the read shape, taught elsewhere in this group), Result.
    • Concept: a two-phase enrollment (start, then complete) so an abandoned setup cannot lock an account out; the same two-phase shape a reader has already seen in other enrollment-style flows in this group.
    • Walkthrough: GetAsync(userId, cancellationToken) (ITwoFactorStore.cs:34) returns null only when the account itself does not exist; an account that never enrolled still returns a state with IsTwoFactorEnabled = false. StartEnrollmentAsync(userId, secret, cancellationToken) (line 47) stores a freshly minted secret WITHOUT activating the factor, per its summary (lines 36-39), so an abandoned enrollment cannot lock the user out. The secret (param doc lines 41-44) arrives already in its protected form (ITwoFactorSecretProtector); the store keeps it as given and returns it unchanged from GetAsync. CompleteEnrollmentAsync(userId, recoveryCodeHashes, cancellationToken) (lines 57-60) activates the factor and stores the first recovery-code hashes, called only after a code from the stored secret has verified. DisableAsync(userId, cancellationToken) (line 69) turns the factor off and clears the secret and recovery codes, so a later re-enrollment starts from a fresh secret. ReplaceRecoveryCodesAsync(userId, recoveryCodeHashes, cancellationToken) (lines 79-82) replaces the whole set, never appends, since regeneration exists to invalidate a list the user believes compromised. ConsumeRecoveryCodeAsync(userId, recoveryCodeHash, cancellationToken) (lines 96-99) removes one hash to spend it, and its remarks (lines 87-91) flag this as security-critical: it must persist before the sign-in it authorized is answered, or the same code could sign in twice.
    • Why it's built this way: splitting StartEnrollmentAsync/CompleteEnrollmentAsync prevents a half-finished enrollment from ever becoming an active, un-verified second factor.
    • Where it's used: implemented by the consuming app, not by Common: AddTwoFactorAuthentication deliberately registers no ITwoFactorStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:31), and registering one alongside that call arms the sign-in challenge (line 37). Called by TwoFactorAuthenticator, by the enrollment/disable/regenerate handler bases in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/, and by TwoFactorControllerBase and UsersAdminControllerBase in MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/.

    IViewAsService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/IViewAsService.cs:10 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the view-as workflow contract: start a grant and mint its token, end a grant, and check whether a token's grant is still live.
    • Depends on: ViewAsGrantResponse, UserIdentifierType, Result.
    • Concept: read-only support access (ADR-137): a staff user gets a short-lived token whose sub is the viewed account, while the act_sub and vag claims name the staff user and the grant row behind it.
    • Walkthrough: StartAsync(staffUserId, targetUserId, reason, cancellationToken) (IViewAsService.cs:22-26) grants and mints; its summary (lines 12-16) lists the refusals (the caller themselves, a missing or soft-deleted account, an account that itself holds users:view-as) and the reason must be 10 to 500 characters. EndAsync(grantId, staffUserId, cancellationToken) (line 33) ends the staff user's grant so its token is refused on the next request, answering not found when the staff user holds no such grant. IsGrantActiveAsync(grantId, staffUserId, targetUserId, cancellationToken) (lines 44-48) is true while the grant exists, names this staff user and this account, was not ended, and has not expired.
    • Why it's built this way: every view-as request is re-checked against the grant row, so ending a grant takes effect immediately rather than when the token expires.
    • Where it's used: implemented by ViewAsService, registered in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:198; IsGrantActiveAsync is called per request by ViewAsGuardMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:137), and the start and end endpoints live on UsersAdminControllerBase and AuthControllerBase.

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/IViewAsGrantStore.cs:11 · Level 4 · interface

    • What it is: the persistence port for ViewAsGrant rows, the audit record of every staff view.
    • Depends on: ViewAsGrant, ViewAsGrantListRequest, UserIdentifierType.
    • Concept: a purpose-built store interface rather than the generic repository, because the grant table is mapped only on the host that holds it (see ViewAsSettings).
    • Walkthrough: AddAsync(grant, ...) (IViewAsGrantStore.cs:17) inserts and saves. FindAsync(grantId, ...) (line 23) reads one row by the token's vag id. EndAsync(grantId, staffUserId, endedAt, ...) (line 34) puts the staff user in the lookup so one staff user cannot end another's grant, and returns true when the grant was found, ended now or before. GetRecentForTargetAsync(targetUserId, maxCount, ...) (lines 41-44) returns the newest grants on one account. DeleteIssuedBeforeAsync(cutoff, ...) (line 50) is the retention sweep and returns the row count. ListAsync(request, now, ...) (lines 62-65) pages the whole support access log newest first; its summary (lines 52-57) notes the status filter is evaluated at now, email filters compare case-insensitively against the display snapshots, and the page size is clamped to ViewAsGrantListRequest.MaxPageSize. ForgetUserAsync(userId, ...) (line 76) is the account-erasure step that blanks the display snapshot on every grant naming the account and, per lines 67-72, saves nothing itself: the erasure's own unit-of-work save persists it.

    • Where it's used: implemented by EFViewAsGrantStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Persistence/Auth/EFViewAsGrantStore.cs:36, registered at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:197) and the test double InMemoryViewAsGrantStore (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing/Support/InMemoryViewAsGrantStore.cs:13). Called by ViewAsService, SignInHistory (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/SignInHistory.cs:55), DeleteUserHandlerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/DeleteUser/DeleteUserHandlerBase.cs:187) and ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase.cs:76).

    • Concept: one filter definition shared by the EF store and the in-memory test double, so the two cannot drift.

ByEmail (line 34) folds each needle with ViewAsGrant.NormalizeDisplay and applies a contains match against StaffDisplay and TargetDisplay. ByWindow (line 49) keeps GrantedAt >= From and GrantedAt < To (inclusive start, exclusive end). ByStatus (line 64) derives Live (not ended, ExpiresAt > now), Ended (EndedAt set) and Expired (not ended, ExpiresAt <= now) at lines 67-69, mirroring ViewAsGrant.StatusAt; no status means no filter.

    ViewAsService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Auth.ViewAs · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsService.cs:42 · Level 9 · class

    • What it is: the shipped IViewAsService: validates and audits a view-as grant, mints its token, ends it, and answers the per-request liveness check.
    • Depends on: IViewAsGrantStore, ITokenService, IPermissionRegistry, ViewAsSettings, TimeProvider, and the optional IViewAsSubjectResolver and ICurrentUserService (ViewAsService.cs:43-49).
    • Concept introduced: impersonation without identity theft. The minted token is an ordinary access token for the viewed account plus two claims, AuthClaimTypes.ViewAsActor and ViewAsGrant (lines 104-108); the command pipeline's ViewAs decorator and the guard middleware use them to keep the session read-only and tied to a live grant (ADR-137). [Rubric §11, Security] (assesses how the design limits and audits privileged access): every view is bounded in time, written to an audit row before a token exists, and refused for accounts that would give lateral or machine access.
    • Walkthrough: Lifetime (lines 55-58) is the configured access-token lifetime when it is positive and below ViewAsGrant.MaxLifetime, otherwise MaxLifetime (the summary says 15 minutes), so a view never outlives an ordinary sign-in token. StartAsync (line 66) first validates self-view and the reason through ViewAsGrant.Create (line 76), returns ViewAs.NotConfigured when no resolver is registered (lines 82-87), then reads the subject (line 89) and runs Refuse (line 90). It rebuilds the grant with the display snapshots (line 99: the staff email from StaffEmail, the viewed email from the subject), sweeps rows older than RetentionDays (line 101) and adds the grant (line 102) BEFORE minting the token with GenerateShortLivedAccessToken (lines 109-115). EndAsync (line 121) answers ViewAs.GrantNotFound when the store found nothing (line 128). IsGrantActiveAsync (line 132) requires the row to exist, match both user ids and be active at now (lines 140-143). StaffEmail (line 153) reads the email claim (mapped ClaimTypes.Email, then raw email, line 161) only when the current user IS the staff user (line 155). Refuse (line 165) answers in order: not found (line 169), deleted (lines 172-174), service account per ADR-140 (lines 178-180), locked (lines 187-189), and an account whose role holds AdministrationPermissions.ViewAsUsers (lines 193-194), so there is no lateral access.
    • Why it's built this way: the remarks (lines 61-65) state the two ordering choices: the row is written before the token so no token exists without its audit record, and the retention sweep rides on grants (which are rare) instead of a hosted service in every process.
    • Where it's used: registered scoped in MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.cs:198; tested in MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsServiceTests.cs, ViewAsTokenTests.cs and ViewAsGuardMiddlewareTests.cs.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the exact value of ViewAsGrant.MaxLifetime is stated here from the summary at lines 51-54, not re-read from ViewAsGrant.

    IPasswordHasher

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces.Infrastructure.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Auth/IPasswordHasher.cs:6 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the password-security port. Two required methods: hash a plaintext password into a separated (byte[] Hash, byte[] Salt) pair, and verify a plaintext against a stored hash plus salt. Two defaulted members follow: NeedsRehash lets the caller ask whether a hash that has just verified was derived with older parameters, and BurnVerificationCost spends one throwaway derivation on a sign-in branch that never reaches a real verification.
    • Depends on: nothing first-party, BCL only (byte[]). Its Infrastructure adapter is PasswordHasher.
    • Concept introduced: hash and salt kept apart. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses credential handling. Returning the hash and the salt as two distinct byte[] members (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Auth/IPasswordHasher.cs:11) rather than one concatenated blob keeps the storage contract explicit: the caller persists two columns, and VerifyPassword (:18) is unambiguous about what it re-derives and compares. Because the algorithm and its parameters live entirely behind this interface, they can be strengthened without touching a single Application handler (ADR-032 sets the current hashing policy, applied inside PasswordHasher).
    • Walkthrough: (byte[] Hash, byte[] Salt) HashPassword(string password) (:11) returns a named value tuple the caller stores as two fields. bool VerifyPassword(string password, byte[] hash, byte[] salt) (:18) re-derives from the supplied salt and compares. bool NeedsRehash(byte[] hash) => false (:28) is a default interface method: it answers whether the stored hash was derived with a format or work factor other than the one HashPassword uses now, and the false default keeps a custom hasher compiling without ever triggering a rehash. void BurnVerificationCost(string password) => _ = HashPassword(password) (:39) is the second default member, and its doc comment (:30-37) names the attack it closes: an unknown address or an account with no password never reaches VerifyPassword, so without a burn those branches would answer measurably faster than a wrong password. The burn must cost what verifying the most expensive stored record costs, so a hasher that still verifies records derived at an older, higher work factor overrides it to burn at that factor; the default (one HashPassword, discarded) is right only for a hasher whose every record uses its current parameters. [Rubric §11, Security] applies directly: this is user-enumeration resistance by timing, expressed as a contract member rather than left to each caller. The interface still declares no iteration count, algorithm identifier, or format version: the concrete decides what "current" means (PasswordHasher overrides NeedsRehash at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/PasswordHasher.cs:127; ADR-133 records the versioned work factor).
    • Why it's built this way: a small port is the [Rubric §1, SOLID] dependency-inversion story in miniature. Swapping the key-derivation function or raising the iteration count is an Infrastructure change, invisible to the register, login, and change-password use cases that only ever see this contract. NeedsRehash closes the loop on such a change: existing records upgrade on their next successful sign-in, while the verified plaintext is still in hand, instead of staying on the old parameters forever.
    • Where it's used: a primary-constructor dependency of AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>, which calls VerifyPassword on the login path (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:212), HashPassword on registration (:335), BurnVerificationCost on the branches that have no credential to verify (:965), and, after tokens are issued, NeedsRehash then HashPassword in its best-effort rehash step (:1016 and :1021) when the app's User implements IPasswordRehashableUser; into the shared ChangePasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>, which verifies the current password (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ChangePassword/ChangePasswordHandlerBase.cs:108) before hashing the new one (:118); into ResetPasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand>, which hashes the replacement after the token redeems (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/ResetPassword/ResetPasswordHandlerBase.cs:110); and into the per-app Identity services, handlers and seeders that derive from those, for example ADC's AuthenticationService (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs:54), its ChangePasswordHandler (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/UseCases/ChangePassword/ChangePasswordHandler.cs:26) and its module seeder (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.API/IdentityModuleSeeder.cs:34, which needs the hasher because seed data carries plaintext credentials).

    ISoftDeletedUserValidator

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces.Infrastructure.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Auth/ISoftDeletedUserValidator.cs:7 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: a single-method port that answers "has this account been soft-deleted?", called after JWT authentication to reject a soft-deleted user who still holds a valid, unexpired token (BR-133, named in the type comment at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Auth/ISoftDeletedUserValidator.cs:4).
    • Depends on: BCL plus the solution-wide UserIdentifierType alias (:15). See primer §2 for the alias convention and ADR-005 for soft-delete versus erasure. The generic implementation is SoftDeletedUserValidator<TUser>.
    • Concept introduced: closing the stateless-token window. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether revocation is timely. A JWT is stateless: once signed it stays valid until exp, even if the account behind it was deleted a minute later. This port lets middleware re-ask the question on every authenticated request and fail the request when the answer is yes, with no per-handler code. The comment at :5 states the second motive: the interface is declared in Application and implemented against the app's own User aggregate precisely so the middleware never takes a cross-module domain reference. That is the same dependency inversion as the other ports in this group, applied to a cross-module read.
    • Walkthrough: one member, Task<bool> IsUserSoftDeletedAsync(UserIdentifierType userId, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default) (:15). One question, one answer, cancellable.
    • Where it's used: SoftDeletedUserMiddleware resolves it lazily from the request scope (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/SoftDeletedUserMiddleware.cs:117 calls context.RequestServices.GetService<ISoftDeletedUserValidator>(), so a host that registers no implementation simply skips the check; the reason is stated at :43) and queries it on a cache miss (:113-115). Both apps register the shared generic against their own user type: MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:43 and MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:43, both as TryAddScoped<ISoftDeletedUserValidator, SoftDeletedUserValidator<User>>().

    ITokenService

    MMCA.Common.Application · MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces.Infrastructure.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Auth/ITokenService.cs:8 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the token-minting port called by the login and refresh use cases. It builds a signed JWT access token from explicit identity facts (with a short-lived variant whose lifetime the caller chooses), generates an opaque refresh token, publishes the two token lifetimes, and recovers the ClaimsPrincipal from an expired-but-validly-signed access token.
    • Depends on: System.Security.Claims (BCL, :1) and the UserIdentifierType alias. Its Infrastructure adapter is TokenService, which signs with the RSA key surfaced by IJwksProvider; SessionStampingTokenService is a second, internal implementation that decorates the first.
    • Concept introduced: token creation as an Infrastructure detail. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses whether library-specific types stay out of the inner layers: the handlers call this contract and never see System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt. GetPrincipalFromExpiredToken (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/Auth/ITokenService.cs:75) is the linchpin of the refresh flow: it validates the signature while deliberately ignoring lifetime, so an expired access token can still identify the user whose tokens are being rotated, returning null when the token is invalid (:74).
    • Walkthrough: GenerateAccessToken(UserIdentifierType userId, string email, string role, string fullName, IEnumerable<Claim>? additionalClaims = null) (:17-22) takes the minimum claim set as typed parameters rather than a ready-made principal, with an escape hatch for module-specific claims. GenerateShortLivedAccessToken(..., IEnumerable<Claim>? additionalClaims, TimeSpan lifetime) (:42-49) is the same mint with an explicit expiry, written for the read-only view-as token, which must never outlive its 15-minute grant (ADR-137, summary at :24-28). It is a default interface member that forwards to GenerateAccessToken and ignores lifetime, so a hand-written token service keeps compiling; the remarks (:29-34) explain why that default is still safe: the view-as guard checks the grant's own expiry on every request, so a longer-lived token is refused once its grant (ViewAsGrant) expires. GenerateRefreshToken() (:53) returns a cryptographically random base64 string. Two more default members publish the lifetimes: AccessTokenLifetime (:60, defaulting to 15 minutes) and RefreshTokenLifetime (:67, defaulting to 7 days), both documented as the BR-205 baseline. The comments at :55-59 and :62-66 explain the split: the real implementation derives both from the bound JWT settings, so the expiry reported to a client matches the token's actual exp, while the defaults keep hand-written test doubles on the baseline instead of forcing every double to implement two more members. That derivation is visible in the concrete: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(_jwtSettings.AccessTokenExpirationMinutes) and TimeSpan.FromDays(_jwtSettings.RefreshTokenExpirationDays) (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TokenService.cs:192 and :129). GetPrincipalFromExpiredToken(string token) (:75) closes the set.
    • Why it's built this way: the explicit-parameter overload is a [Rubric §11, Security] guardrail. The token's contents are a deliberate list, not whatever claims happened to ride in on an inbound principal. Surfacing the lifetimes through the same port removes the duplication where a caller would hard-code an expiry that could drift from the signed exp. Adding GenerateShortLivedAccessToken as a defaulted member rather than a required one follows the same rule as the lifetimes: a new capability on a shared port must not break the hand-written implementations and doubles consumers already have.
    • Where it's used: AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> reads the expired principal on refresh (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:415) through its TokenService property, which exposes a wrapped instance to subclasses. AuthSessionIssuer mints the refresh token when it opens a session (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:476) and when it rotates one (:520), and its wrapping implementation forwards GenerateRefreshToken and GetPrincipalFromExpiredToken to the inner service (:796-800). The short-lived mint has two callers: ViewAsService for the view-as token (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsService.cs:109, its lifetime capped at ViewAsGrant.MaxLifetime, :56-58) and MachineClientService for the client-credentials token (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:109, ADR-140). Each app's Identity service mints access tokens from the base's TokenService property, for example MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Application/Users/AuthenticationService.cs (access token plus the speaker_id claim). The rotated pair produced here is what CookieSessionRefresher later exchanges on the browser's behalf.

    ITwoFactorUserState

    MMCA.Common.Domain · MMCA.Common.Domain.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/ITwoFactorUserState.cs:27 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the two-factor enrollment surface an Identity module's User aggregate exposes: whether the second factor is active, the shared secret the codes are derived from (in protected form), and the hashes of the account's unspent recovery codes (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/ITwoFactorUserState.cs:29-43).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party beyond the BCL IReadOnlyCollection<string> (:1).
    • Concept introduced: two-factor state read through a capability interface, not the concrete User. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses interface segregation: a shared handler that needs to know whether TOTP is enrolled never needs the rest of the app's User shape, so it depends on this narrow contract instead. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the shape of the stored secret itself: TwoFactorSecret (:37) is nullable, meaning "no enrollment started" is representable without a sentinel value, and it is never the plaintext Base32 key: it holds the protected form the framework handed the store (:32-36), so a read of the users table does not yield a working authenticator seed. TwoFactorRecoveryCodeHashes (:43) likewise holds hashes, not the plaintext codes a user was shown once at generation time.
    • Walkthrough: bool IsTwoFactorEnabled (:30) gates whether a code is demanded at sign-in. string? TwoFactorSecret (:37) is the protected shared secret, null until enrollment begins; the protection is applied by ITwoFactorSecretProtector before the secret reaches the store (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs:28, :44; the store contract repeats it at MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorStore.cs:42). IReadOnlyCollection<string> TwoFactorRecoveryCodeHashes (:43) is empty both before enrollment and after every recovery code has been spent, which the doc comment (:40-41) states is a state the user recovers from by regenerating rather than an error condition.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping this state on its own interface, separate from IAuthUser and IPasswordChangeableUser, lets an app opt into two-factor without every existing User aggregate needing new members it never populates. See ADR-116 for the opt-in model this interface belongs to.
    • Where it's used: the generic constraint on BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase<TCommand> (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Users/UseCases/TwoFactor/BeginTwoFactorEnrollmentHandlerBase.cs:65, :80, where a missing state is reported as NotFound targeting this interface), and it is the state ITwoFactorStore returns from GetAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/TwoFactor/ITwoFactorStore.cs:34) against the concrete User. MMCA.Store's User lists it among its capability interfaces (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Domain/Users/User.cs:30), and AuditTrailSaveChangesInterceptor reads it to redact the two-factor material from audit rows.

    IAuthUser

    MMCA.Common.Domain · MMCA.Common.Domain.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/IAuthUser.cs:15 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the deliberately minimal credential surface an Identity module's User aggregate exposes to the shared AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> workflow. Two properties of password material, plus one defaulted flag that marks a machine client's service account. It is the contract that lets the framework's authentication plumbing verify and replace a password without knowing anything app-specific about the user (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/IAuthUser.cs:3-8).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; the BCL only (byte[]). Implemented transitively through IPasswordChangeableUser by each app's User aggregate (see User).
    • Concept introduced: the inverted user contract. Rather than the shared auth workflow depending on a concrete User class, User implements a small interface the framework owns. Profile fields, roles, linked aggregates, and claim sources stay app-specific: the shared workflow reaches those only through per-app hooks (CreateAccessToken, CreateUser), never through this contract (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/IAuthUser.cs:6-8). [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses interface segregation and dependency inversion, and this is a textbook case: the interface is exactly the credential surface and nothing more. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses credential handling, and the whole security-relevant surface of a User aggregate is readable in a dozen lines.
    • Concept: what the contract deliberately leaves out. The <para> block (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/IAuthUser.cs:9-13) records what is deliberately absent: refresh tokens. They are rows in RefreshSession, one per signed-in device, hashed at rest and reached through IRefreshSessionStore, so no usable bearer credential sits in the users table and this interface covers passwords only (ADR-097). [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] applies: documenting an absence on the contract itself stops a later change from "helpfully" putting a token column back on the user.
    • Walkthrough: three members, all read-only.
      • byte[] PasswordHash (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/IAuthUser.cs:19), the PBKDF2 hash produced by IPasswordHasher, documented as either the versioned shape or the header-less legacy shape (:18, ADR-032, ADR-133).
      • byte[] PasswordSalt (:22), the salt paired with it.
      • Both sit inside a scoped #pragma warning disable CA1819 (:17, restored on :23) that knowingly returns arrays, to mirror IPasswordHasher's byte[] tuple and the EF-mapped varbinary columns rather than force a defensive copy on every read. The suppression's justification is written on the disable line itself, which is the convention this codebase uses everywhere it takes an analyzer exception.
      • bool IsServiceAccount => false (:32) is a default interface member marking the service account behind a machine client rather than a person (ADR-140). Its doc comment (:25-31) states the policy: such an account obtains tokens only through the client-credentials grant, so password sign-in, sign-in links, external login and passkeys refuse it, and it can never be viewed as. The false default means an app that has not adopted machine clients implements nothing.
      • There is no mutator. Writing new material is the separate capability IPasswordChangeableUser adds, so an aggregate that only ever authenticates never exposes a way to change its own password.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the contract in Domain and keeping it small is what makes the shared auth workflow reusable across Store and ADC (both User aggregates satisfy it) while each aggregate stays free to model everything else its own way. See ADR-032 for the password-material policy, ADR-004 for the dual-fetch auth model this contract feeds, and ADR-097 for the refresh-token move.
    • Where it's used: it is half the generic constraint on the shared login and registration workflow, where TUser : AuditableAggregateRootEntity<UserIdentifierType>, IAuthUser (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:82), which passes both password properties to VerifyPassword on the login path (:212) and refuses a service account on its sign-in branches (:566, :612, :942). It is also the base of IPasswordChangeableUser, and the shape hand-written test doubles copy. ADC's User overrides the flag with a stored IsServiceAccount { get; private set; } (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/User.cs:145, set to true only when a service account is provisioned, :373), and ViewAsService refuses to view one (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsService.cs:178-180, ViewAs.TargetIsServiceAccount).

    IPasswordChangeableUser

    MMCA.Common.Domain · MMCA.Common.Domain.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/IPasswordChangeableUser.cs:11 · Level 3 · interface

    • What it is: the password-rotation surface an Identity module's User aggregate exposes to the shared ChangePasswordHandlerBase<TUser, TCommand> workflow. It is one method on top of IAuthUser (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/IPasswordChangeableUser.cs:5-9).
    • Depends on: IAuthUser (its base interface, :11) and Result from MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions (:1).
    • Concept: capability interfaces layered by workflow. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses interface segregation, and this is the pattern applied twice over: a User that only ever authenticates satisfies IAuthUser; a User whose app offers self-service password change implements this one and gets PasswordHash and PasswordSalt along with it, because the workflow must verify the current credential before writing the new one (the XML comment states exactly this reason, :7-9). Inheritance here encodes a real dependency between capabilities rather than a taxonomy. [Rubric §4, DDD] also applies: the method returns Result, so the aggregate can refuse the change (an invariant failure) instead of the handler assuming success.
    • Walkthrough: one member, Result ChangePassword(byte[] newPasswordHash, byte[] newPasswordSalt) (:19). The aggregate receives already-hashed material, never a plaintext password: hashing is the handler's job via IPasswordHasher, so no plaintext ever reaches the Domain layer or an EF change tracker.
