    AuthClaimTypes

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/AuthClaimTypes.cs:9 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: the claim-type name constants the framework's own token vocabulary rests on, sitting alongside the standard System.Security.Claims.ClaimTypes values (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/AuthClaimTypes.cs:5-9).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party at runtime. Its doc comments point at IPermissionRegistry for the role-derived half of the permission model (AuthClaimTypes.cs:14) and at the ClaimsPrincipalExtensions readers FindUserIdValue, HasMultiFactor, HasMultiFactorWithheldRole and IsViewAs (AuthClaimTypes.cs:31,57,86,119).
    • Concept introduced, a claim vocabulary owned by the framework rather than by each reader. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses how authentication and authorization are modeled and which facts a principal is allowed to carry; [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses single points of change. A claim type is just a string, so writer and reader agreeing on it is a convention with no compiler behind it. Putting every name in one const holder is what makes the token issuer and every reader provably agree.
      • Permission (AuthClaimTypes.cs:24, value "permission") carries a single granted capability, honored in addition to the permissions a role confers through IPermissionRegistry (AuthClaimTypes.cs:11-14). The doc comment states that TokenService itself is the emitter (AuthClaimTypes.cs:15-22): every access token it mints carries one Permission claim per permission the role's registry entry grants, sorted ordinally so the same role always produces the same token shape. That is what lets a client decide what to show (a navigation entry gating on a required permission) without knowing any role name, while server-side checks still go through the registry, so a host that mints tokens some other way loses nothing. This makes the model in ADR-020 backward compatible with plain role checks: a token still authorizes correctly if a reader ignores the claim entirely.
      • Subject (AuthClaimTypes.cs:34, value "sub") is the single authoritative carrier of the user identifier in every token the framework mints. The doc comment states the trap that follows (AuthClaimTypes.cs:26-33): one value reaches readers under two different claim types, because the JWT bearer handler maps inbound sub onto ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier while a handler that materializes an identity straight from a token's claims leaves the raw sub in place.
      • SessionId (AuthClaimTypes.cs:47, value "sid") is the RFC 7519 / OpenID Connect session id: the identifier of the refresh session the access token was minted for, which is to say the device behind the token (AuthClaimTypes.cs:36-40). It is additive, never required (AuthClaimTypes.cs:41-45): rotation mints a new session and therefore a new sid, a token issued before the claim shipped simply carries none, and nothing validates it. A missing or unparsable value degrades to "no current session known", never to a rejected token.
      • MultiFactor (AuthClaimTypes.cs:63, value "mfa") is an RFC 8176 (amr)-style claim asserting that the access token was minted after a second authentication factor was presented (AuthClaimTypes.cs:49-62). Presence is the assertion, not the value: readers ask whether the claim exists (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.HasMultiFactor), the value exists for audit and for UI copy such as "you signed in with a recovery code". A token issued for an account with no second factor carries no mfa claim at all, which is why a request marked IRequiresMfa denies such a caller rather than degrading to a role check. The value is one of three method names: MultiFactorMethodTotp (AuthClaimTypes.cs:66, value "otp"), MultiFactorMethodRecoveryCode (AuthClaimTypes.cs:69, value "recovery") and MultiFactorMethodPasskey (AuthClaimTypes.cs:76, value "passkey"). A passkey counts as multi-factor by itself, being possession of the device plus the authenticator's own user verification, and a refresh carries the value over like the other two (AuthClaimTypes.cs:71-75).
      • MultiFactorWithheldRole (AuthClaimTypes.cs:89, value "mfa_withheld_role") and MultiFactorWithheldPermission (AuthClaimTypes.cs:96, value "mfa_withheld_permission") are markers, not grants. The API adds one to a validated bearer principal for each role it withheld because the role is listed under Authorization:MultiFactor:RequiredForRoles and the session carries no mfa claim, and one for each Permission claim it removed with that role and did not keep for a role the principal still holds. The token still carries the role; only the request's principal goes without it. The marker lets a reader tell "signed in, role withheld until a second factor" from "no such role", and it never grants anything (AuthClaimTypes.cs:78-95).
      • AuthTime (AuthClaimTypes.cs:111, value "auth_time") is the OpenID Connect sign-in instant, in Unix seconds, stamped when an interactive sign-in opens a session and carried unchanged across every refresh, so unlike iat it does not move when a refresh mints a new access token; a view-as token carries none (AuthClaimTypes.cs:98-104). It is what "recently signed in" is judged by: registering a passkey requires an auth_time within the last ten minutes (ADR-139), so a stolen refresh token cannot keep a session fresh enough to plant one, and a token without the claim reads as not recent (AuthClaimTypes.cs:105-109).
      • ViewAsActor (AuthClaimTypes.cs:122, value "act_sub") names the staff user behind a view-as token, whose sub is the user being viewed (ADR-137). Presence makes the request read-only: every command is refused and every non-safe HTTP method is rejected while it is present (AuthClaimTypes.cs:113-121). ViewAsGrant (AuthClaimTypes.cs:128, value "vag") is the id of the grant the token was minted for, checked on every view-as request so ending the grant ends the token before it expires (AuthClaimTypes.cs:124-127).
      • ClientId (AuthClaimTypes.cs:134, value "client_id", RFC 9068) names the machine client a token was issued to through the client credentials grant, whose sub is the client's service-account user. TokenUse (AuthClaimTypes.cs:140, value "token_use") is carried only by a machine token, with the value TokenUseMachine (AuthClaimTypes.cs:146, value "machine"); a token without it was issued to a person. A machine token has no refresh token, no sid, no auth_time and no mfa (AuthClaimTypes.cs:130-145, ADR-140).
    • Walkthrough: fifteen public const string fields and nothing else (AuthClaimTypes.cs:24-146). const rather than static readonly so the values are usable in attribute arguments and in patterns that require compile-time constants, the same reason RoleNames uses const.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-020 makes the permission layer opt-in, ADR-097 adds the per-device session identity that sid names, the opt-in two-factor completion (ADR-116) adds mfa and its first two method values, ADR-139 adds the passkey method and auth_time, ADR-137 adds the view-as pair, and ADR-140 adds the machine-client pair. Keeping the claim types as shared constants means the writer and the reader cannot drift apart on a string.
    • Where it's used:
      • Permission is written by TokenService itself, one claim per permission the injected IPermissionRegistry grants the token's role, sorted ordinally and deduplicated against any permission claim the caller already supplied (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TokenService.cs:159-171), and is read by PermissionAuthorizationHandler and the CQRS AuthorizationGate, both through ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.HasPermissionClaim (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:31, MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/AuthorizationGate.cs:48).
      • Subject is written by TokenService as JwtRegisteredClaimNames.Sub (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TokenService.cs:146) and read through ClaimsPrincipalExtensions by CurrentUserService, ClaimBasedUserIdProvider, the IdempotencyFilter, and the rate-limit partitioner.
      • SessionId, MultiFactor and AuthTime are stamped by AuthSessionIssuer (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:776,781,787). The method value comes from AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>, which maps a verified TwoFactorOutcome to otp or recovery and a passkey sign-in to passkey (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:624,899-900). sid is read back by FindSessionId for the "my sessions" endpoint (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:262).
      • The withheld markers are written by MultiFactorRoleWithholding (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleWithholding.cs:87-88) and read by MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:67-69).
      • The view-as pair is written by ViewAsService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsService.cs:106-107) and checked by ViewAsGuardMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:127-128).
      • The machine-client pair is written by MachineClientService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:106-107) and refused by RefuseMachineClientsAttribute (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/RefuseMachineClientsAttribute.cs:44).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the Permission claim is written by every token the framework mints (TokenService.cs:159-171); a reader depending on Permission being absent from real tokens would be wrong. The registry lookup remains the authoritative check either way, since the claim path is additive.

    AuthErrorCodes

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/AuthErrorCodes.cs:12 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: the caller-facing error-code strings for registration, sign-in and the multi-factor gate, held in Shared so a client can branch on a refusal without a reference on Application (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/AuthErrorCodes.cs:12-55).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; consumed as an Error code string. Its doc comment points at AuthClaimTypes.MultiFactor (AuthErrorCodes.cs:29).
    • Concept introduced, one code for every path that means the same thing to the caller. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether a caller-facing contract stays stable across an implementation detail; [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether error contracts are explicit. EmailAlreadyExists is returned by both the up-front existence check and the unique-index race recovery during registration, so the two paths stay indistinguishable to the caller (AuthErrorCodes.cs:14-17), and MultiFactorRequired is returned by both the CQRS gate and the HTTP permission check (AuthErrorCodes.cs:27-34). Several constants mirror codes that Application types also define, and the copies are pinned together by tests rather than by a reference (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Application.Tests/Auth/SignIn/AuthErrorCodesAlignmentTests.cs:16-40): TwoFactorRequired and TwoFactorInvalid must equal TwoFactorErrors's codes, EmailNotConfirmed must equal EmailConfirmationErrors's, and MultiFactorRequired must stay the literal "Authorization.MultiFactorRequired".
    • Walkthrough: six public const string fields.
      • EmailAlreadyExists (AuthErrorCodes.cs:19, "Auth.EmailAlreadyExists"): registration refused because the address already belongs to an account; the registration UI keys its "sign in instead" guidance on it.
      • TermsNotAccepted (:25, "Auth.TermsNotAccepted"): registration refused because the host requires Terms of Service acceptance and the request did not carry it; returned only when a current terms version is configured (:21-24).
      • MultiFactorRequired (:35, "Authorization.MultiFactorRequired"): the operation needs a session that signed in with a second factor and the token carries no mfa claim, either because a use case demands a step-up or because the role is listed under Authorization:MultiFactor:RequiredForRoles. A client sends the user to set up two-factor authentication or to sign in again with a code (:27-34).
      • TwoFactorRequired (:42, "Authentication.TwoFactorRequired"): the account has a second factor and the sign-in carried no code. The password has been proved at that point, so a client prompts for the code and retries the same credentials with it (:37-41).
      • TwoFactorInvalid (:48, "Authentication.TwoFactorInvalid"): the second-factor code did not verify; a client keeps the code step and asks for a new one (:44-47).
      • EmailNotConfirmed (:54, "Authentication.EmailNotConfirmed"): the host requires a confirmed address and the account's is not confirmed; a client offers to resend the link (:50-53).
    • Why it's built this way: a race between the registration pre-check and the database's unique constraint is possible under concurrent attempts, and returning the same code from both paths means the caller-facing behavior does not depend on which path lost. The prefixes follow the producing concern (Auth. for registration, Authentication. for sign-in, Authorization. for the gate), and a client matches on the full string.
    • Where it's used: registration codes are returned by AuthenticationServiceBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs), and TermsNotAccepted is re-exposed as LegalAcceptanceErrors.TermsNotAcceptedCode (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Legal/LegalAcceptanceErrors.cs:14); see LegalAcceptanceErrors. MultiFactorRequired is emitted by AuthorizationGate (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/AuthorizationGate.cs:65), by MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:59) and by MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRefusalResultHandler.cs:66), and detected on the client by AuthDelegatingHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/AuthDelegatingHandler.cs:272). The three sign-in codes map to login-page refusals in LoginRefusals (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Auth/TwoFactor/LoginRefusals.cs:57-59).

    Base32

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/Base32.cs:13 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: RFC 4648 section 6 Base32 over the upper-case A-Z2-7 alphabet, the encoding an authenticator app expects a TOTP secret in (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/Base32.cs:3-6,13).
    • Depends on: BCL only (ReadOnlySpan<byte>, ArgumentException).
    • Concept introduced, owning a small codec instead of taking a package for it. [Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain] assesses whether third-party dependencies earn their place. The codec is under a hundred lines of bit shifting with no external dependency, internal to Infrastructure, so neither the framework's public surface nor its consumers take a package for it. [Rubric §14, Testability] applies too: the Infrastructure tests exercise it through RFC vectors (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpRfcVectorTests.cs).
    • Walkthrough:
      • Alphabet (Base32.cs:15), the 32 characters in value order.
      • Encode(ReadOnlySpan<byte>) (:21-57) throws on empty input (:23-26), sizes the output to a multiple of eight characters ((length + 4) / 5 * 8, :28), and feeds each byte into a bit buffer masked to twelve bits, emitting a character every time five bits are available (:34-44). Leftover bits are left-aligned into one last character (:46-49) and the rest is = padding (:51-54).
      • Decode(string) (:65-88) throws on null or empty (:67), trims trailing = (:69), sizes the output as length * 5 / 8 bytes (:70), and emits a byte every time eight bits are buffered (:75-85). Leftover low bits of the last character are ignored, and fewer than eight bits decode to an empty array.
      • ValueOf(char) (:90-96) accepts upper- and lower-case letters and the digits 2-7, and throws for anything else, which includes whitespace and a = that is not trailing.
    • Why it's built this way: the remarks state the leniency policy (Base32.cs:7-12): encoding always pads, while decoding tolerates missing padding and either letter case, because that is how authenticator secrets are typed and stored; anything else is rejected rather than guessed at.
    • Where it's used: TotpTwoFactorService encodes new secrets and recovery codes with it and decodes the stored secret before verifying (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:39,70,107).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: its exceptions are not part of any public contract; TotpTwoFactorService.VerifyCode catches ArgumentException and answers false (TotpTwoFactorService.cs:72-78).

    DeviceMetadata

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/DeviceMetadata.cs:24 · Level 0 · record (sealed, positional)

    • What it is: what a native client reports about the device it runs on, recorded on the caller's current refresh session so a "signed-in devices" list and a sign-in history can name the device in its owner's words. The same shape is the body of PUT auth/sessions/current/device and the Device member of the session responses (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/DeviceMetadata.cs:3-7).
    • Depends on: nothing; seven string? positional members.
    • Concept introduced: none new; it is the device half of the per-device refresh session model taught at RefreshSession (ADR-097). [Rubric §11, Security] applies in one sentence: every member is informational only, so nothing validates a session against it, and the server truncates each value to its column width and stores a blank one as null (DeviceMetadata.cs:8-12).
    • Walkthrough: DeviceId, a per-install identifier the client generates (a random GUID, since iOS exposes no stable device id; not a hardware serial, :14-17); DeviceName, the owner's name for the device when the platform exposes it (:18); DeviceModel (:19); DeviceManufacturer (:20); DevicePlatform, such as Android, iOS or WinUI (:21); DeviceFormFactor, such as Phone, Tablet or Desktop (:22); and DeviceType, Physical or Virtual (:23). The record is declared at :24-31.
    • Why it's built this way: browser clients report nothing and are described from the user-agent instead (DeviceMetadata.cs:10-11); a native client knows more about itself than a user-agent string says, so it reports a structured shape and the server stores it on the session row.
    • Where it's used: sent by MauiDeviceMetadataReporter (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI.Maui/Services/MauiDeviceMetadataReporter.cs:34) and accepted by AuthControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:292); passed through AuthSessionIssuer (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/AuthSessionIssuer.cs:333) to RefreshSession.RecordDevice (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Domain/Auth/RefreshSession.cs:273); read back by RefreshSessionDevice.ToDeviceMetadata (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Sessions/RefreshSessionDevice.cs:22) into RefreshSessionSummaryResponse and SignInSummaryResponse (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Responses/RefreshSessionSummaryResponse.cs:35, .../SignInSummaryResponse.cs:50); and labeled in the UI by UserAgentSummary.

    OidcDiscoveryResponse

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.ExternalProviders · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ExternalProviders/OidcDiscoveryResponse.cs:10 · Level 0 · record (sealed, positional)

    • What it is: the home-realm discovery answer from GET auth/oauth/discover?email=: the configured OIDC provider whose Domains list holds the address's domain. The sign-in page then starts the challenge at auth/oauth/{Provider} (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ExternalProviders/OidcDiscoveryResponse.cs:3-7,10).
    • Depends on: nothing; two string members, Provider (the provider name, which is also its scheme name and route segment) and DisplayName (the name shown to the user, :8-9).
    • Concept introduced: none new; it belongs to the external-login flow of ADR-036. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] applies: the response carries only the two values the sign-in page needs to route the user, not the provider's configuration.
    • Walkthrough: a one-line positional record (OidcDiscoveryResponse.cs:10).
    • Where it's used: returned by DiscoverOidcProvider on OAuthControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/OAuthControllerBase.cs:177-184) and read by OidcDiscoveryUIService for the login page.

    PasswordComplexity

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/PasswordComplexity.cs:18 · Level 0 · class (static partial)

    • What it is: the one definition of the strong-password rule: the two length bounds, four source-generated character-class regexes, and an Evaluate predicate that combines them (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/PasswordComplexity.cs:5-18).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; BCL System.Text.RegularExpressions and the [GeneratedRegex] source generator (PasswordComplexity.cs:1,34).
    • Concept introduced, one rule evaluated on both sides of the wire. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] assesses validation parity: the client form must give the verdict the API would. The doc comment states the purpose directly (PasswordComplexity.cs:5-10): the server validator (StrongPasswordRules<T> in MMCA.Common.Application) and the client attribute (PasswordComplexityAttribute in MMCA.Common.UI) both read this type, so they cannot disagree on the same input. It lives in Shared because Shared is the one project both of those layers may reference (UI depends on Shared only). The character classes are Unicode-aware (PasswordComplexity.cs:11-16): an accented or CJK letter counts as a letter, never as the "special" character.
    • Walkthrough: MinimumLength is 8 (PasswordComplexity.cs:28) and MaximumLength is 128 (PasswordComplexity.cs:31), both const int measured in UTF-16 code units, so they are usable in attribute arguments. Four public static partial Regex properties are source-generated by [GeneratedRegex], each with a 1000 ms match timeout: Uppercase (\p{Lu}, PasswordComplexity.cs:34-35), Lowercase (\p{Ll}, :38-39), Digit (\p{Nd}, :42-43), and SpecialCharacter ([^\p{L}\p{Nd}], anything that is neither a letter nor a decimal digit, :49-50). Evaluate(string? password) (PasswordComplexity.cs:52-57) returns true only when the input is non-null, at least MinimumLength long, and matches all four regexes. It deliberately does not check MaximumLength: the upper bound is a separate rule with its own message on both sides (PasswordComplexity.cs:52-56).
    • Why it's built this way: a client rule and a server rule written separately are two copies of one policy that drift independently. Exposing the regexes (not only Evaluate) lets the server's FluentValidation chain keep one message per failed class, while the client attribute asks the single yes/no question. Source-generated regexes avoid runtime regex construction, and the match timeout bounds evaluation of untrusted input.
    • Where it's used: StrongPasswordRules<T> feeds both length constants and all four regexes into its rule chain (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Validation/CommonValidationRules.cs:195-200); PasswordComplexityAttribute calls Evaluate, leaving empty input to [Required] (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/PasswordComplexityAttribute.cs:25); RegisterModel and ResetPasswordModel pair that attribute with [StringLength(PasswordComplexity.MaximumLength)] to supply the separate upper-bound rule (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/RegisterModel.cs:27-28, MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Auth/ResetPasswordModel.cs:25-26); pinned by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared.Tests/Auth/PasswordComplexityTests.cs.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the server's error messages still hard-code the numbers ("at least 8 characters", "longer than 128 characters") rather than interpolating the constants (CommonValidationRules.cs:195-196), and so does the attribute's default message (PasswordComplexityAttribute.cs:19); changing a bound means editing those strings too. The plain PasswordRules<T> sibling in the same file still uses literal 8/128 (CommonValidationRules.cs:179-180) and does not read this type.

    Totp

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/Totp.cs:24 · Level 0 · class (internal static)

    • What it is: RFC 6238 time-based one-time passwords over HMAC-SHA1 with RFC 4226 dynamic truncation, "the variant every authenticator app implements" (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/Totp.cs:8-11,24).
    • Depends on: BCL only: HMACSHA1.HashData, BinaryPrimitives, CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals and MemoryMarshal from System.Security.Cryptography, System.Buffers.Binary and System.Runtime.InteropServices.
    • Concept introduced, a one-time code is an HMAC of the clock. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether credentials are verified without side channels. A TOTP code is the HMAC of a shared secret over a counter, where the counter is "the whole Unix seconds of the instant divided by the period", so a code is live for exactly one period (Totp.cs:13-17). The server holds the same secret, recomputes the code for the current step and its neighbors, and compares. Comparison is fixed time: every candidate step is computed and compared with CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals, without stopping at a match, so the reply time does not say which step matched (Totp.cs:18-22). [Rubric §32, Dependency & Supply-Chain] applies as for Base32: the algorithm is about a hundred lines of BCL calls rather than a package.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Compute(key, utcInstant, periodSeconds, digits) (Totp.cs:32-33) computes the code for the step containing an instant.
      • Verify(key, code, utcInstant, periodSeconds, digits, windowSteps, out matchedStep) (:47-75) null-checks its inputs (:56-57), takes the current step (:59) and the presented code's bytes (:60), then walks every candidate step, computing the expected code and comparing in fixed time; the && !matched guard records the first match without leaving the loop early (:64-72). matchedStep is zero when nothing matched.
      • TimeStep (:77-82) rejects a non-positive period and divides whole Unix seconds by it.
      • Candidates (:84-97) yields the current step, then each earlier step out to the window but never below step zero (currentStep >= offset, :88), then each later step.
      • ComputeForStep (:99-124) bounds digits to 1..9 (:101-102), writes the step as a big-endian 64-bit counter into a stack buffer (:104-105), HMAC-SHA1s it (:107-110, with a scoped CA5350 suppression whose justification is that authenticator apps speak HMAC-SHA1 and HMAC does not rely on SHA-1 collision resistance), applies the RFC 4226 section 5.3 dynamic truncation (the low nibble of the last byte picks four bytes, read big endian with the top bit cleared, :112-115), and reduces modulo 10^digits, left-padding with zeros (:117-123).
    • Why it's built this way: two-factor authentication is opt-in (ADR-116); the algorithm is internal to Infrastructure, so Application, Domain and Shared take no dependency for it and TotpTwoFactorService is its only production caller.
    • Where it's used: TotpTwoFactorService.VerifyCode (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:87-94); checked against the RFC test vectors by MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Tests/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpRfcVectorTests.cs.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: replay inside the window is not this type's concern; it only reports the matched step, and TwoFactorAuthenticator refuses a step it already accepted.

    ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:18 · Level 0 · class (sealed attribute)

    • What it is: a marker for a read-only gRPC service, or a single method of one, that may be called under a view-as token. gRPC is always POST, so without this mark ViewAsGuardMiddleware refuses every view-as read that fans out over gRPC (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:3-10,18).
    • Depends on: BCL Attribute; AttributeUsage(Class | Method, AllowMultiple = false, Inherited = true) (ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:17).
    • Concept introduced, an exemption the host asserts and nothing verifies. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether a read-only mode is enforced by construction. The guard treats a POST to a marked endpoint as safe for the HTTP METHOD rule only: any other method is still refused, ViewAs:Enabled and the grant-liveness check still apply, and the command decorator still refuses every command (ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:6-9). The remarks are candid that the mark "is an assertion the host makes, which nothing can verify", so a host applies it deliberately and only to code that performs no write; there is no exemption by content type and none for gRPC in general (:11-16). See ADR-137.
    • Walkthrough: an empty sealed class deriving from Attribute (:18).
    • Why it's built this way: it lives in Shared "so a gRPC service project can apply it without taking a reference on the API package" (ViewAsReadOnlyEndpointAttribute.cs:14-15).
    • Where it's used: read from the routed endpoint's metadata by ViewAsGuardMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:119); ADC's services tests check the posture of its gRPC endpoints against it (MMCA.ADC/Tests/Services/MMCA.ADC.Services.Tests/Live/GrpcViewAsPostureTests.cs).

    ClaimsPrincipalExtensions

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:18 · Level 1 · class (static)

    • What it is: the one place the framework reads identity claims off a ClaimsPrincipal: the raw user-id value, the parsed user id, the caller's roles, an explicit permission claim, the refresh-session id, whether a second authentication factor was presented, whether the request comes from a view-as token, which roles were withheld pending a second factor, and the sign-in instant (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:6-18).

    • Depends on: AuthClaimTypes for the claim names it reads (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:27 Subject, :98 Permission, :112 SessionId, :129,148 MultiFactor, :138 ViewAsActor, :165,175 MultiFactorWithheldRole, :191 AuthTime); the solution-wide UserIdentifierType alias; BCL System.Security.Claims and System.Globalization (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:1-2).

    • Concept introduced, one reader for a claim that arrives under two names. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether identity resolution is correct and uniform, and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses whether a fragile detail is centralized or copy-pasted. The trap is ASP.NET Core's inbound claim mapping. Tokens carry the user identifier in the standard sub claim only, but that single value reaches readers under two different claim types depending on which pipeline produced the principal (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:8-16):

      • the JWT bearer handler maps inbound sub onto ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier, the long http://schemas.xmlsoap.org/... URI;
      • a handler that materializes an identity straight from a token's claims leaves the raw sub in place. SessionCookieAuthenticationHandler is exactly that case: it builds new ClaimsIdentity(jwt.Claims, ...) from the decoded token (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/SessionCookies/SessionCookieAuthenticationHandler.cs:60-61).

      A reader that hard-codes either name works under one pipeline and silently returns "anonymous" under the other, and "silently anonymous" in an authorization path is the worst failure shape available. Routing every framework reader through FindUserIdValue makes both shapes resolve identically, and means a consumer that changes its claim mapping does not lose the current user (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:13-15). FindAuthTime applies the same two-shape rule to auth_time. Note the deliberate use of C#'s classic this-parameter extension methods here rather than the extension(T) blocks the codebase uses for DI registration: these are plain static helpers on a BCL type.

    • Walkthrough: twelve extension methods, all null-tolerant by construction (every parameter is ClaimsPrincipal?, so a null principal yields null, empty, or false rather than throwing).

      • FindUserIdValue(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:26-28) is the primitive: principal?.FindFirst(AuthClaimTypes.Subject)?.Value ?? principal?.FindFirst(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)?.Value. Raw sub wins, the mapped NameIdentifier is the fallback, and a principal carrying neither yields null.
      • GetUserId(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:40-44) parses that value into the module's UserIdentifierType and returns null when the claim is absent or unparsable. It parses through IParsable<TSelf>.TryParse in CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, which the remarks justify twice over (:34-38): it matches the writer (claims are formatted invariantly) and it stays correct if the solution-wide identifier alias changes shape, so the helper does not have to be rewritten when an app moves from int to Guid.
      • GetRoleValues(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:60-68) returns every role value the principal carries under any of three claim types: the standard ClaimTypes.Role URI, or the raw role/roles claim an identity provider emits with inbound-claim mapping off. The remarks mark it SECURITY: it is the framework's one definition of "the caller's roles", because the narrower BCL ClaimsPrincipal.IsInRole(string) sees only the identity's own role claim type and can therefore disagree with the authorization handler about who is privileged. The rule is scoped to access decisions (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:55-57): every role read that gates access goes through here, while the UI NavMenu's BCL IsInRole calls only decide which nav links are shown, not what the caller may do.
      • HasRole(this ClaimsPrincipal?, string) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:76-78) is GetRoleValues().Contains(role, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase), guarded against a blank role.
      • HasPermissionClaim(this ClaimsPrincipal?, string) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:95-98) checks for an AuthClaimTypes.Permission claim matching the given permission, independently of role. The remarks mark it SECURITY too: both authorization gates, the HTTP policy handler and the CQRS pipeline gate, read it, so a grant the minting host stored and emitted as a claim is honored identically at both boundaries; in a multi-service deployment the claim is the only way such a grant reaches a service that does not own the grant table. It is additive, never a denial: a principal without the claim still passes on a role the registry grants.
      • FindSessionId(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:110-114) reads the sid claim and Guid.TryParses it. The remarks make the degradation explicit (:104-108): null is an ordinary answer, not an error, because tokens issued before sid shipped carry no such claim, and every reader treats its absence as "the caller's own session is unknown". Nothing authenticates on this value.
      • HasMultiFactor(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:128-129) is principal?.FindFirst(AuthClaimTypes.MultiFactor) is not null. The remarks mark it SECURITY: presence is the whole test, and absence denies rather than falling back to a role check, because only the sign-in flow stamps the claim, and only after a code verified.
      • IsViewAs(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:137-138) is the same presence test on ViewAsActor: true means the principal comes from a view-as token and the request is read-only.
      • FindMultiFactorMethod(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:147-148) returns the value of the MultiFactor claim, or null when the principal carries none, for audit and UI copy such as "signed in with a recovery code".
      • GetMultiFactorWithheldRoles(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:162-165) returns the values of every MultiFactorWithheldRole marker in recorded order, or an empty list. The remarks are precise that a withheld role is not held: GetRoleValues and HasRole do not see it, and this member exists so a caller can say "set up two-factor authentication to use this role" instead of treating the account as one without the role (:155-159).
      • HasMultiFactorWithheldRole(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:174-175) is the presence test for at least one such marker.
      • FindAuthTime(this ClaimsPrincipal?) (ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:189-197) reads the raw auth_time first and falls back to ClaimTypes.AuthenticationInstant, the type the JWT bearer handler's inbound claim map renames it to (:182-186), then parses whole Unix seconds into a DateTimeOffset. It returns null for a token minted before the claim shipped and for a view-as token.

    • Why it's built this way: TokenService records the other half of the story in a comment (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TokenService.cs:140-143): a duplicate custom user-id claim used to ride alongside sub, which meant two values that could disagree and two claim names every reader had to know. Collapsing the writer to one claim (TokenService.cs:146) is only safe because one reader absorbs the mapping difference, which is this type. The sid half comes from ADR-097, the view-as test from ADR-137, and the sign-in instant from ADR-139.

    • Where it's used: broadly, and always instead of a hand-rolled claim lookup. CurrentUserService resolves the ambient user id through GetUserId() (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/CurrentUserService.cs:20); ClaimBasedUserIdProvider uses FindUserIdValue() to key SignalR connections (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Context/ClaimBasedUserIdProvider.cs:15); the IdempotencyFilter uses it to scope an idempotency key to a caller (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Idempotency/IdempotencyFilter.cs:540); CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor uses it for feature-flag targeting (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/FeatureManagement/CurrentUserTargetingContextAccessor.cs:121); the opt-in "UserPolicy" rate-limit partition keys on httpContext.User?.Identity?.Name directly rather than on GetUserId() (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Startup/WebApplicationBuilderExtensions.RateLimiting.cs:197-202); AuthControllerBase uses FindSessionId() to tell the session list which row is the caller's own (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/AuthControllerBase.cs:262); AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser> uses GetUserId() on the principal recovered from an expired access token during rotation and FindAuthTime() to carry the sign-in instant forward (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:425,455); PasskeyStepUp judges recent sign-in with FindAuthTime() (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/Passkeys/PasskeyStepUp.cs:27); and TestPrincipal writes sub precisely so test principals resolve the same way real ones do (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.UI/Infrastructure/TestPrincipal.cs:19,27). HasPermissionClaim backs both PermissionAuthorizationHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:31) and the CQRS AuthorizationGate (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/AuthorizationGate.cs:48), whose IRequiresMfa check is HasMultiFactor (AuthorizationGate.cs:60); IsViewAs backs ViewAsGuardMiddleware (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Middleware/ViewAsGuardMiddleware.cs:58) and the view-as command decorator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/Decorators/ViewAsCommandDecorator.cs:38); the withheld-role readers back MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/MultiFactor/MultiFactorRoleAuthorizationHandler.cs:67-69).

    • Caveats / not-in-source: MMCA.Store's Sales UI module defines its own unrelated ClaimsPrincipalExtensions in a different namespace (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Sales/MMCA.Store.Sales.UI/Extensions/ClaimsPrincipalExtensions.cs:9); do not confuse the two when reading a using list. Also note GetUserId returns a nullable value type, so is { } userId pattern-matching (as the framework's controllers use, for example MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/TwoFactor/TwoFactorControllerBase.cs:100) is the idiomatic call shape, not a ! dereference.

    TotpTwoFactorService

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:33 · Level 2 · class

    • What it is: the RFC 6238 TOTP implementation of ITwoFactorService: secret generation, provisioning-URI construction, code verification, and recovery-code generation/hashing/matching (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TotpTwoFactorService.cs:9-12,33-164).
    • Depends on: ITwoFactorService (the contract it implements); TwoFactorSettings injected as IOptions<TwoFactorSettings>; RecoveryCodeSet as its return shape; the internal Totp (RFC 6238 over HMAC-SHA1) and Base32 (RFC 4648) in the same folder, no third-party package; System.Security.Cryptography (RandomNumberGenerator, SHA256, CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals).
    • Concept introduced, constant-time comparison for a secret the caller does not control the timing of. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether the codebase avoids timing side channels around secret comparison. TryMatchRecoveryCode never exits its scan early on a match: the loop "runs to the end so the answer takes the same time whichever code in the list was presented" (TotpTwoFactorService.cs:145-146), and each comparison itself goes through CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals rather than == or SequenceEqual (:147). A byte-for-byte comparison that stops at the first differing byte leaks how many leading bytes an attacker guessed correctly across repeated attempts; a fixed-time comparison over a full linear scan removes that channel entirely. The type remarks add why the recovery hash is a plain SHA-256 rather than a key derivation: the codes are high-entropy random values, not user-chosen secrets, so stretching buys nothing an attacker cannot skip and would cost a derivation per stored code on every sign-in (:14-20).
    • Walkthrough: internal sealed class with a primary constructor taking IOptions<TwoFactorSettings> settings (:33), caching .Value once (:35).
      • GenerateSecret() returns Base32.Encode of RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(_settings.SecretByteLength) (:38-39).
      • BuildProvisioningUri rejects a blank secret or account name, URL-escapes the issuer and account name, and formats the standard otpauth:// URI a QR code encodes: the algorithm is fixed at SHA1, while digit count and period are read from settings (:42-53). The remarks explain why it is composed in one visible place: the issuer:account label and the redundant issuer parameter, which older authenticator apps read, are part of what a user's app has to accept (:26-30).
      • VerifyCode comes in two overloads. The two-argument form is a one-line forward to the three-argument form, discarding the step (:56). The three-argument form reports the matched TOTP time step through out long matchedStep, initialized to 0 so every early false leaves it defined (:59-61). It returns false for a blank secret or code (:62-65), then decodes the stored secret with Base32.Decode, catching ArgumentException and returning false rather than throwing when the value is not valid Base32: "a stored secret that is not Base32 can never mint a code, so it verifies nothing. That is a data fault, not a caller fault" (:67-78). A secret that decodes to no key (padding alone, or fewer than eight bits) verifies false for the same reason (:80-85). It then calls Totp.Verify with DateTime.UtcNow, the configured period and digit count, and a window of _settings.VerificationWindowSteps steps on each side of now, every candidate compared in fixed time, writing the step the code matched into matchedStep (:87-94). The window tolerates clock drift between the server and the user's authenticator app; the reported step is what lets TwoFactorAuthenticator refuse a replay of the same code inside that window. The secret it receives is plaintext: unprotecting the stored value is the caller's job (DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector).
      • GenerateRecoveryCodes produces _settings.RecoveryCodeCount codes, each a Base32-encoded random byte string of _settings.RecoveryCodeByteLength bytes with the = padding trimmed, alongside their SHA-256 hashes computed by HashRecoveryCode (:98-114). Base32 rather than Base64: "the alphabet has no case ambiguity and no characters a user has to guess at while copying a code off paper" (:105-106). Only the hashes and the caller-facing codes are returned as a RecoveryCodeSet (:113); nothing persists the plaintext codes here.
      • HashRecoveryCode normalizes the code (keeps letters and digits, upper-cases) then SHA-256-hashes it to an upper-case hex string (:117-122).
      • TryMatchRecoveryCode normalizes and hashes the presented code once, skips null stored entries, then fixed-time-compares it against every stored hash, returning the matched hash (not the code) through an out parameter (:125-154).
      • NormalizeCode is the shared helper both verification paths route through: it strips whitespace and separators a user types or a password manager inserts and upper-cases what remains, "so a code is matched the way it was generated" (:156-163).
    • Why it's built this way: two-factor authentication is opt-in (ADR-116), registered by AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config). The one-time-password algorithm and the Base32 codec are internal Infrastructure types rather than a package, so Application, Domain and Shared take no dependency for them, and this type, rather than anything in Application, is what computes and verifies codes.
    • Where it's used: registered in DI (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:55, a TryAddSingleton) as the ITwoFactorService implementation behind AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config) (DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:47), and consumed by TwoFactorAuthenticator for both TOTP and recovery-code verification.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: internal sealed, so it is reached only through the ITwoFactorService abstraction; a consumer cannot construct or type-check against this class directly.

    RoleValue

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/RoleValue.cs:26 · Level 3 · class (abstract)

    • What it is: the abstract base for a role value object. It stores one canonical string, gives it case-insensitive value equality and hashing, and offers a shared validation helper against a per-app set of known role names (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/RoleValue.cs:6-26).

    • Depends on: Result and Error from MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions (RoleValue.cs:2), plus System.Collections.Frozen from the BCL (RoleValue.cs:1). Its doc comments point at RoleNames for the canonical strings (RoleValue.cs:9) and at ICurrentUserService.IsInRole for the comparison semantics it matches (RoleValue.cs:17). Conceptually a value object (see ValueObject) but deliberately not derived from that base, for a reason the next bullet unpacks.

    • Concept introduced, a value object as an abstract class with type-guarded equality. [Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design] assesses whether identity-less concepts are modeled as value objects rather than bare primitives, and [Rubric §1, SOLID] applies to how an open hierarchy is left safe to extend. A role has no database identity: two "Organizer" values are the same role, so the type is defined by its value, which is exactly the value-object shape. Two design decisions make this base unusual, and both are written into the source:

      1. No IEquatable<T> on the base (RoleValue.cs:18-24). The remarks cite Sonar S4035: an unsealed type implementing IEquatable<T> breaks the equality contract, because a subclass instance compared through the base-typed interface can report an equality the derived type would reject. Instead equality is the plain object.Equals override, and it is type-guarded: GetType() == other.GetType() before the value comparison (RoleValue.cs:91-94), so a role of one concrete type is never equal to a same-valued role of another. A sealed derived type is then free to layer a strongly-typed IEquatable<TSelf> plus ==/!= on top, which is what ADC's UserRole does (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:18,78-84).
      2. It does not derive from ValueObject, and that is a fitness-rule consequence, not an oversight. ValueObjectsAreImmutableSealedInShared requires every concrete class whose base type starts with MMCA.Common.Shared.ValueObjects.ValueObject to be sealed, immutable, and to live in the Shared layer (MMCA.Common/Source/Hosting/MMCA.Common.Testing.Architecture/Rules/Domain/ArchitectureRules.Immutability.cs:56-72). A concrete role type lives in its app's Domain layer (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:6), so deriving from ValueObject would fail that rule in every app. Keeping the base in MMCA.Common.Shared with its own equality also keeps it dependency-free and therefore usable from Blazor WebAssembly and UI code as well as Domain (RoleValue.cs:12-17). The same trade-off is made by Enumeration<TEnumeration>, whose own remarks name RoleValue as the shipped precedent (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/ValueObjects/Enumeration.cs:34).

      [Rubric §11, Security] applies too, because role strings arrive as JWT claim values whose casing is not under this codebase's control. Every comparison here is OrdinalIgnoreCase, so an authorization check does not silently miss on "organizer" against "Organizer".

    • Walkthrough: a get-only Value (RoleValue.cs:29) assigned by the protected constructor (RoleValue.cs:33), so an instance is immutable and only a derived type can create one. The static Validate(role, knownRoles, source) (RoleValue.cs:43) null-guards the supplied set (RoleValue.cs:45), then returns Result.Success() when the role is known, otherwise a Result failure carrying an Error of kind Invariant, coded User.Role.Invalid, with the caller's method name as source and role as target (RoleValue.cs:47-53). The membership test is the private IsKnown (RoleValue.cs:64-66) and it is more careful than it first looks: the fast path is the supplied set's own Contains (correct and O(1) for the intended OrdinalIgnoreCase sets, with a role ?? string.Empty coalesce so a null role becomes a clean failure rather than a NullReferenceException), and a miss falls back to an explicit case-insensitive Any scan, so a set built with the default ordinal comparer still validates case-insensitively as the contract promises (RoleValue.cs:56-63). Role sets hold a handful of entries, so the fallback is negligible and only ever runs on a miss. The protected generic BuildLookup<TRole>(params TRole[] roles) (RoleValue.cs:76) freezes the supplied singletons into a case-insensitive FrozenDictionary keyed by Value (RoleValue.cs:81-84), so a derived type can back its FromString/IsValid members with interned instances instead of re-allocating on every parse. ToString returns the value (RoleValue.cs:88), and GetHashCode uses the ordinal-ignore-case hash (RoleValue.cs:97) so it stays consistent with Equals, which is the contract any dictionary or HashSet key depends on.

    • Why it's built this way: the abstract-class-plus-type-guard shape is how you share equality behavior across an open hierarchy of value objects without violating the equality contract, and the S4035 rationale is documented inline (RoleValue.cs:18-24) so a future reader does not "helpfully" add IEquatable<T> to the base. The comparer-agnostic IsKnown fallback exists because Validate accepts any IReadOnlySet<string>: the type cannot see how the caller built the set, so it enforces its own promise instead of trusting the caller's comparer. That behavior is pinned by test, including the default-comparer case (MMCA.Common/Tests/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared.Tests/Auth/RoleValueTests.cs:24), the OrdinalIgnoreCase case (RoleValueTests.cs:36), a null role (RoleValueTests.cs:65), and a null role set throwing (RoleValueTests.cs:73).

    • Where it's used: the two apps consume it differently, and the difference is instructive. ADC derives a full sealed value object, UserRole, which fixes three roles (Organizer, Attendee, ContentEditor), interns them through BuildLookup (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:21-34), exposes FromString returning a Result<UserRole> and IsValid over that frozen lookup (UserRole.cs:52-66), and adds a case-insensitive IsOrganizer for raw claim strings (UserRole.cs:76) plus the sealed-type IEquatable<UserRole> and ==/!= operators the base leaves to subclasses (UserRole.cs:78-90). Store's UserRole is a static class, not a subclass: it fixes Admin and Customer as string properties over an OrdinalIgnoreCase set and calls the shared RoleValue.Validate helper for its IsValid (MMCA.Store/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.Store.Identity.Domain/Users/UserRole.cs:14,26-30,37), so it inherits the rule set (case-insensitive membership, the User.Role.Invalid code) without inheriting the type. Both key their known-role sets off the RoleNames constants, and PermissionRegistryBuilder keeps its role keys on the same case-insensitive comparer to match (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/PermissionRegistryBuilder.cs:11).

    DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:15 · Level 4 · class (internal sealed)

    • What it is: the default ITwoFactorSecretProtector, which encrypts a TOTP secret at rest with the host's ASP.NET Core data-protection key ring under the purpose MMCA.Common.Auth.TwoFactor.Secret.v1 (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:8-13,15).
    • Depends on: ITwoFactorSecretProtector (the contract); the framework's Result<T> and Error; Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection (IDataProtectionProvider, IDataProtector); BCL CryptographicException.
    • Concept introduced, an unreadable secret is a result, not an exception. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether secrets are protected at rest; [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether a key-management fault degrades instead of crashing a hot path. A multi-replica host needs the shared key ring (ADR-069), or a replica cannot read a secret another one wrote, and the remarks require that this "surfaces as a failed unprotect, never as an exception" (DataProtectionTwoFactorSecretProtector.cs:10-12). Unprotect therefore returns Result<string> and maps both failure exceptions to one coded failure.
    • Walkthrough:
      • Purpose (:18), "MMCA.Common.Auth.TwoFactor.Secret.v1", documented as part of the stored format, "so it never changes" (:17); the protector is created from it once (:23).
      • SecretUnreadableCode (:21), "Authentication.TwoFactorSecretUnreadable".
      • Protect(string) (:26-30) throws on null or empty and returns the protected payload.
      • Unprotect(string) (:33-52) answers a blank input as unreadable (:35-38), returns Result.Success with the plaintext (:40-43), and catches CryptographicException (:44-47) and FormatException (:48-51) into the same failure.
      • Unreadable() (:54-58) builds Error.Failure(SecretUnreadableCode, "The two-factor secret cannot be unprotected with this host's key ring.", nameof(Unprotect)).
    • Why it's built this way: the sign-in path treats an unreadable secret as "no time-based code can verify" and keeps the recovery codes usable, so the owner still has a way in (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:77-78); that is only possible because this type answers with a Result rather than throwing.
    • Where it's used: registered with TryAddSingleton behind AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config) (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:59), so a host can register its own protector first; consumed by TwoFactorAuthenticator.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: Not determinable from source read for this section: which caller invokes Protect when an enrollment stores the secret; the type is referenced directly only by its DI registration and by tests.

    TwoFactorAuthenticator

    MMCA.Common.Infrastructure · MMCA.Common.Infrastructure.Auth.TwoFactor · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:43 · Level 5 · class

    • What it is: the ITwoFactorAuthenticator implementation that turns a raw code plus a user's stored two-factor state into one of four challenge outcomes (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/TwoFactor/TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:43-208).
    • Depends on: ITwoFactorService (code verification and recovery-code matching); ITwoFactorStore (loading state and consuming a recovery code); ITwoFactorSecretProtector (unprotecting the stored secret before a code is verified against it); ICacheService (remembering the last accepted TOTP time step per account); TwoFactorSettings via IOptions<T> (period and window size); IDistributedLock (serializing both code paths per account); TwoFactorErrors; TwoFactorOutcome; the framework's Result<T>; the UserIdentifierType alias.
    • Concept introduced, a challenge is answered with an outcome enum, not a bare boolean. [Rubric §1, SOLID] and [Rubric §11, Security] both bear on the shape of ChallengeAsync's return: Result<TwoFactorOutcome> distinguishes "not enrolled" (a success carrying TwoFactorOutcome.NotEnrolled, not a failure) from a missing code, an invalid code, and the two ways a valid one can be accepted, VerifiedTotp versus VerifiedRecoveryCode. Collapsing those five states into one boolean would force the caller to re-derive which one happened from side effects, and a login path that cannot tell "not enrolled" from "denied" cannot decide whether to prompt for enrollment or reject the sign-in.
    • Walkthrough: internal sealed class taking ITwoFactorService, ITwoFactorStore, ITwoFactorSecretProtector, ICacheService, IOptions<TwoFactorSettings>, and IDistributedLock as primary constructor parameters (:43-49), with two static lock timings: StepLockTimeToLive of 10 seconds (:51) and StepLockWait of 5 seconds (:53). It implements ChallengeAsync(userId, code, cancellationToken) (:56-87) and VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync (:90-105).
      • Loads the user's state from the store first (:61). If the state is missing or IsTwoFactorEnabled is false, the challenge succeeds trivially with NotEnrolled: "an account that never enrolled, and an account whose row vanished between the password check and here, are both 'nothing to challenge'" (:63-69).
      • An enrolled account with no presented code fails with TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorRequired (:71-75).
      • The code is checked first against the stored TOTP secret, but only after secretProtector.Unprotect succeeds with a non-empty plaintext; the plaintext goes to the out long matchedStep overload of ITwoFactorService.VerifyCode, and a match is not accepted outright but handed to AcceptTimeStepOnceAsync with the step it matched (:79-84). "A stored secret this host cannot unprotect verifies no time-based code; the recovery codes stay usable, so the owner still has a way in" (:77-78).
      • Otherwise the challenge goes to RedeemRecoveryCodeOnceAsync (:86).
      • VerifyEnrollmentCodeAsync(userId, secret, code, cancellationToken) (:90-105) checks the first code of an enrollment against a candidate secret that is not yet stored. The candidate arrives protected: a blank secret, one that does not unprotect to a non-empty plaintext, or a code that fails VerifyCode against the plaintext returns false (:96-101); a match is passed through the same AcceptTimeStepOnceAsync and returns whether that step was accepted (:103-104), so the code that confirms enrollment cannot then be replayed as the first sign-in challenge.
      • The private RedeemRecoveryCodeOnceAsync (:117-151) takes the same per-account lock the time-based path takes, lock:{StepKey(userId)} with StepLockTimeToLive and StepLockWait, and answers a submission that cannot take it with TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalid (:122-128). Inside the lock it re-reads the state and fails as invalid when the account is gone, no longer enrolled, or the code matches no stored hash through ITwoFactorService.TryMatchRecoveryCode (:130-139). A match is then consumed, not just verified: store.ConsumeRecoveryCodeAsync persists the redemption, and if that persistence fails, the challenge is answered as a failure rather than a success: "letting the sign-in through would hand out a code that is still live" (:141-149). Only a persisted consumption returns VerifiedRecoveryCode. Re-reading inside the lock is what makes two concurrent redemptions of one code yield exactly one success: the second reads the state after the first spent it (:107-112).
      • The private static StepKey(userId) (:156-157) builds the per-account key twofactor:laststep:{userId} that both paths lock on (:153).
      • The private AcceptTimeStepOnceAsync makes a TOTP code single use (:167-188). It takes the distributed lock on lock:{key} (:176-178), because "the read, the compare and the write below are one critical section: without it, two submissions of one code that both read before either writes would both pass" (:174-175). A submission that cannot take the lock within the wait gets a null handle and fails with TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalid (:179-182), never a second success. Holding the handle in an await using block, it delegates to AcceptIfNewerAsync (:184-187).
      • The private AcceptIfNewerAsync(key, matchedStep, cancellationToken) (:190-207) reads the last accepted step with GetFromSharedStoreAsync, deliberately bypassing a local copy: "a step accepted on another replica must be seen here, or a replayed code would pass against a stale local copy inside its window" (:195-197). A matched step not newer than the stored one fails with TwoFactorErrors.TwoFactorInvalid (:198-201). Otherwise the step is written back with a lifetime of PeriodSeconds * (2 * VerificationWindowSteps + 2) seconds, long enough to outlast every step the verification window could still accept, and the challenge returns VerifiedTotp (:203-206).
    • Why it's built this way: this is the runtime half of the opt-in two-factor feature (ADR-116). The type remarks give the order: the time-based code is tried first because it is the ordinary path and costs one HMAC, and walking the recovery list only on failure keeps a six-digit code from being compared against the recovery hashes in the common case (TwoFactorAuthenticator.cs:15-19). Both kinds of code are made one-time inside the challenge rather than left to the caller, because a caller that forgot would leave a code live for a second sign-in (:20-26). A TOTP code would otherwise stay valid for its whole verification window, so a code seen over someone's shoulder could be replayed; remembering the last accepted step closes that window. Remembering alone is not enough under concurrency, so the read, compare and write of that step, and the match and spend of a recovery code, run under an IDistributedLock on the account's step key (ADR-108), and a submission that cannot take the lock is answered as invalid, the same shape PasswordResetTokenService uses (:27-35).
    • Where it's used: registered in DI (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/DependencyInjection.Auth.cs:63, a TryAddScoped) as the ITwoFactorAuthenticator behind AddTwoFactorAuthentication(config); the resolved instance is passed to AuthenticationServiceBase<TUser>, which answers Authentication.TwoFactorRequired or mints the mfa claim depending on the outcome, mapping VerifiedTotp and VerifiedRecoveryCode to the claim's method value (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/AuthenticationServiceBase.cs:899-900).

    AdministrationPermissions

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/AdministrationPermissions.cs:15 · Level 0 · class (static)

    • What it is: the seven permission-string constants the framework's own opt-in administration controller bases gate on: ManageUsers ("users:manage"), ManageRoles ("roles:manage"), ViewAsUsers ("users:view-as"), ManageFeatures ("features:manage"), ManageClients ("clients:manage"), ViewAuditTrail ("audit:view") and ManageWebhooks ("webhooks:manage") (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/AdministrationPermissions.cs:15-55).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; it is a plain const string holder consumed by the permission-authorization pipeline. Its doc comment points at IPermissionRegistry and PermissionRegistryBuilder as the way these names are granted (AdministrationPermissions.cs:3-7).
    • Concept introduced, the framework shipping its own permission vocabulary for the administration surface it also ships. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the authorization model for built-in capabilities. The administration controller bases are framework code, so they need permission names that exist before any consuming app declares its own; these constants are those names, defined once so the base controllers and every host that wires a role to them agree on the string. They follow the same area:capability naming as a host's own permissions, and the remarks record the failure direction: a host that mounts one of the bases but grants none of these permissions serves endpoints that deny everyone (AdministrationPermissions.cs:3-14).
    • Walkthrough: seven public const string fields, each documented with the operation it gates (AdministrationPermissions.cs:17-54): ManageUsers (:18) for listing, inspecting, locking, unlocking and re-roling accounts; ManageRoles (:21) for listing roles and editing their stored permission grants; ViewAsUsers (:27) for read-only view-as of another account for at most 15 minutes, where an account holding it can never itself be viewed, so staff cannot view each other; ManageFeatures (:33) for listing feature flags and setting or clearing their stored overrides; ManageClients (:40) for creating, rotating, promoting and revoking machine clients, documented as to be granted as sparingly as ManageUsers because creating a client creates a service-account user; ViewAuditTrail (:46) for reading recorded entity change history; and ManageWebhooks (:54) for the outbound webhook subscription lifecycle, documented as to be granted as sparingly as the data the subscribed events carry.
    • Why it's built this way: part of the opt-in identity completions (ADR-116), extended by each later opt-in surface: view-as (ADR-137), feature-flag overrides (ADR-031), machine clients (ADR-140), the audit trail (ADR-075) and outbound webhooks (ADR-142). Naming them in the framework is what lets each shared controller base carry its own [HasPermission] attribute, so a host adopting a built-in screen grants a role the constant rather than inventing its own string (AdministrationPermissions.cs:9-14).
    • Where it's used: the controller bases carry them as class or action attributes: RolesAdminControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/RolesAdminControllerBase.cs:60), UsersAdminControllerBase<TUserDto> (ManageUsers at MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Administration/UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:67, ViewAsUsers on its view-as action at UsersAdminControllerBase.cs:161), ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase (ViewAsGrantsAdminControllerBase.cs:39), FeatureFlagsControllerBase (FeatureFlagsControllerBase.cs:37), AuditHistoryControllerBase (AuditHistoryControllerBase.cs:47), MachineClientsControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:38) and WebhookSubscriptionsControllerBase (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/Webhooks/WebhookSubscriptionsControllerBase.cs:39). MachineClientService refuses a client role that grants ViewAsUsers, ManageUsers, ManageRoles or ManageClients (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:52-57); ViewAsService checks ViewAsUsers on the subject's role (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/ViewAs/ViewAsService.cs:193); StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService refuses to grant ManageRoles through a stored row, since it guards the role-administration surface itself (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/Administration/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs:147-151), and RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs disables that permission in the edit UI for the same reason (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Pages/Administration/RoleAdminEdit.razor.cs:260,272). In ADC, IdentityPermissions aliases ManageUsers, ManageRoles, ViewAsUsers and ManageClients (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Shared/Authorization/IdentityPermissions.cs:26,41,52,64), IdentityPermissionGrants grants ViewAuditTrail (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.Shared/Authorization/IdentityPermissionGrants.cs:50), and IdentityUIModule uses ManageUsers and ManageClients as the RequiredPermission of its Support Access and Machine Clients nav entries (MMCA.ADC/Source/Modules/Identity/MMCA.ADC.Identity.UI/IdentityUIModule.cs:39,44).

    CreateMachineClientRequest

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:15 · Level 0 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the body of the create-machine-client call: a Name, the Role the service-account user behind the client is created with, and an optional SecretExpiresOn (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:3-15).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; BCL DateTime.
    • Concept: a machine client is a program that authenticates with a client id and secret (the OAuth client credentials grant) and acts as a dedicated service-account user (ADR-140). [Rubric §11, Security] assesses least privilege: the request carries a role rather than a permission list, so the client's tokens carry exactly that role's permissions, and the doc comment records that a role granting users:view-as, users:manage, roles:manage or clients:manage is refused (CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:7-11).
    • Walkthrough: three positional members (CreateMachineClientRequest.cs:15): Name, documented as 1 to 100 characters (:6); Role (:7-11); SecretExpiresOn, a UTC instant, defaulting to null for no expiry (:12-14).
    • Why it's built this way: the refusal list in the comment is enforced server-side by MachineClientService's ForbiddenPermissions, which names the matching AdministrationPermissions constants (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientService.cs:52-57), so a program can never be minted with the power to create more programs or impersonate staff.
    • Where it's used: the [FromBody] of MachineClientsControllerBase.CreateAsync (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Controllers/MachineClients/MachineClientsControllerBase.cs:75-76), passed on to IMachineClientService; sent from the UI by MachineClientAdmin through MachineClientAdminService (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.UI/Services/Administration/MachineClientAdminService.cs).

    IPermissionCatalog

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionCatalog.cs:24 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the read-only enumeration half of the permission model: every role the compiled registry grants something to, and every permission it grants to anyone, both sorted ordinally (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionCatalog.cs:24-31).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; it is a companion abstraction to IPermissionRegistry.
    • Concept introduced, separating "does this role grant that permission" from "what roles and permissions exist at all". [Rubric §1, SOLID] applies to interface segregation: IPermissionRegistry answers a per-request authorization question, IPermissionCatalog answers an administration-screen enumeration question, and a consumer that only needs to render a permission-grant matrix does not have to depend on the authorization interface at all.
    • Walkthrough: two get-only properties, Roles and Permissions, both IReadOnlyList<string>.
    • Why it's built this way: PermissionRegistry already holds the closed set of roles and permissions compiled into the host, so the catalog is a second, narrower interface the same class implements explicitly, rather than a second source of truth that could drift.
    • Where it's used: implemented explicitly by PermissionRegistry; read by StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Infrastructure/Auth/Administration/StoredPermissionRoleAdministrationService.cs), PermissionCatalogResponse (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Responses/PermissionCatalogResponse.cs), and AuthorizationExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs); registered alongside IPermissionRegistry in both MMCA.Common.Application and MMCA.Common.Infrastructure DependencyInjection.cs.

    IPermissionRegistry

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.Permissions · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionRegistry.cs:14 · Level 0 · interface

    • What it is: the abstraction that maps roles to the fine-grained permissions they grant, and the single place that knows which roles confer which capabilities (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/Permissions/IPermissionRegistry.cs:3-14).
    • Depends on: nothing first-party; its remarks reference RoleNames for the case-insensitivity rule.
    • Concept introduced, permission (capability) authorization over role checks. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses the authorization model, and [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses dependency inversion: endpoints depend on an abstraction, not on a role name. Instead of scattering [Authorize(Roles = "Organizer")] across endpoints, code authorizes against a permission (a capability such as sessions:manage) and this registry translates a principal's roles into the permissions they hold. The payoff is decoupling: adding a role or reshaping who-can-do-what is a registry change, not an edit to every endpoint (IPermissionRegistry.cs:4-7). The remarks also fix the comparison rules (IPermissionRegistry.cs:9-13): role lookups are case-insensitive, permission values are compared ordinally, and implementations are expected to be immutable and thread-safe. Those three sentences are what let the implementation be a frozen, lock-free structure.
    • Walkthrough: two members. GetPermissions(string role) (IPermissionRegistry.cs:21) returns the permission set for a role, or an empty set for an unknown role, never a throw (IPermissionRegistry.cs:16-18). HasPermission(IEnumerable<string> roles, string permission) (IPermissionRegistry.cs:29) answers whether any of a principal's roles grants the permission: the hot path the authorization handler calls per request.
    • Why it's built this way: ADR-020 records the decision. An empty-set-on-miss contract keeps callers branchless, and pushing the who-grants-what knowledge behind one interface is the capability-security expression of the framework's habit of hiding decision logic behind an abstraction.
    • Where it's used: implemented by PermissionRegistry (built via PermissionRegistryBuilder); registered as a lazily-built singleton by AuthorizationExtensions (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/AuthorizationExtensions.cs:78) and injected into PermissionAuthorizationHandler (MMCA.Common/Source/Presentation/MMCA.Common.API/Authorization/PermissionAuthorizationHandler.cs:14).

    MMCA.Common.Shared · MMCA.Common.Shared.Auth.MachineClients · MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientResponse.cs:15 · Level 0 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: one machine client as the administration surface lists it: its ClientId, Name, ServiceAccountUserId, CreatedOn, SecretExpiresOn, RevokedOn, LastUsedOn and HasSecondarySecret (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Shared/Auth/MachineClients/MachineClientResponse.cs:3-23).

    • Walkthrough: eight positional members (MachineClientResponse.cs:15-23). ClientId is the value a program presents as client_id (:7); the three nullable instants mean "no expiry", "still active" and "never used" when null (:11-13); HasSecondarySecret says a rotated secret is waiting to be promoted (:14), which is the state an operator needs to see between a rotate and a promote.
